Title: The G20 agenda under the Russian chairmanship
text: The G20 Agenda under the Russian Chairmanship Luncheon Keynote Address Agustin Carstens  Governor Banco de Mexico Moscow, Russia, February 15, 2013 First of all, allow me to thank the IIF for having invited me to participate in this very relevant conference, organized in partnership with the Ministry of Finance of the Russian Federation, at the outset of the G20 ministerial meetings. It is a great pleasure for me to have the opportunity to address this distinguished audience again. **** Let me start by presenting my view on the world economy, focusing on the epicenter of the crisis  the advanced economies. The crisis erupted in full in late 2008, at the time of the Lehman Brothers collapse. The virulence of the consequences of this event brought a sense of common purpose among the most important countries in the world. In foras like the G20 and the Funds IMFC a coordinated policy response was instrumented, having as main objectives to stabilize financial markets, and to implement countercyclical fiscal and monetary policies to contain the contractionary forces in economic activity and 1 employment. At the same time, the process of the dearly needed redesign of the international financial architecture was initiated. The signs in 2009 and 2010 were relatively encouraging. The forceful measures implemented in the United States to backstop its financial markets and institutions were successful; it seemed at the time that the contagion to European financial institutions and economies was under control, and some advanced economies (like Singapore, Australia and Canada) and a broad number of emerging economies (like China, India and Mexico) were experiencing a very strong rebound in economic activity. As a matter of fact, towards the end of 2009 and 2010, a sense of achievement started to appear. But during the second half of 2011 two unprecedented events brought us back to a period of heightened uncertainty in financial markets and significantly deteriorated global economic prospects: first, the downgrade of the US sovereign debt by one credit rating agency in early August, and second, the worsening of the sovereign debt crisis in Europe, followed by the increasing risk of contagion across markets and countries. These events, along with the respective authorities difficulties to implement immediate credible policies to address the 2 ongoing fiscal and financial problems, led to a noticeable deterioration in confidence among economic agents. The perceived increase in the probability of a tail risk event, such as a sovereign default episode in some Euro zone member countries and, to a lesser extent, in the United States, produced great disruptions in international financial markets and economic activity worldwide. In turn, weak economic activity further deteriorated fiscal positions and the health of banking institutions, leading to an even worse situation, making it clear that we were in an adverse feedback loop. Given tight trade and financial linkages across countries, the decoupling in terms of growth between advanced and emerging economies that was apparent after the first quarter of 2009, disappeared. Needless to say, the situation required immediate policy response by authorities. In the United States, given that entrenched political positions made it impossible to make meaningful progress in the fiscal front, the Federal Reserve continued to carry the brunt of the adjustment, as it expanded its accommodative monetary policy stance, using extensively quantitative easing combined with prospective interest rate guidance. All this with the objective of taking the pressure 3 off the bond market, flattening the yield curve and by these means stimulate aggregate demand and employment. The situation in Europe, at least from my point of view, was, and still is, more challenging. The main reason was that the drastic deterioration of the fiscal position and the health of the banking system in some peripheral countries in the Eurozone elevated to hazardous levels what has been called fragmentation risk, which in plain English means the risk of a breakdown of the European currency union as we know it. This led to sudden stops in the financing of some sovereigns and their banking system, triggering also massive capital outflows. All this in turn fed back into higher fragmentation risks, creating a very pervasive vicious cycle. The materialization of sudden stops in the Eurozone caught many by surprise. This type of phenomenon was not supposed to happen in mature economies protected by a supposedly strong anchor in the form of a credible exchange regime, i.e. the European currency union. But the problem precisely was that the perception of a strong external anchor made it feasible for some countries to let their guard down, 4 manifested in policy complacency in the good years when huge and persistent net capital inflows were the norm. This situation resulted in: a) unprecedented external indebtedness in some countries, and b) banking institutions with bloated balance sheets supported by very fragile funding. This combination of factors made the sudden stops in some European countries much more pronounced than the ones experienced in previous decades in Latin America or during the Asian crisis in the nineties. The financial sector and sovereign distress in Europe demonstrates once more that an exchange rate regime per se cannot be a substitute for policy discipline. As a matter of fact, the problems faced by Europe since mid-2011 are not different from the ones resulting from a speculative attack against an exchange rate regime sparked by the loss of consistency between the token regime and the rest of the macroeconomic framework. When such inconsistencies appear, the confidence in the sustainability of the regime is lost, and the attack by market participants is immediately unleashed. The sudden stops in capital flows in some European countries provoked steep increases in sovereign and financial institutions 5 borrowing costs and CDS spreads, and a noticeable deterioration in liquidity conditions in the regions money markets. Access to the interbank funding market for many banks was abruptly interrupted, and the government securities market of the weakest European countries dried up for practical purposes. As the perception of the likelihood of a catastrophic event in Europe increased, major reallocation of portfolios took place, as resources were diverted to safe assets. Emerging markets were not spared of this reallocation of assets: their currencies depreciated and borrowing costs increased. More importantly, the contraction in economic activity in the most advanced economies reduced emerging markets exports and their rates of growth. Contagion in international financial markets was rampant. Urgent policy response by the Eurozone became unavoidable. But I think it is fair to say that the European Union was not prepared to respond to a challenge of this magnitude, basically because of what I already mentioned that by design the problems that they confronted then, caused by the surge in fragmentation risk, were not supposed to happen in the first place. An obvious additional complication was that any solution would have to be agreed by the seventeen Eurozone member countries through their political instances. After many months 6 of hesitation and confusion, a successful two-pronged stabilization strategy was finally implemented: First, through different facilities, the European Central Bank eventually guaranteed the provision of sufficient liquidity to backstop the interbank and government debt markets; it is worth mentioning the unlimited financing through the Target 2 mechanism, the LTRO (LongTerm Refinancing Operation), and the OMT (Outright Monetary Transactions). Second and more fundamentally, structural reforms in the European Union were credibly committed to firmly establish the congruency between the exchange rate regime and the rest of the macroeconomic and institutional framework of the Eurozone. Here I would like to highlight the following policy decisions: - The creation of a strong European Financial Stability Mechanism; - The reinforcement of fiscal policy governance, falling just short of the establishment of a fiscal union; - A proposed banking union, supported by centralized supervision and a Eurozone-wide resolution regime; and 7 - A major drive to enhance competitiveness in the region, to increase potential growth and employment creation. No less important has been the gigantic political drive by the European leadership to stick together and ratify their joint commitment to a single currency. A cornerstone in all this construct has been the OMT facility, since it bridged the short-term emergency liquidity provision and backstopping measures with the more long term, fundamental reforms that is anchoring the so far credibility of the single currency. Recall that through the OMT facility the ECB is willing to acquire unlimited amounts of sovereign debt, provided that the issuer has basically accepted the conditionality established by the European Union, and it is acting in accordance. This was a master stroke by the ECB. After all these difficulties and tribulations, we started 2013 with more optimism about the future of the world economy. Key factors to improve market sentiment have been: - In the United States, the avoidance so far of the fiscal cliff; - The permanence of Greece in the Eurozone; 8 - That many countries in the periphery have made sustained progress in their fiscal and external sector adjustments, regaining market access; - The gradual but steady progress in the design and implementation in the structural reforms in Europe; and - The faster growth in China. Risk appetite among investors has returned and the search for yield is in full force. There have been substantial capital inflows to Europe, together with an internal redistribution of resources in the Eurozone, which has produced a remarkable improvement in the borrowing costs for peripheral economies. Resources have also poured into emerging markets generating a compression of spreads and domestic currencies appreciation. The mood swing has been so strong, that some fears have been expressed about financial markets being too optimistic, with the potential of mispricing in some asset classes. Concern of asset price bubbles fed by credit booms are starting to appear in some economies, although not yet in Mexico, I would like to clarify. 9 A word of caution is in order though. Substantial vulnerabilities and downside risks still persist. Let me cite the most significant: - The United States economy still could be affected by the fiscal cliff. Not only the potential fiscal adjustment is a matter of concern, but also investment and expenditure decisions are being postponed due to the related uncertainty; - Stability in the Eurozone is still fragile, given that it continues to be dependent on massive support from authorities, in particular from the ECB; - Even though progress has been made in delineating the substantive policy actions that are essential to reestablish the consistency of the Eurozone exchange rate regime with the rest of the macroeconomic and institutional framework, relevant details are still in the drawing board, and once they are decided, they need to be legislated and implemented. Delays and/or incomplete adjustments could trigger the erosion of incipient market confidence. - The Eurozone has been in a recession for quite some time with very high unemployment, with the expectation that this 10 will continue to be the case for 2013. Reigniting growth has been a challenge given the fiscal constraints that many European countries face, the need for households balance sheet repair and the present limitations of credit institutions which are in the process of deleveraging. - It is to be noticed an incipient trend led by some advanced countries, like Japan, but including also some emerging markets economies, to use exchange rate policy as an instrument to enhance (or at least defend) competitiveness, promote exports and by these means growth. The problem with this approach is that by manipulating nominal exchange rate adjustments the impact on effective competitiveness tends to be temporary at best, while incurring in two big risks: a) that the pursuit of a short cut towards growth and prosperity could delay the adoption of structural reforms that genuinely would generate the desired effects on competitiveness and growth, and b) the possibility of retaliation by other countries, which would trigger severe turbulence in international financial markets. 11 - In emerging markets economies, even though most of them have structurally sound economies, large capital inflows can generate financial stability vulnerabilities through credit booms and asset price bubbles, and the concomitant domestic currency appreciation in real terms could affect growth, in particular given that as I already pointed out, independently some important advanced economies are actively pursuing a depreciating real exchange rate strategy. As I mentioned in a recent speech in Singapore, my fear is that a perfect storm might be forming as the result of: first, massive capital flows to some emerging market economies and some strong performing advanced economies; second, the surge of bubbles, characterized by asset mispricing; and third, the potential reversal in flows when the major advanced economies start exiting their accommodative monetary policy stance. This oversimplified sequence of potential events poses a major financial stability challenge for many capital recipient countries. **** 12 Needless to say, what I just outlined makes still at best for a sobering picture. This is the background scenario that we are facing today here in Moscow at the outset of Russias G-20 Presidency. I would rate this starting situation as better that the one the world was at the beginning of Frances and Mexicos G-20 Presidencies, but certainly not better enough that would allow us to declare victory. Therefore major challenges are still present, leaving no room for complacency. What does this mean for the G-20? At a minimum we should persevere in accomplishing the main commitments we made in Mexico last year. The agenda is comprehensive and ambitious, and it is urgent that we deliver. But that does not take away the possibility of new issues being brought to the fore, nor that we shouldnt concentrate our efforts in some specific, more pressing goals. In this regard, let me mention, from my point of view, which should be our priorities. First, the G-20 should regain its sense of common purpose. As the business and credit cycles in different parts of the world have diverged, the consensus and drive towards policy coordination and collaboration have been weakened. We should not forget that we live in an interconnected world, thus a collaborative solution to the 13 problems we face today would be far more rewarding in terms of benefits manifested in faster economic growth and employment creation in the context of financial stability, as well as in terms of minimizing the unavoidable adjustment costs. In this regard, it will be of the essence for countries to avoid the use of proactive exchange rate policies in pursuit of relative competitive advantages. In the same vein, we should avoid weakening the potential of the major reforms in financial sector regulation and supervision that are under way, by countries in the implementation face deviating from the level playing field objective that has been a keystone in our discussions and decisions. To illustrate what I mean, I find it a source of uncertainty that is delaying the full recovery of international financial markets the surge of different expressions of the reform in the form of the Volker rule, the Vickers solution or the one contained in the Liikanen report. Regulatory harmonization would benefit everybody, so deviating from this objective would be detrimental to the recovery process. Second, in terms of the international financial architecture, we should not weaken our commitment to strengthen key international financial institutions, like the IMF. In Mexico, we delivered in terms of enhancing the Funds lending capacity by many countries committing 14 to lend resources to the institution, but this came with the understanding that we would move forward also with the quotas review and the redesign of the quotas formula. I am a firm believer that the Fund will remain relevant as long as its lending capacity is quota based, and as long as the quota distribution gives legitimacy to the institution. I regret the lack of progress in the front, and I hope that this process can be reinvigorated here in Moscow. I also think we have not made enough progress in our collective efforts to prevent crises. This is a very important workstream in the reform process of the international financial architecture. Sometimes I have the sense that we are not inquisitive enough in actively asking ourselves from where the next crisis will come from. I say this because more often than not we are caught by surprise as a crisis erupts from an unsuspected source. Financial crises tend to mimic strokes trigged by high blood pressure. As you now, high blood pressure is referred in the medical jargon as the silent killer. I fear that we are exposed to too many silent killers in modern financial systems, and it is our duty to enhance our capabilities to uncover them in time. In this sense, I feel very keenly that we need to improve our early warning systems, broaden the practice of stress testing and dwell further in multilateral 15 surveillance and the identification of spillover effects of major economies policy decisions. Third, we should be able to react on a timely fashion to the threats to financial stability that might be brewing today and that we have identified already. I refer for example to the probability of a perfect storm that I alluded before. There is no doubt that the monetary policy implemented by major advanced economies have contributed to create an environment for huge capital reallocations among countries and markets, guided by the search for yield. But at the same time, I believe that those policies have been essential in the resolution of the crisis, and they will continue to be, so we need to learn to live with them. Also, emerging markets have to accept the fact that given the two-speed recovery process, with emerging markets growing much faster and on a stronger footing than advanced economies, some degree of currency appreciation is to be expected. On the other hand, capital recipient economies, primarily emerging ones, have a limit to the amount and speed of capital inflows that they can manage, after which asset mispricing can result, including non-equilibrium currency appreciations, which could generate financial stability vulnerabilities. What can be done then in this respect? 16 To start with, recipient countries could try to expand their capacity to accommodate capital inflows, by adjusting their fiscal stance and by implementing structural reforms to amplify the potential productive use of additional resources. But regretfully, there is also a limit to this. As a matter of fact, some countries have already exhausted this instance. The only alternative left would be the application of macroprudential policies. These policies can be implemented by using three types of instruments: a) capital-based instruments, like countercyclical capital buffers, or dynamic provisioning; b) liquidity-based instruments, like countercyclical liquidity requirements; and c) asset-side instruments, like LTV and DTI restrictions. Intervention in the forex markets and lowering of reference interest rates should also be considered, in particular if the zero-bound is not yet a restriction, but I would be less inclined towards the use of capital controls. Now in all this what can a fora like the G-20 contribute? I would say that in two aspects. Fist, even though I already said that we should be in general supportive of advanced economies monetary policies, I think that we are entitled to request their upmost effort to implement them, in particular when the time to exit comes, in a way to minimize volatility in international financial markets; and 17 Second, to develop a consensus towards good practices in macroprudential policies implementation and design so that they are transparent and targeted to prevent exclusively financial stability vulnerabilities, avoiding their use to introduce protectionist measures through the back door. Thank you very much for your attention. 18

Title: Central Banking: New Challenges and New Responses
text: "CENTRAL BANKING: NEW CHALLENGES AND NEW ANSWERS". SPEECH BY MR. JAVIER GUZMaN CALAFELL, DEPUTY GOVERNOR OF THE BANK OF MEXICO, AT THE 3RD INTERNATIONAL SEMINAR OF THE CENTRAL BANK OF ECUADOR "FROM PRIVATE CURRENCIES TO CENTRAL BANKING: 90 YEARS OF POLICY AND ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT SINCE THE CREATION OF THE ECB". Quito, Ecuador, October 25, 2017.1 I am very honored to participate in this International Seminar commemorating the 90th anniversary of the creation of the Central Bank of Ecuador. My sincere congratulations to all the staff of the Institution, and my thanks to the organizers for the invitation to share some points of view at this important event. We are experiencing a period of greater optimism about the world economic situation, which at the same time is accompanied by profound changes in the work of central banks. Undoubtedly, some of the most important adjustments are being observed in the implementation of monetary policy in advanced economies. On this occasion, I would like to concentrate my speech on this subject, which I consider to be of enormous importance, not only because of the lessons it may entail for our central institutes, but also because of the repercussions it may have for the evolution of the world economy in the coming years. Having reached its lowest reading in the aftermath of the 2008-2009 global financial crisis last year, the global GDP growth rate is expected to register a rebound in 2017 that could mark the beginning of a 1 The opinions and views expressed in this document are the responsibility of the author and do not necessarily represent the institutional position of the Bank of Mexico or its Governing Board as a whole. 1 stage of acceleration, although gradual and at still moderate levels, over the next few years. In addition to the higher rate of expansion that emerging and developing economies have generally been showing, this is due to a performance of advanced economies that has been better, both in its magnitude and in its coverage, than previously anticipated, thus laying firmer foundations for global economic recovery. Naturally, this has also given rise to the expectation and, in some cases, the materialization, of the beginning of a cycle of efforts aimed at the normalization of monetary policy stances by the central banks of the major advanced economies. It should be recalled that, in response to the negative effects of the global financial crisis on both inflation and economic activity in their respective economies, these central institutes implemented monetary easing measures of unprecedented magnitude and scope. On the one hand, benchmark interest rates were reduced to levels close to, and in some cases even lower, to zero percent. Also, as a result of the asset purchase programs put in place, the size of its balance sheets expanded significantly, from pre-crisis figures equivalent to 10 percent of GDP in the economies of the United States, Japan, the euro area and the United Kingdom as a whole, to 37 percent today. While it is possible to anticipate that the normalization of monetary policy in these economies will take place gradually and over a relatively long period, some differentiation can also be expected in terms of both their rate of progress and the specific order in which the various stimulus measures will be withdrawn. To date, the 2 The greatest progress has been shown by the US Federal Reserve since, in addition to having increased by 100 basis points the target range for the federal funds rate since the end of 2015, it has also begun, as of this month, the reduction of the size of its balance sheet. Likewise, although the European Central Bank has been clear about the possibility of extending, either in magnitude and/or duration, its asset purchase program if it deems it necessary, it has also indicated that as soon as this autumn some decisions could be taken to start its decline. For its part, the Bank of England has indicated that, if the economy maintains a consistent evolution with additional reductions in its idle capacity and an increase in inflationary pressures, its monetary stance could require a tightening in the coming months. In principle, these actions contribute to strengthening the feeling of greater optimism about the trajectory of the world economy in the coming years. On the one hand, to the extent that it is well supported, the normalization of the monetary policy positions of these central banks would reflect a sustainable strengthening of economic activity in their respective countries. On the other hand, a lower monetary lassitude would mitigate latent risks to global financial stability, derived from risk-taking by international investors in search of higher yields, as well as high levels of indebtedness in various economies and sectors, induced by an environment of low interest rates. 3 However, the normalization of monetary policy in advanced countries is also accompanied by significant challenges, with potential adverse repercussions on the world economy and, consequently, with a significant potential impact on emerging and developing economies. I would now like to refer to some of the main ones among them. First, the normalization of monetary policy in the major advanced economies will imply a tightening of global financial conditions. The downward pressures on low-risk asset yields introduced by the sharp monetary easing of the major central banks in recent years, both on the side of reductions in their benchmark rates and by purchases of government bonds, have led to a simultaneous compression in the corresponding term premiums and other risks. It should be noted by way of example that a recent study by the Federal Reserve estimates that, as a result of the quantitative stimulus measures put in place in that country, the term premium for 10-year Treasury bonds showed a compression close to 100 basis points towards the end of 2016.2 Of course, this process is expected to reverse as monetary stimulus withdraws, but there is a high level of uncertainty as to the magnitude and speed of adjustment. The foregoing by virtue of the special circumstances in which this will occur, particularly as a result of the size of the balance sheets of the respective central banks, the 2 Ver Bonis, Brian, Jane Ihrig, y Min Wei (2017): "The Effect of the Federal Reserve's Securities Holdings on Longer-term Interest Rates", FEDS Notes, Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, April. 4 intensity and duration of the period of monetary easing, and the absence of historical precedents. Likewise, the aforementioned environment of low interest rates, coupled with the relative scarcity of assets considered safe in advanced economies, has led to a reallocation of the portfolios of international investors towards more profitable but also riskier instruments, including those of emerging and developing economies. Indeed, according to recent estimates by the International Monetary Fund,3 about 85 percent (about 315 billion) of portfolio capital flows to emerging economies accumulated since 2010 can be attributed to external factors, such as global risk appetite, quantitative stimulus measures by the Federal Reserve, and expectations regarding the monetary policy to be implemented by that Central Institute. Therefore, it is logical to anticipate that the normalization of monetary policy in advanced economies will lead to movements in the opposite direction of these flows, a trend that could be accentuated by the possible overvaluation of some assets in emerging economies. Also, in a situation of tighter financial conditions, the vulnerabilities that still affect various economies of this group may become more evident. Secondly, to the complications that this represents for the management of monetary policy, it is possible to add a series of elements of uncertainty derived from changes of a possibly structural nature in the world economy. In particular, I would like to highlight the decrease in 3 International Monetary Fund (2017): "Global Financial Stability Report", October. 5 over the last few decades, real interest rates have been recorded, both in emerging economies and, in particular, in advanced economies. While this phenomenon has been extensively studied, there is no clear explanation for the relative importance of its determinants.4 Thus, the low level of real interest rates appears to be attributable to a variety of factors acting simultaneously. These have highlighted the role of global savings and investment patterns (resulting, for example, from high income growth in emerging economies, the decline in investment as a proportion of output in advanced economies or demographic aspects), and the interaction of demand and supply of assets considered safe (driven by factors such as the accumulation of international reserves in emerging economies or more financial regulation). strict). While the relevance of some of these elements, including the existence of an excess of savings at the global level, seems to be decreasing, and in the case of others it is anticipated that they will show some reversal in the future, it is generally considered unlikely that in the long term real interest rates on a global scale will reach levels close to those observed, for example, in the final decades of the last century. The prospect of real interest rates below their long-term average, combined with a low inflation rate, points to a picture of relatively low nominal interest rates in the coming years. However, the increases that can be expected as a result of the 4 Ver, por ejemplo, International Monetary Fund (2014): "Perspectives on Global Real Interest Rates", Capitulo 3 de "World Economic Outlook", April; Carney, Mark (2017): "[De]Globalisation and Inflation", 2017 IMF Michel Camdessus Central Banking Lecture, September; y Goodhart, Charles y Manoj Pradhan (2017): "Demographics Will Reverse Three Multi-decade Global Trends", BIS Working Paper No. 656, August. 6 This process of normalization poses significant challenges for the management of monetary policy, given the difficulties that exist in reducing short-term interest rates below zero. In other words, under these circumstances the room for manoeuvre needed to cope with both sharp slowdowns in economic activity and deflationary pressures is considerably reduced. Of course, one possibility is to resort again to the central bank's messages on the orientation of monetary policy ("forward guidance"), as well as the deployment of quantitative stimulus measures such as those adopted in recent years, although the latter faces the risk of propitiating the adverse effects already mentioned. Other options on the table include targeting the yield curve (implemented, with little impact on inflation so far, by the Bank of Japan), defining higher inflation targets (which may be seen as incompatible with the mandate of central banks or not very credible by virtue of the difficulties they have had in achieving, even the current ones) and the introduction of targets for the price level (difficult to implement and with serious communication challenges).5 This is undoubtedly a crucial issue for the implementation of monetary policy in advanced economies, for which there is still no answer. Third, it's important to note that, as I noted earlier, a low interest rate environment can also have 5 Ver Blanchard, Olivier y Lawrence Summers (2017): "Rethinking Stabilization Policy. Back to the Future", y Bernanke, Ben (2017): "Monetary Policy in a New Era", documentos presentados en la conferencia "Rethinking Macroeconomic Policy" del Peterson Institute for International Economics, October. 7 implications for the functioning and stability of financial systems. In particular, cutting short-term interest rates can incentivize excessive risk-taking, especially in a context where some intermediaries and other participants in the system perceive a high willingness or even the obligation of the central bank to provide emergency financing and liquidity in its role as lender of last resort.6 While research on the various elements related to financial stability has increased significantly in the wake of the global financial crisis, the level of knowledge on the subject remains relatively modest. This is also evident in the difficulty that still exists in reaching conclusions that could be considered definitive, as to the role that monetary policy must assume in the containment of risks in the financial system. However, and highlighting the still preliminary nature of both the evidence and the theoretical developments of recent years, the dominant point of view seems to lean towards a stance against the active use of monetary policy for financial stability purposes, among other reasons due to the limitations in identifying financial bubbles, the lags with which monetary policy operates and its impact beyond the financial system. In this context, it has been argued that the primary responsibility should lie with micro and macroprudential policies, which by their nature are more directly focused. 6 Ver Weidmann, Jens (2017): "Monetary Policy after the Crisis", IMFS Distinguished Lecture, September; Diamond, Douglas y Raghuram Rajan (2012): "Illiquid Banks, Financial Stability, and Interest Rate Policy", Journal of Political Economy, 120(3):552-591; y Farhi, Emmanuel y Jean Tirole (2012): "Collective Moral Hazard, Maturity Mismatch, and Systemic Bailouts", American Economic Review 102(1):60-93. 8 in the objective of financial stability. On the other hand, given the many questions that still persist in this field, it is important to be aware of the limitations facing policy decision-making and to maintain a position open to future progress.7 Fourth, the monetary authorities of the major advanced economies have found it difficult to accurately assess the determinants of inflation in their economies, in a context in which inflation remains low, in concurrence with indicators of employment and economic activity that have continued to strengthen. At present, the so-called "Phillips curve", which establishes the changes in the rate of growth of prices or wages that could be expected as a result of reductions in unemployment levels or, more generally, of an increased use of resources in the economy, represents a fundamental piece in the implementation of monetary policy of numerous central banks. However, this relationship seems to have weakened over the course of the past few decades as a result of a combination of factors. Among these, the role of globalization has been pointed out, by allowing slack in the global labor market to become more relevant than that in the domestic market, especially in a context in which technological progress facilitates the transfer of the production of goods and services to places with ample resources. 7 Ver International Monetary Fund (2015): "Monetary Policy and Financial Stability", IMF Policy Paper, September; y Haldane, Andrew, David Aikman, Sujit Kapadia y Marc Hinterschweiger (2017): "Rethinking Financial Stability", documento presentado en la conferencia "Rethinking Macroeconomic Policy" del Peterson Institute for International Economics, October. 9 this is reflected in the reduced capacity of producers and workers (or unions) to increase prices and wages, respectively, in the face of latent competition from abroad. The effect of the successful implementation of anti-inflationary strategies in many economies has also been highlighted, which has diluted the impact on prices of episodes of less slack in the economy. In addition, some authors have stressed that the revival in employment that has been observed in recent years seems to have been concentrated in lower-paid sectors, thus containing the average increase in wages, while others do not rule out the possibility of reductions in the natural unemployment rate as a result, for example, labour market reforms or demographic changes.9 Obviously, the difficulties in determining the determinants of inflation accentuate the margins of error in the implementation of monetary policy and increase the possibility of surprise adjustments. Likewise, the apparent weakening of the relationship between inflation and unemployment on the Phillips curve has led to a discussion about the merits of maintaining very low interest rates, given circumstances in which slack in the labor market seems to have little impact on inflation, and the maintenance of very loose monetary policies may lead to risks to the 8 Sin embargo, se ha senalado que el sustento empirico para esta hipotesis parece ser debil en el caso de Estados Unidos y otras economias avanzadas. Ver Yellen, Janet (2017): "Inflation, Uncertainty, and Monetary Policy", Remarks at the 59th Annual Meeting of the National Association for Business Economics, September. 9 Ver, por ejemplo, Leduc, Sylvain y Daniel Wilson (2017): "Has the Wage Phillips Curve Gone Dormant?", Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco Economic Letter No. 2017-30, October; y Aaronson, Daniel, Luojia Hu Arian Seifoddini y Daniel Sullivan (2015): "Changing Labor Force Composition and the Natural Rate of Unemployment", Chicago Fed Letter No. 338. 10 financial stability.10 The situation is further complicated by the possibility that the neutral interest rate (i.e., the rate that allows the economy to operate at full capacity without inflationary pressures) in advanced economies has declined considerably in recent years, further raising the technical complexity inherent in estimating this variable. Fifth, the environment of persistently low inflation rates, particularly in advanced economies, has led to doubts about the merits of central bank independence in these countries. This, mainly on the grounds that the fundamental motivation for providing monetary policy institutions with independence, namely the removal of incentives to stimulate employment and economic activity at the expense of price stability, might have lost its validity under the current circumstances.11 The independence of central banks has also been called into question in the face of unfavourable developments in economic activity in economies. Advanced after the global financial crisis, as well as by the proposition that, under quantitative easing schemes, the distinction between monetary and fiscal policy has become more tenuous, without the former having the legitimacy derived from approval by bodies subject to an electoral process. 10 Ver Borio, Claudio (2017): "Through the Looking Glass", OMFIF City Lecture, September. 11 Ver Eggertsson, Gauti (2013): "Fiscal Multipliers and Policy Coordination", en Cespedes, Luis y Jordi Gali (eds.), "Fiscal Policy and Macroeconomic Performance", pp. 175-234. 11 In this regard, several authors have pointed out the following:12 (a) monetary policy decisions must be made in a timely manner in an environment of continuously and rapidly changing economic and financial conditions. Subjecting monetary policy to a process of scrutiny and political discussion such as that which typically accompanies other economic policy decisions would detract from its effectiveness; (b) an independent central bank has a long-term vision that is alien to the political cycle, which is indispensable in the light of the lags with which monetary policy operates in the economy; c) achieving the institutional credibility of the central bank necessary for the efficient implementation of monetary policy is more difficult in the absence of such independence; (d) it is precisely the independence of central banks that has made it possible to put in place the measures required to mitigate the costs of the global financial crisis; (e) the experience of recent years shows that the coordination of fiscal and monetary policies, where necessary and justified, is not impeded by the central bank operating independently. In sum, despite the recent improvement in the global economy and a generally more encouraging outlook, the challenges facing monetary policy in advanced economies raise questions about the ability of their central banks to weather shocks of different kinds, as well as the possibility that their own monetary policy responses will become a destabilizing factor at the global level. However, I believe that it is possible to identify some concrete actions that could 12 Ver, por ejemplo, Bernanke, Ben (2017): "Monetary Policy in a New Era", documento presentado en la conferencia "Rethinking Macroeconomic Policy" del Peterson Institute for International Economics, October; y Walsh, Carl (2011): "Central Bank Independence Revisited", Economic Papers 30(1):18-22, March. 12 adopt in these countries with a view to promoting a more orderly behavior of both their economies and the world: ? The implementation of clear and effective communication strategies on monetary policy actions. As noted, one of the main sources of anxiety in the markets stems from the potential implications of the interest rate adjustment process and the exit of the quantitative stimulus measures put in place by the main central banks of this group. To the extent that changes in their respective positions are adequately communicated to the public, the risk of episodes of high volatility and disorderly adjustment in the markets would be mitigated. ? The adoption of more balanced policy approaches. The complexities that characterize the environment we currently face are largely due to an over-reliance on monetary policy to ensure the recovery of economic activity and combat deflationary pressures. Indeed, had a more balanced distribution of the burden of adjustment among the various policy instruments been resorted to, both the required reduction in interest rates and the unintended effects on the world economy would have been smaller. It is true that many advanced economies do not have fiscal space. However, the above does not apply to all of them, particularly under the current conditions of low interest rates.13 The margin of action is 13 Ver Auerbach, Alan y Yuriy Gorodnichenko (2017): "Fiscal Stimulus and Fiscal Sustainability", NBER Working Paper No. 23789, September. 13 much higher in the area of structural change, as efforts in this regard in this group of countries leave much to be desired. ? Greater awareness of the global impact of their policy actions. This is not only by virtue of the aforementioned indirect effects that these can generate, particularly in emerging and developing economies, but also in the self-interest of advanced economies, taking into account the possibility of "boomerang" effects. This implies, of course, promoting greater research efforts that allow us to obtain robust conclusions and direct applicability for economic policy. In conclusion, I would just like to point out that the challenges being faced by the central banks of advanced countries can leave lessons of great relevance for emerging and developing economies. While the problems faced by the monetary authorities of these two groups of countries differ in multiple areas, in others their nature is similar. Such is the case, for example, of existing doubts about the appropriate policies to preserve financial stability, or the more tenuous relationship between inflation and unemployment, which also seems to be present in some emerging economies. I believe that it is also necessary to take note of the challenges that may arise for the independence of central banks in our countries, either due to questions about the management of monetary policy as in advanced economies or simply as a reflection of pressures of this nature in those nations. In addition, emerging and developing economies should be involved in efforts to have 14 a stronger analytical rationale for the impact of economic policy measures on advanced economies on the rest of the world. And what is even more urgent. In the face of the above challenges and other well-known risk factors, both economic and political, for global economic performance in the short and long term, it is imperative that emerging and developing economies take advantage of the space provided by current circumstances in the global economy to strengthen their economic fundamentals. Undoubtedly, efforts in recent years have improved the growth bases and the ability of many of these economies to cope with shocks. However, it is also true that the task is incomplete, and that there are still too many cases in which there are significant macroeconomic imbalances and a considerable lag in structural adjustment. 15
