En suma, durante el complejo entorno de la emergencia sanitaria, el Banco de Mxico coadyuv de manera importante a generar un clima de estabilidad y certidumbre, que contribuy a mitigar los efectos econmicos de la pandemia y posibilit que los ciudadanos pudieran tomar mejores decisiones. Resultados Respondiendo a la convocatoria con la temtica ya indicada, este ao se inscribieron 1064 personas (15% ms inscritos que el ao anterior) de 28 Estados de la Repblica y recibimos 609 entradas. La distribucin 7 por genero fue de 55% mujeres, 44% hombres y 1% personas que prefirieron no indicar su gnero. El proceso de inscripcin y seleccin es importante pues ratifica la transparencia e imparcialidad que le ha dado prestigio y credibilidad al premio. Los alumnos se inscriben desde la plataforma del Premio, misma que reguarda sus datos y les proporciona un folio para mantener el anonimato ante el Jurado. En la misma plataforma, responden un cuestionario sobre temas econmicos y adjuntan su trabajo o video, que en las bases del concurso son denominados entradas. Los miembros del Jurado revisan alrededor de 150 entradas, seleccionadas. Los 10 mejores promedios de cada categora (semifinalistas) tienen una sesin de interaccin con el Jurado (entrevista de 10 minutos), a partir de la cual se seleccionan a los 5 finalistas y, posteriormente, al ganador de cada categora. Compaeras y compaeros participantes: Es un gusto encontrarme con jvenes estudiantes que, desde muy temprano, empean su inteligencia, visin prospectiva y dinamismo en 8 el estudio de temas cruciales para que en el futuro tengamos un mejor pas. Como siempre, la gran cantidad y calidad de los trabajos recibidos ponen en aprietos al jurado, a quien agradecemos su generosidad y profesionalismo. La mayora de los trabajos combinan seriedad analtica y frescura expositiva y contagian entusiasmo y optimismo. Por eso, me congratulo de la gran reserva de talento con la que contamos en nuestras ms recientes generaciones y felicito a todos los participantes y, por supuesto, a nuestros finalistas y ganadores. 9

Title: 2011 AFI Global Policy Forum: Taking stock. Setting goals. Moving forward
text: Opening remarks for the 2011 AFI Global Policy Forum Taking Stock. Setting Goals. Moving Forward. Cancun, September 28, 2011 1. Welcome remarks and introduction It is a pleasure to have you here in this beautiful resort in the south east part of Mexico. I welcome all the participants to this Global Policy Forum organized by the Alliance for Financial Inclusion. As all of you know, during this year, and in particular the last few weeks, many of us have been deeply involved in discussing issues related to fiscal consolidation, financial stability and low economic growth mostly in advanced economies. These issues are certainly very important and deserve a great part of our time and efforts, since lack of financial stability in the developed countries can represent a serious impediment of growth to the rest of the world. However, I am very pleased that we gather here today to devote part of our time to another important topic, which is also part of the G20 agenda. Certainly, financial inclusion does not seem as pressing as crisis management, but it as relevant for its long term implications on economic growth and population wellbeing. Looking at this Forums program it is very gratifying to see that the drive towards financial inclusion around the world have been resilient to the financial crises. Many countries have been working hard and dedicating economic and human resources during this last three years, in spite of the turbulent times in the global financial markets. I will focus todays address in three topics. First, I will make some considerations about the importance of financial inclusion. Second, I will describe the efforts that Banco de Mexico has done 1 to promote financial inclusion; and third, I will mention the challenges we face, not only in Mexico but worldwide in this regard. I will end with brief concluding remarks. 2. Importance of financial inclusion  In recent years there has been an increasing interest in Financial Inclusion. It has been argued that it helps reduce poverty and that it promotes economic development. Recent evidence supports this argument showing that not only does a correlation exist between financial development and economic growth but also that the former causes the latter.  Reductions in inequality, increased growth rates, and productivity gains are in part the consequence of financial deepening. Furthermore, randomized controlled trials conducted in several countries have shown that financial inclusion leads to wider investment options for small enterprises and better terms for wealth transfers to low-income individuals.  There is not a universally accepted definition of financial inclusion. Some definitions imply that all people should have access to financial services, while others define a vulnerable group, usually with lower income, as the inclusion target. Some definitions consider inclusion to all types of financial services, others to a subset of them.  A definition that seems appropriate for the purpose of policy is that used by the World Bank. Financial inclusion is defined as the absence of barriers to access; such barriers may be lack of infrastructure, customers' ineligibility or lack of information, inadequate product design, customers' lack of trust in financial intermediaries, and high prices and interest rates. Inadequate or excessive regulations could also constitute a barrier for financial inclusion. 2 3. The Mexican case  Financial inclusion in Mexico has been growing in recent years according to all the merits that are available.  Nonetheless, a significant number of Mexicans is still excluded from the financial system. In many cases exclusion is not due to the lack of physical infrastructure. Additionally, people with access to the financial system tend to make marginal use of it. To illustrate this, there are more than 80 million debit cards issued in Mexico, but in a given quarter only 38 million of them (less than 48%) are used. Moreover, the number of transactions performed with banking cards at points of sale in Mexico is lower than in Brazil, let alone more developed countries.  Given the impact that financial deepening has on economic growth, I believe that the limitations on financial inclusion have reduced Mexicos growth potential.  The trend for wider financial inclusion in Mexico was not interrupted by the world financial crisis. For instance, the number of deposit accounts did not stop growing during the last years; only credit card accounts dropped but they are already recovering.  The already existing trend toward wider financial inclusion constitutes a solid base for future developments in this account. 3.1. Banco de Mexicos mandate and financial inclusion  Financial inclusion is not explicitly part of Banco de Mexico's mandate; price stability is its first and foremost goal. Nevertheless, other important goals of the Mexican central bank are related to financial inclusion issues.  Banco de Mexico's law mandates the central bank to promote sound and efficient financial and payment systems. Additionally, the Transparency and Financial System Restructuring Law 3 (Transparency law) establishes obligations to Banco de Mexico that have a direct and indirect impact on financial inclusion.  An essential element for financial development is price stability. When there is no price stability, people stop using formal intermediation channels. Price stability allows agents to get into long term financial transactions, like buying a house or saving for retirement. High level of inflation affects severely the wellbeing of the poor because they are not able to hedge against the evasion of purchasing power of their salaries and scout saving. High level of inflation inhibits financial inclusion. Therefore, the main contribution that Banco de Mexico could do to financial inclusion is to promote price stability.  Wider financial inclusion is consistent with price stability in another way. Inclusion results in better functioning financial markets with fewer informational asymmetries. Also, by incorporating more individuals into the financial sector, more people acquire the means to smooth consumption over time, and to insure against adversity. These may act as automatic stabilizers during crises and recessions.  Regarding the promotion of a sound financial system, greater financial inclusion allows for a more efficient allocation of resources. In a sense, lending is a matching problem; intermediaries match amounts, terms (plazos) and risks between borrowers and depositors. By including more consumers in the system, banks, and financial intermediaries in general, have a wider pool to solve the mismatch problem.  Fostering an efficient payment system is an integral part of financial inclusion. Customers with a deposit account, and the payment options usually associated to it, are able to choose the most efficient means of payment available to them. Additionally, access to efficient payments vehicles reduces customers transaction costs and increases payment security; this impacts 4 productivity positively since customers have more time to dedicate to other activities, at the same time that risks are abated providing an essential element of any entrepreneurial activity: certainty. 3.2. What Banco de Mexico has done regarding financial inclusion  Banco de Mexico has also participated decisively, within the scope of its authority, in the development of regulation to eliminate the barriers that households, small and medium enterprises, and providers face when interacting in the financial system.  One of the most relevant recent developments for financial inclusion in Mexico has to do with payments through mobile means. This year, Banco de Mexico issued regulation to contribute to the development of payments through these means by defining several types of bank accounts.  The logic behind these accounts is that their regulatory treatment should be proportionate to the risks and benefits involved in offering the services; it reflects the international Anti-Money Laundering standards, and it takes advantage of the banking correspondents regulation recently issued. Additionally, it is consistent with the nine principles for innovative financial inclusion endorsed by the G20.  Four types of bank accounts have been contemplated by regulation by regulation. The documents required to customers to open such accounts and the associated monitoring are negatively related to its transaction capabilities. That is, the least risky accounts have lower information and monitoring requirements.  Mobile services and banking correspondents hold enormous potential to expand financial inclusion. On the supply side, tside 5 options reduce the cost of service provision, give that there is no need to open branches or deploy ATMs. On the demand side, transaction costs faced to users are significantly diminished. A very powerful side benefit for development purposes is that people in isolated areas will now have a chance to be part of the financial system.  In addition, this scheme promotes customer confidence in the financial system since their deposits are protected under the deposit insurance system. Also, payments through mobile means are settled through the banking network and are subject to the transparency and protection rules applied to any other payments made through the banking system.  Banco de Mexico established also the terms and conditions of basic accounts, which banks are obliged to offer accounting to Mexicos Transparency Law. Basic accounts contemplate restricted services that are not subject to any fees or commissions. Since they are offered by all deposit taking institutions, they are widely available. The offering of basic accounts eliminated some product design and price barriers that used to deter access to the system. These accounts have been rather successful: there are now more than 16 million of them.  We have also indirectly promoted inclusion by regulating banking fees and commissions. This strategy, implemented since 2010, eliminated charging practices that were not consistent with competitive market behavior. The principles followed in this regulation include: charges have to be related to actual services provided to the consumer; there cannot be two charges for the same service; there must be at least one channel free of charge through which customers may have access to their deposits; fees should not constitute a barrier to customer mobility; and information about fees should be transparent for customers. 6  In accordance with the Transparency Law, Banco de Mexico keeps a "Register of Fees and Commissions"; any increase in fees has to be reported and justified to the Central Bank. Banco de Mexico can issue objections if proposed fee increases are deemed unjustified. Objections are made public thereby affecting institutions' reputation.  Additionally, Banco de Mexico has promoted trust and competition in the banking system by means of publishing reports containing a wide range of indicators of consumer credit. These reports promote competition among providers and customers mobility.  Also, Banco de Mexico has taken steps to promote the adoption and usage of electronic means of payment, which indirectly favors financial inclusion. Among them, there is a permanent campaign to foster the use of SPEI, our interbank electronic payment system, which is extremely cost effective even for small scale transactions. 4. Challenges ahead 4.1. Challenges for Mexico  Mexico has made progress in all of the nine principles endorsed by the G20 regarding financial inclusion; however, there are still challenges ahead.  Reaching isolated, rural areas with low population density is probably the main challenge for the Mexican financial system. Although 95% of the population lives in municipalities in which financial infrastructure is available, there are many small and isolated municipalities that lack physical access to financial services. The recent drive in favor of mobile banking and banking correspondents is designed to face heads on this problem, but it is still too soon to know its impact. 7  The promotion of access for people that live in places with financial services availability, i.e. in urban areas, also represents a huge challenge. Many reasons may explain this phenomenon, among them: lack of trust in financial institutions (in a 2009 Banxico survey, 56% of respondents said they had little or no trust in banks); lack of financial education (26% said they were not familiar with checking or savings accounts); poor consumer protection; high prices; and inadequate services. 4.2. Global challenges  On the international agenda, I firmly believe that the main challenge we face ahead on financial inclusion is to be sure that the overhaul of the financial regulation agreed by the G20, mostly oriented to prevent financial instability, do not affect the efforts and long term process of promoting financial inclusion.  I do endorse H.R.H Princess Maximas proposal to include the following text in the foreword of the revised draft of the Basel Core Principles: Recognizing the complementarity among financial stability, integrity and inclusion, as well as the positive effects that financial inclusion has on growth and sustainable development, it is encouraged to implement the principles in ways that do not unnecessarily limit access to finance.  Other challenge is to promote technological and institutional innovation that lower transactions costs and make financial services readily available. Recent developments in correspondent banking and mobile services seem to be a promising avenue for expanding financial penetration. Regulation should be adapted constantly so that these schemes have a continuous impact on financial inclusion. 8  Another challenge is to find a balance between promoting financial inclusion while keeping the adequate Anti-Money Laundering (AML) restrictions. 5. Concluding remarks I believe that through financial inclusion, the general population and, above all, the poorest can share the benefits of a stable, efficient and competitive financial system. This is particularly so in todays world in which it is expected that economic growth in advanced economies will slow down, forcing emerging and developing economies to look for opportunities to enhance domestic growth, and an obvious candidate to do so is through financial inclusion. Thank you very much. 9

Title: Global financial stability and cooperation between central banks: what have we learned?
text: "Global Financial Stability and Central Bank Cooperation: What Have We Learned?" Remarks by Dr. Manuel Sanchez Gonzalez, Deputy Governor of the Bank of Mexico, at the Conference "Cooperation between Central Banks at the Beginning of the XXI Century", on the occasion of the 60th Anniversary of the Center for Latin American Monetary Studies (CEMLA), in Mexico City, on July 20, 2012. It is an honor for me to participate in this conference commemorating the 60th Anniversary of the Center for Latin American Monetary Studies (CEMLA), and to exchange ideas with distinguished personalities in this panel entitled "Global Financial Stability and Cooperation among Central Banks: What Have We Learned?" CEMLA has been a key organization for collaboration between issuing institutes, promoting research, understanding and training on monetary and financial issues. I congratulate this Centre on its anniversary and on the excellent initiative of organizing this conference, and I wish it many more years of success in its work for the benefit of our countries. The importance of financial stability and economic policy As we know, the proper functioning of any economy requires that the different components of its financial system operate in a continuous and orderly manner, without suffering significant interruptions or alterations despite the possible emergence of shocks of various nature. This is what we usually describe as financial stability. 1 In the pursuit of this stability, central banks play a fundamental role. By their very nature, issuing institutes must create a currency that serves as a reliable means of payment to society, which involves the task of controlling inflation. Empirical evidence confirms that price stability is a prerequisite for the stability of the financial system and even for sustained economic growth. Also, the law often assigns central banks other responsibilities, including those related to the development of the financial system and payment systems. Also, in many countries, authorities other than central banks have broad responsibilities for substantive aspects of the regulation and supervision of the financial system. The proper exercise of these functions should promote stability. The shared nature of the supervisory functions of the financial system between central banks and other entities at the national level has made collaboration between authorities of the same country indispensable. Interaction has manifested itself in multiple forms, including the exchange of information, the requests for opinion of one authority on the decisions of another, the participation of members of central banks in the boards of various authorities and, recently, in joint participation within financial stability boards. However, national financial systems and markets are highly interconnected, which, to a large extent, makes financial stability an inherently global notion. The implications of international links can be significant. For example, financial instability in one country can affect the stability of other regions if they operate branches of banks whose parent companies are in troubled countries. In turn, the weakness of a parent bank in one country may imply higher capital costs for subsidiaries in other countries. 2 Likewise, measures taken by some nations can impact the financial systems of others, for example, in the form of monetary stances that induce capital flows to other economies, or regulations of international banks that limit the development of certain markets in other countries. In addition, the economic situations and policies of some countries may provoke economic policy reactions in others, such as the imposition of controls on the entry or exit of capital considered "excessive". Cooperation between central banks The growing financial interconnection explains why, in recent years, dialogue and collaboration between authorities and, in particular, between central banks in different jurisdictions has intensified. The avenues of this collaboration are well known, including the exchanges of information, opinions and experiences, bilaterally or within international organizations and groups.1 It is worth noting the arduous coordination effort to jointly strengthen banking regulatory and supervisory frameworks, led by the Financial Stability Board (FSB) and the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (BCBS). The scope of work has been broad, including stricter capital and liquidity standards, international resolution mechanisms, expansion of the regulatory perimeter, cross-border transactions, additional capital requirements for banks considered systemically important globally and locally, the creation of supervisory colleges, standardization. 1 For a comprehensive account of central bank cooperation, see Borio, C. and G. Toniolo (2006). "One hundred and thirty years of central bank cooperation: a BIS perspective." BIS Working Papers No. 197. 3 of OTC derivatives and the use of central counterparties to trade such assets. There is perhaps no better example of effective collaboration than that emerged during the recent global crisis in the form of reciprocal and temporary mechanisms for the exchange of currencies in order to provide liquidity, known as "swap lines". In particular, central banks' response to the lack of liquidity in specific currencies was to establish these lines so that central banks of scarce currencies could offer them to commercial banks in those countries that required them.2 Lessons and outstanding questions Experience in the tasks of financial stability and cooperation between central banks allow us to derive relevant lessons, which are the topic of discussion of this panel. Just to invite the debate I would like to identify some lessons and questions. The first lesson is that collaboration between central banks has been fruitful in sharing knowledge about monetary and financial practices and policies. The second lesson is humility. Although links have been strengthened and central banks' methods of analysis and communication have become sophisticated, neither the frequency nor the intensity of financial crises has diminished. Obviously, the most dramatic case in many decades has been the great global crisis whose epicenter was the United States, which was neither diagnosed nor prevented by the financial authorities. 2 The lines used as intermediaries the central banks of the commercial banks that needed that liquidity, so that the credit risk fell on the intermediary central banks. For an analysis of the effectiveness of these lines, see Allen, W.A. and R. Moessner (2010). "Central bank co-operation and international liquidity in the financial crisis of 2008-9." BIS Working Papers No. 310. 4 The third lesson is that we still have a long way to go on how to keep systemic risk low without hindering the healthy development of the financial system. In particular, we seem to be better at managing a crisis than at preventing it. These and other possible lessons lead us to ask ourselves substantive economic policy questions, among which I arbitrarily select four: First, what would be a minimum agenda of understanding on the possible causes of financial crises and the mechanisms of contagion? For example, what is the real relevance of the so-called global imbalances that seem to be inherent in harnessing specialization and investment opportunities in a world with countries of different levels of development? Second, what are the best policies to combat these problems? In particular, what would be the optimal mix between domestic and international policies to address the possible causes of instability? Third, in economic policy, where should the focus of the jurisdiction itself end and the global one begin? For example, under what conditions should central banks incorporate the potential impacts of their policies on other economies? Fourth, what should they avoid and, if so, what would be the best reaction of the monetary authorities to policies in other countries that are making their decisions difficult? Finally, I would like to reiterate my congratulations and thanks to CEMLA and express my hope that, with better understanding and collaboration together, those of us who work in central banks can better contribute to the financial stability of our countries in the future. 5
text_original: Estabilidad financiera global y cooperacin entre bancos centrales: Qu hemos aprendido? Palabras del Dr. Manuel Snchez Gonzlez, Subgobernador del Banco de Mxico, en la Conferencia Cooperacin entre bancos centrales a principios del Siglo XXI, con motivo del 60 Aniversario del Centro de Estudios Monetarios Latinoamericanos (CEMLA), en la Ciudad de Mxico, el 20 de julio de 2012. Es para m un honor participar en esta conferencia conmemorativa del 60 Aniversario del Centro de Estudios Monetarios Latinoamericanos (CEMLA), e intercambiar ideas con distinguidas personalidades en este panel titulado Estabilidad financiera global y cooperacin entre bancos centrales: Qu hemos aprendido?. El CEMLA ha sido una organizacin clave para la colaboracin entre institutos emisores, promoviendo la investigacin, el entendimiento y la capacitacin sobre temas monetarios y financieros. Felicito a este Centro por su aniversario y por la excelente iniciativa de organizar esta conferencia, y le deseo muchos aos ms de xito en sus labores en beneficio de nuestros pases. La importancia de la estabilidad financiera y poltica econmica Como sabemos, el funcionamiento adecuado de cualquier economa requiere que los diferentes componentes de su sistema financiero operen de manera continua y ordenada, sin sufrir interrupciones o alteraciones significativas a pesar del posible surgimiento de choques de diversa naturaleza. Esto es lo que generalmente describimos como estabilidad financiera. 1 En la bsqueda de esta estabilidad, los bancos centrales juegan un papel fundamental. Por su propia naturaleza, los institutos emisores deben crear una moneda que sirva como medio confiable de pago a la sociedad, lo cual implica la tarea de controlar la inflacin. La evidencia emprica confirma que la estabilidad de los precios es un prerrequisito para la estabilidad del sistema financiero e incluso para el crecimiento econmico sostenido. Tambin, con frecuencia la ley asigna a los bancos centrales otras responsabilidades, incluyendo las relacionadas con el desarrollo del sistema financiero y de los sistemas de pagos. Asimismo, en muchos pases algunas autoridades diferentes a los bancos centrales tienen responsabilidades amplias sobre aspectos sustantivos de la regulacin y supervisin del sistema financiero. El ejercicio adecuado de estas funciones debe promover la estabilidad. El carcter compartido de las funciones de supervisin del sistema financiero entre bancos centrales y otras entidades a nivel nacional ha hecho indispensable la colaboracin entre autoridades de un mismo pas. La interaccin se ha manifestado de mltiples formas, incluyendo el intercambio de informacin, los requerimientos de opinin de una autoridad sobre las decisiones de otra, la participacin de miembros de los bancos centrales en los directorios de diversas autoridades y, recientemente, en la participacin conjunta dentro los consejos de estabilidad financiera. Ahora bien, los sistemas y mercados financieros nacionales se encuentran sumamente interconectados, lo que, en buena medida, convierte a la estabilidad financiera en una nocin inherentemente global. Las implicaciones de los enlaces internacionales pueden ser significativas. Por ejemplo, la inestabilidad financiera en un pas puede afectar a la estabilidad de otras regiones si en stas operan sucursales de bancos cuyas matrices se encuentran en pases con problemas. A su vez, la debilidad de un banco matriz en un pas puede implicar mayores costos de capital para las subsidiarias en otros pases. 2 Asimismo, las medidas adoptadas por algunas naciones pueden impactar los sistemas financieros de otras, por ejemplo, en la forma de posturas monetarias que induzcan flujos de capital hacia otras economas, o regulaciones de bancos internacionales que limiten el desarrollo de ciertos mercados en otros pases. Adems, las situaciones y polticas econmicas de algunos pases pueden provocar reacciones de poltica econmica en otros, como por ejemplo, la imposicin de controles a la entrada o salida de capitales considerados excesivos. Cooperacin entre bancos centrales La creciente interconexin financiera explica por qu, en los aos recientes, se ha intensificado el dilogo y la colaboracin entre las autoridades y, en particular, entre los bancos centrales de diferentes jurisdicciones. Las avenidas de esta colaboracin son bien conocidas, incluyendo los intercambios de informacin, de opiniones y de experiencias, de manera bilateral o dentro de los organismos y grupos internacionales.1 Vale la pena destacar el arduo esfuerzo de coordinacin para fortalecer de forma conjunta los marcos de regulacin y supervisin bancarias, encabezado por el Consejo de Estabilidad Financiera (FSB) y el Comit de Basilea para la Supervisin Bancaria (BCBS). El alcance del trabajo ha sido amplio, incluyendo estndares ms estrictos de capital y liquidez, mecanismos de resolucin internacional, ampliacin del permetro regulatorio, transacciones transfronterizas, requerimientos de capital adicionales para los bancos considerados sistmicamente importantes a nivel global y local, la creacin de colegios de supervisin, la estandarizacin 1 Para un recuento amplio de la cooperacin entre bancos centrales, vase Borio, C. y G. Toniolo (2006). One hundred and thirty years of central bank cooperation: a BIS perspective. BIS Working Papers No. 197. 3 de derivados extraburstiles y el uso de contrapartes centrales para comerciar dichos activos. Tal vez no exista un mejor ejemplo de colaboracin eficaz que la surgida durante la reciente crisis global en la forma de mecanismos recprocos y temporales para el intercambio de divisas con el fin de proveer liquidez, conocidos como lneas swap. En particular, la respuesta de los bancos centrales a la falta de liquidez en monedas especficas fue establecer estas lneas para que los bancos centrales de las monedas que escaseaban pudieran ofrecerlas a los bancos comerciales de aquellos pases que las requeran.2 Lecciones y preguntas pendientes La experiencia en las tareas de estabilidad financiera y cooperacin entre los bancos centrales nos permiten derivar lecciones relevantes, las cuales son el tema de discusin de este panel. Solo para invitar al debate me gustara identificar algunas lecciones e interrogantes. La primera leccin es que la colaboracin entre los bancos centrales ha sido fructfera en cuanto al intercambio de conocimientos sobre prcticas y polticas monetarias y financieras. La segunda leccin es de humildad. A pesar de que se han estrechado los vnculos y se han sofisticado los mtodos de anlisis y comunicacin de los bancos centrales, no ha disminuido ni la frecuencia ni la intensidad de las crisis financieras. Obviamente, el caso ms dramtico en muchas dcadas ha sido la gran crisis global cuyo epicentro fue Estados Unidos, la cual no fue diagnosticada ni prevenida por las autoridades financieras. 2 Las lneas usaron como intermediarios a los bancos centrales de los bancos comerciales que necesitaban esa liquidez, con lo que el riesgo crediticio recay en los bancos centrales intermediarios. Para un anlisis de la efectividad de estas lneas, vase Allen, W.A. y R. Moessner (2010). Central bank co-operation and international liquidity in the financial crisis of 2008-9. BIS Working Papers No. 310. 4 La tercera leccin es que todava nos falta mucho por entender sobre la forma de cmo mantener reducido el riesgo sistmico sin entorpecer el sano desarrollo del sistema financiero. En particular, parece que somos mejores para manejar una crisis que para prevenirla. Estas y otras posibles lecciones nos llevan a plantearnos preguntas sustantivas de poltica econmica, entre las que arbitrariamente selecciono cuatro: Primera, cul sera una agenda mnima de entendimiento sobre las posibles causas de las crisis financieras y los mecanismos de contagio? Por ejemplo, cul es la verdadera relevancia de los llamados desequilibrios globales que parecen ser inherentes al aprovechamiento de la especializacin y las oportunidades de inversin en un mundo con pases de diferente nivel de desarrollo? Segunda, cules son las mejores polticas para combatir esos problemas? En particular, cul sera la mezcla ptima entre polticas internas e internacionales para abatir las posibles causas de la inestabilidad? Tercera, en la poltica econmica, dnde debe terminar el foco de la propia jurisdiccin y empezar el global? Por ejemplo, bajo qu condiciones los bancos centrales deberan incorporar los posibles impactos de sus polticas sobre otras economas? Cuarta, qu deberan evitar y, en su caso, cul sera la mejor reaccin de las autoridades monetarias ante polticas de otros pases que les estn dificultando sus decisiones? Finalmente, me gustara reiterar mi felicitacin y agradecimiento al CEMLA y expresar mi deseo de que, con un mejor entendimiento y colaboracin en conjunto, los que trabajamos en los bancos centrales podamos contribuir mejor a la estabilidad financiera de nuestros pases en el futuro. 5

Title: Inauguration of National Financial Education Week 2012
text: Remarks by the Governor of the Bank of Mexico, Agustin Carstens, during the inauguration of the National Financial Education Week 2012. Monday, October 1, 2012 Good morning. I would like to begin my speech by thanking the Secretary of finance, Dr. Jose Antonio Meade, for his kind words. I pay tribute to Dr. Meade, because although under my time at the Ministry of Finance and Public Credit this national financial education program began, it has been during Dr. Meade's period as Secretary that this initiative has been taken to unusual levels, with the support, of course, of all public and private institutions that deal with financial matters. The participation of Dr. Luis Pazos and the Condusef has also been very outstanding. In particular, as seen by this full auditorium, every year the National Week dedicated to Financial Education summons more enthusiastic participants eager to spread and learn. This fact alone reveals that financial education is here to stay and is already an irreplaceable element in the map of financial activity in Mexico. I have no doubt that in the coming years this trend of steady growth will continue to be the guideline. This means that efforts are bearing fruit and that they are becoming more abundant. A year ago, I allowed myself to recall in this same auditorium that for central banks in the world financial education has become a matter of first importance. Increasingly, central banks engage in activities dedicated specifically to financial education and designed to disseminate among the most diverse audiences the knowledge necessary to take advantage of all the benefits of financial products and systems. And we certainly don't do it alone. With the leadership of the Ministry of Finance and the Condusef, all the institutions represented here have enthusiastically joined this great purpose of raising financial education in our country. This involvement of central banks in efforts for greater and better financial education is due to the fact that this is a factor that has a decisive impact so that we can better comply with our legal mandates. In the specific case of the Bank of Mexico, we are aware that to the extent that the benefits of price stability and a healthy functioning of the financial and payment systems are disseminated with increasing depth and clarity, and with an increasing number of people, we will achieve, for example, that the monetary policy decisions taken by the Governing Board meet their objectives more effectively. Fortunately, the times when the Central Bank could be a very respectable but definitely arcane institution, unknown to the majority of the population, are already behind us for many years. Also left in the past, the times when the officials of the Issuing Bank secretly decided on interest rates, growth of monetary aggregates or 1 foreign exchange reserves, convinced that disseminating their decisions and the reasons that gave them foundation would cause bewilderment and confusion in a public unfamiliar with the functioning of money and the financial system. Today, on the contrary, communication and full transparency are vital for a modern central bank. Today central banks arguably yearn, for example, for our internal discussions about monetary policy to be attended, understood and analyzed by more and more people. Since 2011, the Bank of Mexico has disseminated the minutes of the Governing Board regarding monetary policy decisions. This task of dissemination is eminently educational and today each member of the Governing Board of the Bank of Mexico has before him the challenge of being clear, precise, eloquent even in the presentation of his arguments and reasons, because he knows that, in the end, his words will potentially reach the entire public. This effort to communicate is a genuine task of financial education. And to the extent that good financial education spreads among more people, the Central Bank will be forced to ensure that its decisions have the highest standards of quality, good judgment, opportunity and information, for the benefit of the entire economy and each of the Mexicans. The same reasoning applies to the other tasks of the Bank of Mexico: to promote the proper functioning of the financial system, the Central Institute has no better tool than financial education. Better and greater financial education reinforces the tasks of the Bank of Mexico in terms of regulation and supervision of the financial system. Thus, in close interaction with financial education efforts, the Bank of Mexico verifies that consumers of financial products and services have complete, truthful and timely information or that financial institutions comply with the legal provisions on the collection of commissions. The contribution of financial education to the proper functioning of payment systems is also decisive. Disseminating with clarity and opportunity among the public the variety of payment options, their respective costs, their advantages and their limits - which is, clearly, a task of financial education - allows the Bank of Mexico to better fulfill this other function. Along the same lines, the Contacto Banxico award, which for the fourth consecutive year the Bank of Mexico is calling for high school students from all over the country has as its theme in this year 2012 precisely payment systems. In these constant and growing efforts to spread financial education, the Bank of Mexico has used the most modern communication technologies available. Hence the accumulation of timely economic and financial information that we disseminate on our Internet portal; hence also the constant communication with increasingly diverse and extensive audiences through the so-called social networks. In less than a year, for example, we have doubled the number of our active followers on Twitter reaching last Friday to more than 59 thousand. This constant and growing interest in knowing first-hand timely financial information on interest rates, exchange rates, presentations by the Governing Board of the Bank of Mexico, reports on financial activity or on inflation, reveals the immense and fertile ground for growth that financial education in Mexico has before it. 2 On the other hand, the Bank of Mexico allocates many educational and communication resources to another task of financial education that may seem trivial, but that in reality is of great importance for its extensive social impact. I am referring to the disclosure that we constantly make of the characteristics of our banknotes and coins and the security elements that characterize them so that all people can easily distinguish, for example, between a genuine banknote of the Bank of Mexico and a counterfeit. In fact, in Mexico we have a very low rate of counterfeits with respect to the total of banknotes in circulation, but even that very low incidence can be reduced through greater financial education, since it is precisely the users who can most effectively safeguard the integrity of the cash when delivering to the Bank of Mexico or send it through its delivery in bank branches, the allegedly false pieces. It is also worth mentioning the important work of disseminating financial culture carried out by the Interactive Museum of Economics, MIDE. A pioneering concept in museography, which was an initiative of the Governing Board of the Bank of Mexico, and which, now with the invaluable contribution of all Mexican banks, puts daily within the reach of all the foundations of a good economic and financial culture. In parallel to these purely educational tasks, it should be recalled that Congress has given the Bank of Mexico powers to protect the rights of consumers of financial products and services. This is how we have regulated the so-called basic accounts and how we have prohibited financial practices that are harmful to consumers or contrary to free competition. It is clear to us that financial education is crucial for users of financial services to take full advantage of these legal and regulatory provisions that have been designed precisely for their benefit. The challenge of financial education is immense and we would do badly to declare ourselves satisfied with what we have achieved so far. Financial education is everyone's task, we all have a lot to contribute and we all have a lot to gain if we generalize and intensify these efforts. The virtue of this National Financial Education Week is to bring together these multiple efforts, give them greater cohesion, and above all, inject them with a renewed impetus in the face of the great challenges that we still have to come. Thanks a lot. 3
