Title: Inauguration of the International Forum on Financial Inclusion
text: Remarks by the Governor of the Bank of Mexico, Agustin Carstens, during the inauguration of the International Forum on Financial Inclusion (National Palace, Mexico City) June 26, 2014 ? Mr. President of the United Mexican States, Mr. Enrique Pena Nieto, ? Ms. Christine Lagarde, Managing Director of the International Monetary Fund, ? Mr. Secretary of Finance and Public Credit, Dr. Luis Videgaray Caso, ? Madam Secretary of Social Development, teacher Rosario Robles Berlanga, ? Madam Secretary of Health, Dr. Mercedes Juan Lopez, ? Mr. Secretary of Economy, Mr. Ildefonso Guajardo Villarreal, ? Mr. Director General of the Alliance for Financial Inclusion, Dr. Alfred Hannig, Ladies and gentlemen legislators, ? Representatives of the business sector, the social sector and the financial sector, ? Ladies and gentlemen, 1 First of all, I would like to welcome the convening of the Government of President Pena Nieto to this International Forum on Financial Inclusion, in particular because of the great social content it has. I also wish, like the Secretary of finance, to welcome Mrs. Christine Lagarde to our country and to thank her for her special interest in promoting financial inclusion and for her great willingness to have an always positive interaction between the International Monetary Fund and Mexico. Talk of financial inclusion inevitably forces us to recognize the hard lessons we still have to digest about the economy of poverty. As a starting point, it must be accepted that a low coefficient of financial inclusion is associated with high poverty rates. The exclusion of the formal financial markets that still suffer large population centers, in Mexico and in the world, constitutes one of the most iron obstacles to overcoming poverty. It is very expensive for those who are poor not to have access to savings and credit instruments. This is because who 2 they suffer from the scarcity of resources, they also suffer severe restrictions to undertake productive businesses, finance projects to improve human capital, plan for reasonable terms to acquire a home or to successfully face adversities and natural disasters. In the life sentence of poverty, the lack of financial inclusion is a link that is always present. But to break that link, it is necessary to avoid two more or less frequent conceptual errors both among economists and among those in charge of the execution of public policies. The first of these errors is to assume, with a certain arrogance, that the main problem of the lack of financial inclusion is first and foremost an educational or cultural problem; that is, it would be enough to undertake large financial education campaigns for the poor to discover the benefits of financial intermediation and, consequently, come ready to join formal financial institutions as clients. This assumes that any 3 The person has immediate and cost-free access to financial services, which is clearly not the case. On the other hand, it is common to find the thesis that the poor do not carry out financial transactions on a daily basis, under the argument that they do not have enough resources. Nothing more false. Just as the intermediation of resources between lenders and debtors is almost as old as the history of mankind itself, financial activity is known and practiced on a daily basis by all social groups in the world, whether rich or poor. As early as 1979, upon receiving the Nobel Prize in Economics, Professor Theodore W. Schultz drew attention to the fact that many economists make the conceptual error of thinking that the economy of poverty obeys different laws and standards than those applicable to the rest of the economy. Not so: the need to make the best use of scarce resources and apply them efficiently is equally imperative for a large company as for a tiny family business. 4 The difference between them, rich and poor, basically does not lie in the lack of basic knowledge or interest in obtaining better living conditions. The abysmal difference between those who have full access to modern, efficient, regulated, formal financial intermediation and those who have to resort to inefficient, expensive, uncertain savings mechanisms, lacking regulation and guarantees, lies fundamentally in the very high transaction costs that the latter must face. Thus, one of the first steps to successfully face the great problem of financial exclusion is to know and understand the multiple mechanisms of informal financial intermediation that ingenuity, necessity and customs have created in Mexico. Many of these mechanisms, for example the spontaneously organized batches in many workplaces and colonies, are a response to the need to save and obtain credit that many families have. This type of financial intermediation bears a resemblance to 5 made by the merchants organized in ancient Mexico in the great market of Tlatelolco, who invested their surpluses in the sponsorship of celebrations and invitations that would ultimately facilitate their mobility in a stratified and rigid society, as was that one. Therefore, the great challenge that the financial authorities have is to create the conditions so that these savings and financing needs find modern, reliable and efficient channels that allow popular savings and credit models to evolve towards formal channels. These formal financial intermediation networks must lower transaction costs for the user. The recent financial reform certainly pays significantly in this regard. It is about breaking down information barriers, giving greater strength to development banking, facilitating the mobility of users between different intermediaries to take advantage of the best alternatives, considerably strengthening the protection of users of financial services and multiplying the points of access to them. 6 Along with the financial reform, there is another reform also promoted by the government of President Pena Nieto that will allow the full exploitation of technological potential for the benefit of greater financial inclusion. I am referring to the reform in telecommunications. Greater competition in telecommunications will generate a significant reduction in transaction costs in multiple financial intermediation operations, from basic to the most complex. Telecommunication services that are cheaper in cost, more efficient, with a wider geographical coverage and of higher quality will mean more frank access to financial intermediation for the population with fewer resources and, therefore, will increase the possibilities of various financial operations. Another crucial element in sustaining greater financial inclusion is trust. In this sense, have stable and solid macroeconomic fundamentals through 7 both a responsible fiscal policy and a monetary policy committed to the stability of the purchasing power of the currency, together with constant respect for the rule of law, are indispensable foundations for extending financial inclusion, foundations that Mexico already has. On this platform of trust we can undertake the great challenge of massifying financial intermediation mechanisms, following a strategy of constant and progressive reduction of transaction costs, through better regulation and the full and intelligent use of technological advances. Only in this way, by enduring and sustainably reducing transaction costs and democratizing the benefits of modern financial intermediation, can we break the vicious circle between poverty and financial exclusion. Only in this way - through the synergies between structural reforms, regulation and responsible and sound public policies - will we end up with the perverse paradox that there is no more expensive and costly condition than that of being poor. Thanks a lot. 8
text_original: Palabras del Gobernador del Banco de Mxico, Agustn Carstens, durante la inauguracin del Foro Internacional de Inclusin Financiera (Palacio Nacional, Ciudad de Mxico) 26 de junio de 2014  Seor Presidente de los Estados Unidos Mexicanos, licenciado Enrique Pea Nieto,  Seora Christine Lagarde, Directora-Gerente del Fondo Monetario Internacional,  Seor Secretario de Hacienda y Crdito Pblico, doctor Luis Videgaray Caso,  Seora Secretaria de Desarrollo Social, maestra Rosario Robles Berlanga,  Seora Secretaria de Salud, doctora Mercedes Juan Lpez,  Seor Secretario de Economa, licenciado Ildefonso Guajardo Villarreal,  Seor Director General de la Alianza para la Inclusin Financiera, doctor Alfred Hannig, Seoras y seores legisladores,  Representantes del sector empresarial, del sector social y del sector financiero,  Seoras y seores: 1 Antes que nada, quisiera celebrar la convocatoria del Gobierno del Presidente Pea Nieto a este Foro Internacional de Inclusin Financiera, en particular debido al gran contenido social que reviste. Tambin deseo, al igual que el Secretario de Hacienda, darle la bienvenida a nuestro pas a la seora Christine Lagarde y agradecerle su especial inters por promover la inclusin financiera y su gran disposicin a tener una interaccin siempre positiva entre el Fondo Monetario Internacional y Mxico. Hablar de inclusin financiera obliga inevitablemente a reconocer las duras lecciones que an debemos digerir sobre la economa de la pobreza. Como punto de partida se debe aceptar que un bajo coeficiente de inclusin financiera se asocia con altos ndices de pobreza. La exclusin de los mercados financieros formales que padecen an grandes ncleos de la poblacin, en Mxico y en el mundo, constituye uno de los ms frreos obstculos para la superacin de la pobreza. Es muy caro para quien es pobre no tener acceso a instrumentos de ahorro y crdito. Esto debido a que quienes 2 sufren la estrechez de recursos, padecen tambin severas restricciones para emprender negocios productivos, financiar proyectos de mejora del capital humano, planear a plazos razonables la adquisicin de una vivienda o para afrontar exitosamente adversidades y catstrofes naturales. En la cadena de perpetuacin de la pobreza, la falta de inclusin financiera es un eslabn que siempre est presente. Pero para romper ese eslabn, es preciso evitar dos errores conceptuales ms o menos frecuentes tanto entre economistas como entre quienes tienen a su cargo la ejecucin de polticas pblicas. El primero de estos errores consiste en suponer, con cierta arrogancia, que el problema principal de la falta de inclusin financiera es ante todo un problema de ndole educativa o cultural; es decir, que bastara emprender grandes campaas de educacin financiera para que los pobres descubriesen las bondades de la intermediacin financiera y, en consecuencia, acudiesen prestos a incorporarse como clientes a las instituciones financieras formales. Esto supone que cualquier 3 persona tiene acceso inmediato y sin costos a los servicios financieros, lo cual, a todas luces, no es el caso. Por otro lado, es comn encontrar la tesis de que los pobres no llevan a cabo cotidianamente transacciones financieras, bajo el argumento de que no tienen suficientes recursos. Nada ms falso. As como la intermediacin de recursos entre prestamistas y deudores es casi tan antigua como la misma historia de la humanidad, la actividad financiera es conocida y practicada de forma cotidiana por todos los grupos sociales en el mundo, sean ricos o pobres. Ya en 1979, al recibir el Premio Nobel de Economa el profesor Theodore W. Schultz llam la atencin sobre el hecho de que muchos economistas incurren en el error conceptual de pensar que la economa de la pobreza obedece a leyes y estndares diferentes que los aplicables al resto de la economa. No es as: la necesidad de aprovechar de la mejor manera los recursos escasos y aplicarlos con eficiencia es igualmente imperiosa para una gran empresa que para un minsculo negocio familiar. 4 La diferencia entre unos y otros, ricos y pobres, en lo fundamental no radica en la falta de conocimientos bsicos o de inters en obtener mejores condiciones de vida. La diferencia abismal entre quienes tienen acceso pleno a la intermediacin financiera moderna, eficiente, regulada, de carcter formal y quienes tienen que recurrir a mecanismos de ahorro ineficientes, caros, inciertos, carentes de regulacin y garantas, radica fundamentalmente en los elevadsimos costos de transaccin que los segundos deben afrontar. As pues, de los primeros pasos para enfrentar con acierto el gran problema de la exclusin financiera es conocer y entender los mltiples mecanismos de intermediacin financiera informal que el ingenio, la necesidad y las costumbres han creado en Mxico. Muchos de estos mecanismos, por ejemplo las tandas organizadas de forma espontnea en muchos centros de trabajo y colonias, son una respuesta a la necesidad de ahorrar y obtener crdito que tienen muchas familias. Este tipo de intermediacin financiera guarda semejanza con el 5 que hacan los comerciantes organizados en el Mxico antiguo en el gran mercado de Tlatelolco, quienes invertan sus excedentes en el patrocinio de festejos y convites que a la postre facilitaran su movilidad en una sociedad estratificada y rgida, como era aquella. Por tanto, el gran reto que tenemos las autoridades financieras es crear las condiciones para que estas necesidades de ahorro y financiamiento encuentren cauces modernos, confiables y eficientes que permitan evolucionar los modelos populares de ahorro y crdito hacia canales formales. Estas redes de intermediacin financiera formal deben abatir para el usuario los costos de transaccin. La reciente reforma financiera sin duda abona de manera significativa en este sentido. Se trata de derribar barreras de informacin, dar una mayor fuerza a la banca de desarrollo, facilitar la movilidad de los usuarios entre distintos intermediarios para aprovechar las mejores alternativas, fortalecer considerablemente la proteccin de los usuarios de los servicios financieros y multiplicar los puntos de acceso a los mismos. 6 A la par de la reforma financiera, hay otra reforma igualmente promovida por el gobierno del Presidente Pea Nieto que permitir explotar a plenitud el potencial tecnolgico en beneficio de una mayor inclusin financiera. Me refiero a la reforma en telecomunicaciones. Una mayor competencia en telecomunicaciones generar un importante abatimiento de los costos de transaccin en mltiples operaciones de intermediacin financiera, desde las bsicas hasta las ms complejas. Servicios de telecomunicacin ms baratos en costo, ms eficientes, con una cobertura geogrfica ms amplia y de mayor calidad significarn un acceso ms franco a la intermediacin financiera para la poblacin de menores recursos y, por ende, elevar las posibilidades de diversas operaciones financieras. Otro elemento crucial para sustentar una mayor inclusin financiera es la confianza. En este sentido, contar con fundamentos macroeconmicos estables y slidos a travs 7 tanto de una poltica fiscal responsable como de una monetaria empeada en la estabilidad del poder adquisitivo de la moneda, junto con el respeto constante al estado de derecho, son cimientos indispensables para extender la inclusin financiera, cimientos con los que Mxico cuenta ya. Sobre esa plataforma de confianza podemos emprender el gran desafo de masificar los mecanismos de intermediacin financiera, siguiendo una estrategia de constante y progresivo abatimiento de los costos de transaccin, a travs de una mejor regulacin y del uso pleno e inteligente de los avances tecnolgicos. Slo as, abatiendo de forma perdurable y sostenida los costos de transaccin y democratizando los beneficios de una intermediacin financiera moderna, podremos romper el crculo vicioso entre pobreza y exclusin financiera. Slo as  mediante las sinergias entre reformas estructurales, regulacin y polticas pblicas responsables y slidasterminaremos con la perversa paradoja de que no hay condicin ms cara y costosa que la de ser pobre. Muchas gracias. 8

Title: Participation in the event organized by The Aspen Institute
text: Remarks by Dr. Agustin Carstens, Governor of the Bank of Mexico, during his participation in the event organized by The Aspen Institute Mexico City, March 24, 2014 Good afternoon. First of all I want to thank Juan Ramon De la Fuente for his kind invitation to this event. As he said, I'm familiar with the Aspen Institute, I've been attending for about 10 years or more, not every year, but several times. to the World Economy forum in Aspen, and I can say that it is a forum of the highest quality. For me personally and professionally, it has contributed a lot. I would also like to salute and thank Walter Isaacson for the support he always gives to this program and, obviously, for having facilitated the Aspen Institute to move to Mexico. Let's say, then, that I've been involved in the discussions about the global economy at the Aspen Institute, and I think that precisely the state of the global economy is a good starting point for my comments, which are aimed at describing what the 1 challenges and opportunities that Mexico has in the immediate future and in the medium term. As I mentioned, a little over ten years ago, around the beginning of this century, I started attending the forums of the Aspen Institute and it has been really very interesting to see how the theme in those events has evolved. I remember that in the first meetings, around the years 2002 and 2003, still a topic that dominated the discussion was the situation of the emerging countries. In fact, the origin of that interest came, in some way, from 1994 with the crisis process that Mexico suffered at the end of that year, but also, then there was the Asian crisis, the crisis in Russia in 1998 and then there was a crisis in South America with Brazil and Argentina. Arguably, that is why the debate was always focused on the representatives of the emerging countries. First because the representatives of the advanced economies wanted to understand a little more about the pathologies, so to speak, of the emerging economies and also, of course, because they gave us a lot of advice on what we should do to establish better practices and so that our economies became reliable and we could enter a process of stability. 2 economic, which is a necessary but not sufficient condition for economic growth. Over the years, what was very curious is that somehow the roles were reversed. In 2008 crises began to emerge in advanced countries. No two crises are really exactly the same. Each crisis has its particularities, this because countries and their political institutions are different. However, at least from a scientific point of view (I must warn, by the way, that we economists, we like to consider ourselves scientists, although many do not think that possible), an effort can be made to try to identify what could be the causes of crises and it was always very interesting to discuss, for example, whether such causes were manifesting themselves in advanced countries. I think there is common ground there: we in emerging economies have learned the hard way, but at the end of the day we have learned that any financial crisis is the result of financial imbalances. These imbalances can often be generated over time, and giving signs that anticipate a crisis; but many other times the imbalances are generated 3 without one noticing them. In the end, in both cases, they end up in a situation where public finances are questioned, the stability of the currency is questioned, and the authorities have to do abnormal things to stabilize the macroeconomy and usually generate quite high social costs. Obviously without trying to draw an exact parallel, it can be said that the source of the crisis in 2007 was the weakness of the financial system in the United States, originating from novel and relatively bold financial practices. That, in turn, and because many other countries follow the leadership of the United States, led to those financial practices beginning to become widespread. Here I warn that from a point of view of the financial authority, something that is very important is always to think proactively, where the next financial crisis is going to come from; be cautious precisely when the environment is more optimistic and even euphoric. In this regard, I would dare to propose a simile taken from medicine. Here we have two brilliant doctors, Dr. Jose Narro and Dr. De la Fuente and with your permission let me tell you that banking crises are something very similar to sudden deaths whose origin is high blood pressure, hypertension, and there you 4 Doctors could correct me, but I think in the United States hypertension is called the silent killer. Well, something very similar happens with crises in the financial system: they are brewing silently, without previous and notorious discomforts that allow them to be anticipated and prevented. If you go back to the years from 2003 to 2006, you will remember that in the United States everything was going very well in appearance: interest rates were at an extraordinarily low level, there was a very high growth, many families were receiving credit for the first time, people were more "leveraged", that is: with greater borrowing capacity, therefore they bought more, and really that was seen as a new paradigm, in which many of the precautions that one usually must take, because they are simply not taken, because there is the conviction, more or less implicit, that things are now different. When one spoke with the authorities of the United States, already closer to the outbreak of the crisis, it is true that they were no longer so happy, but there was no great alarm either, because at the end of the day, the vulnerabilities in the system were given without there being a clear manifestation. For example, in crises of a more 5 traditional or typical, macroeconomic crises, such as those we had in Mexico, in the seventies and eighties of the last century, first there were very high fiscal deficits, then there were deficits in the balance of payments, very high inflations, and so on. That is: there were many more signals in advance, but in crises in the financial system, the truth is that before they burst, everyone feels very good, because credit is growing, the economy is growing. It is necessary that there is a clash or that there is a disturbance, an unusual phenomenon, almost like a black swan (like the simile used by Nassim Nicholas Taleb), and that this begins to detonate problems, a domino effect is generated until finally it is obvious to everyone that what has happened is very perverse. Something that was undoubtedly novel in the crisis of 2008-2009 was its global reach. What really surprised in a very important way was the degree of interconnectivity of the global financial system. It was also surprising, of course, the very high degree of leverage that had occurred and that has been occurring in both the regulated and unregulated financial systems. This combination of interconnection with very broad leverage facilities generated extreme vulnerability in all areas. 6 financial systems. In addition, the problem lay not only in the manifestation of the crisis itself, but in the high costs that society has to pay for a relatively long time. A large part of these costs are derived from the surprise factor, that is, when there is a crisis of this nature, such as an unanticipated crisis, the authorities are slow to make an accurate diagnosis and make the appropriate decisions to stabilize the situation, there are hesitations and in many of the advanced countries in mid-2008, some of the initial responses contributed more to destabilizing than stabilizing, as was the case with the bankruptcy of Lehman Brothers. And even when the ideal solutions are already reached to achieve greater stability, these solutions also generate consequences that last over time; consequences that to this day we still suffer. For example, most advanced countries adopted very aggressive fiscal and monetary policies; that certainly helped solve immediate problems and prevent further collapse, and they made very one-off interventions to prop up the most fragile financial institutions. However, on the other hand, weaknesses of a macroeconomic and more traditional nature were created, such as imbalances. 7 Tax. Thus, there was talk of public debt problems in advanced countries. Also when implementing unconventional monetary policies that also generated a whole series of problems, from which we still do not get out. In fact, we can draw an interesting parallel with the history of some crises in Mexico. We already know from experience that when there is a crisis of this nature, it takes seven or eight years to get out of it, but when many of these things were discussed in Aspen and the question arose of how long the crisis is going to last, many people said: "well, it's going to last three years." And, in fact, many of the fiscal responses were: "We are going to boost the economy fiscally for three years, then it will stabilize and then the private sector will continue to drive growth." With that idea in mind, several of the countercyclical measures were taken. But the reality is that we are already in 2014, six years have already passed and we still cannot declare that the period of crisis has been overcome. In fact we are still in a situation where the Federal Reserve in the United States has to start gradually undoing a monetary policy. 8 highly expansionist. A situation in which public finances have yet to be completed. In Europe, the global crisis really called into question the regime of a single currency. There, the question is whether a single currency can survive with a single instrument of coordination, which is monetary policy, when there is not necessarily coordination or clear and sufficiently strong rules in fiscal and banking matters. Europe, fortunately, has been moving in that direction lately; in fact last Friday there was good news about the process on the way to a banking union in Europe. But it is a process that is still underway and that is having repercussions on all countries of the world. This brings me to the current situation and the outlook for emerging economies. Certainly at first the crisis of 2008 found almost all emerging countries in very good circumstances. The vast majority of emerging countries did not have major macroeconomic imbalances, and a very important reason for this was precisely the fact that we had already gone through 9 those problems, we had already learned our lesson and had already done our homework. Thus, at first the consequences of the crisis were not so noticeable in the emerging economies, however, as time has progressed, it is much more difficult to say that the emerging countries are running in a different lane than the advanced countries. In fact, one of the issues that is affecting many emerging countries today is precisely that the economic slowdown and, above all, the corrective measures being taken by advanced countries, are affecting world economic growth, and are limiting the growth of emerging economies. According to the IMF, today the world economy is growing between 0.75 and one percentage point below its potential GDP, and that is certainly reflected in all economies, including of course emerging economies. So, it is very difficult to think that when the advanced countries that represent perhaps about 50% of the world's GDP are in a situation of weakness, the rest of the countries, including the emerging countries, will not be affected by that. Today, for example, the fact that Europe and the United States are in a process of 10 Fiscal consolidation, and the fact that there is a great effort at monetary normalization in the United States, also imply that emerging countries face headwinds. There are some emerging countries that have entered a more complex situation, in part, because after 2008, they somehow declared victory, thought they had more degrees of freedom than they actually had, and didn't take care of their economic fundamentals. All this led to a certain weakness, to the extent that to this day some emerging countries have had to make costly and important macroeconomic adjustments. Another issue that has added to this picture, and which has hindered the situation of the emerging countries, is the fact that China, which has been a very significant growth engine, especially after 2009, also incurred excesses from a macroeconomic point of view. Now, they have had to contain their economy, and have gone from growing from rates of more than 12 percent to rates of between 7 and 7.5 percent. All of that, given its size and low growth in advanced economies, has caused the prices of many commodities and commodities to fall, which has affected 11 several of the emerging economies, whose growth in recent years was strongly supported by the export of these goods. Although the emerging countries at the beginning of the global crisis came out relatively well spared, we now have very important challenges ahead. The main challenge is: how can economic growth in our countries be accelerated without jeopardizing financial stability? Let's look at the scenario again: one, we are living in a time of lower economic growth, largely because of what is happening outside of emerging economies. Two, the corrections that advanced economies are now making to the policies they resorted to to deal with the crisis in recent years are generating some degree of turbulence, especially as they begin to emerge from periods of historically low interest rates, which will now begin to rise or have already begun to rise in the case of long-term periods. Given this environment, the question is: how can emerging countries not only preserve stability but accelerate growth? And this question has an added one which is how to face, 12 in turn, a scenario where there will be higher interest rates globally. At the end of the day, in my opinion, there will be three key factors that emerging countries will have to concentrate on: 1.- They have to maintain very strong macroeconomic fundamentals. Today there is no room for weak economic fundamentals. This means, first, low inflations, and in this sense, and for the specific case of Mexico, we assume in the Bank of Mexico the responsibility that touches us. Today the inflation of the first half of March was announced and it is very good news that it has been, in annual terms, 3.89%. This means that, as we had anticipated, the initial shock of the tax reform and the increase in public transport fares in the largest cities, which brought inflation to an annual rate of 4.63 in the month of January, has been diluted; we are under the roof of our reference band. On the other hand, public debt must be preserved at sustainable levels, and in this field, the government has also made efforts and made clear commitments, especially through the law of fiscal responsibility. All the plans that have been made towards 13 in the medium term, they contemplate maintaining public debt at a sustainable level, so that Mexico's public indebtedness will be, even taking the broader definition of debt (which is the historical balance of the financial requirements of the public sector), below 40% of GDP. In the same area of macroeconomic fundamentals, it is very necessary to preserve the stability of the banking system and there I return to the issue of hypertension or the "silent killer". There we have to be us, the financial authorities, and the bankers themselves, very prudent in the way credit will expand. In Mexico there is a lot of room for the banking system to lend more and make a greater contribution to economic growth, but it must also be done very prudently. This aspect seems to me to be of the highest priority as well. On this first point, which is to maintain strong macroeconomic pillars, I believe that Mexico is doing relatively well. 2.- The second great pillar is to maintain the strength of the external sector and have the ability to face shocks from abroad. These shocks can come from price variations of some goods and 14 basic goods, or they could also arise through the reallocation of portfolios. How do you build that strength to deal with such clashes? First, with a floating exchange rate regime that is based on sound economic fundamentals; and that has really been the case as far as Mexico is concerned. In the last two or three months during which the currency markets have had some volatility, the peso has been well behaved; in fact, it has appreciated against virtually all the currencies of other emerging countries. Similarly, if one analyzes Mexico's sovereign risk, it has been improving if we evaluate it with market indicators or by the ratings of specialized agencies. The second component to building strength in the face of external shocks is having flexibility in interest rates. This is a very important point, especially in an environment where there may be portfolio adjustments. A third element is to have high international reserves, and there we also have historically high levels today, of around 180 billion dollars, in addition to the line of 15 flexible credit with the IMF, for approximately 73 billion dollars. Flexible credit lines are one of the few programs the IMF has for well-behaved countries, rather than exclusively on bailing out troubled economies. That is: the IMF sees that a country has a healthy macroeconomic program and grants it a line of credit so that it continues like this and can face shocks from abroad. This encourages the country itself, in order to keep that line of credit open, to strive to maintain its sound macroeconomic fundamentals. Thus, it is a good vehicle for countries to preserve their macroeconomic strength. In short, taking into account the flexible line of credit and reserves, we have more than 250 billion of "park," so to speak. On the other hand, both the public and private sectors have met their financing needs well; have taken good advantage of the circumstances of historically low interest rates in international financial markets to extend the terms of their debts and improve their conditions. So it does not seem that there are short-term financing needs that could be destabilizing. 16 3. The third pillar is to find a way to stimulate economic growth without losing macroeconomic stability or the strength of the balance of payments. That brings us to structural reforms. It is clear that in Mexico today we are immersed in the issue of reforms. I believe that it has been a great achievement for Mexico to have moved in this direction in recent months. For example, at the last G20 meeting in Sydney, Australia, the big commitment that countries made was to set a goal of stimulating global growth by two percentage points over the next five years. Among the measures identified for Mexico to contribute to that goal, we have already done so to a large extent through the structural reforms of recent months. This is a great advantage over the other members of that select group of countries. What the reforms seek is to change the structure of the Mexican economy to make it more competitive, which we are only achieving by increasing the total productivity of the factors of production in the country. That must translate into a better distribution of income. Obviously this process has not concluded, the task that remains pending is that the secondary laws that are approved are solid 17 and suitable for this purpose, send the right signals and establish the right incentives. In the end, there has to be a good implementation process. This is, in my opinion, the map that emerging countries must follow to navigate this time of low global growth and with a scenario of potential instability in financial markets. In Mexico it seems to me that we have a well-planned horizon, we have a plan that has a lot of potential going forward. Of course, the path is not always as smooth and smooth as one would like, but generally speaking the direction we are taking is the right one. So I hope that it is a matter of time before these reforms that we have agreed to begin to generate much clearer signals and to convince everyone, especially ourselves Mexicans, that we have everything we need to build a very good future. Thanks a lot. 18
