Title: Inauguration of the Fourth National Convention of AFORES
text: Remarks by Mr. Alejandro Diaz de Leon, Governor of the Bank of Mexico, during the inauguration of the Fourth National Convention of AFORES. Arturo Herrera, Secretary of Finance and Public Credit; Bernardo Gonzalez, President of the Mexican Association of AFORES, (AMAFORE); Abraham Vela, President of the National Commission of the Retirement Savings System (CONSAR); Zoe Robledo, Director General of the Mexican Social Security Institute; Ladies and gentlemen, Deputies and Senators; Presidents of the regulatory bodies of the financial sector and leaders of guilds and associations; Directors of the Retirement Fund Administrators; Ladies and gentlemen: 1 I am very pleased to participate in this Fourth National Convention of Retirement Fund Administrators (Afores). Pension funds have a mission of social justice for the benefit of those who complete their work and, in turn, contribute to the effective operation of labour markets and the economy as a whole. In recent decades, global demographic trends, technological evolution and accelerated changes in labor markets have forced pension systems to adapt in order to ensure their financial sustainability and the fulfillment of their social objectives. In Mexico, more than 20 years ago, the Social Security Law was reformed and a pension system was established that replaced the defined benefit scheme with one of defined contributions. This change was extended in 2007 for a large part of the workers in the public sector. Although the system of defined contribution pensions with full asset control of workers is adequate, 2 The system still faces significant challenges. In particular, it is necessary to move forward with measures that consolidate the empowerment of workers and place them at the center of the system. The long period of time and uncertainty surrounding retirement make it necessary to have a system that accompanies workers throughout their working lives, so that they can plan and save for their retirement stage. To this end, the most common strategy has been to develop retirement systems that contemplate the mandatory savings of workers, employers and the State. However, the challenge is not only the contribution of resources, since the remoteness with which most workers perceive retirement leads to a lack of vigilance and monitoring towards the intermediaries who manage their resources. Thus, while in the administration of voluntary savings, savers take a more active attitude to choose and monitor the performance of the institutions to which they entrust their resources, in a mandatory savings scheme these incentives are significantly reduced, which tends to lead to a lower quality of services and fiduciary management that the worker receives. Thus, in 3 multiple times, in a relatively closed system, market forces and innovation operate weakly and insufficiently. Therefore, the regulation must seek the best way to correct these distortions and introduce the appropriate measures to bring the costs and quality of services closer to that of the voluntary. Beyond the regulation, it is essential that the guild of administrators fully assumes the responsibility of serving the workers in the best possible way. In this sense, the union must not only comply with the regulation and its own corporate goals, but act proactively and adopt international best practices to carry out its fiduciary mission and contribute to improving the retirement conditions of millions of workers. Let me refer to some key elements that must be present in a functional retirement savings system, sustainable over time and that promotes the full empowerment of workers. 4 One: the system should promote labour mobility and flexibility in favour of promoting greater productivity and efficiency in the use of the economy's resources. For example, it is important to ensure that labour migration between different sectors does not undermine the conditions of retirement, which points to the full universality of the system. Two: the system must give workers clear and well-defined rights over their resources, so that they constitute an incentive to the formation of a patrimony throughout their working life. In this regard, technology offers unprecedented opportunities to promote greater proximity of managers and authority with the worker, offering timely and accessible information about their resources and expanding their range of options. Three: the system must encourage both workers and employers to contribute to consolidating retirement savings. This encourages co-responsibility and generates incentives for voluntary savings. 5 Four: the system must provide workers with excellent fiduciary and resource management, equivalent to that of the largest private investors. This means making the most of the investment regime's options and permanently modernizing it to maintain portfolios that offer attractive returns in a sustainable manner. This also means overcoming lags and achieving greater agility. Responses have sometimes been slow: for example, the adoption of reference portfolios took several years, when it is an essential element of current retirement fund management. Five: the system should seek that the areas of housing and retirement interact flexibly and help the worker both to build their real estate assets and to increase their income when they retire, according to their needs and preferences. Six: the system must ensure that its contribution parameters in amount and frequency are those necessary for the worker's pension requirements. In this regard, it is essential to stimulate voluntary contributions with appropriate incentives and greater flexibility. 6 in its management, as well as analyzing the possibility of gradually increasing contributions, making aware that small increases can translate into a better retirement situation. Seven: The system should focus on providing a comprehensive and top-notch offering in its financial and fund management services, rather than focusing efforts on business strategies. Eight: the system must ensure that the options of annuity and scheduled retirement are more flexible and allow the worker to combine them so that he can reach the pattern of pension flows that best reflects his needs in the different stages of his retirement. Nine: the system must promote greater competition, more information and better services, as well as contribute to overcoming behavioral biases, so that workers have more and better alternatives to build their wealth and have greater control of the conditions at the time of retirement. 7 A system such as the one described, which empowers workers, not only results in benefits for them, but, by promoting increasing savings over time, provides greater and better opportunities for employment and economic growth. The Afores play a key role in achieving the aforementioned elements and, in general, for the future viability of the pension system. These entities face the permanent challenge of improving their operation and establishing financial strategies and suitable incentives to more efficiently mediate the resources of workers, capture more voluntary savings and offer an adequate balance between profitability and safety. Therefore, I note with interest that, in this year's program, the Convention contemplates the discussion of key issues in the evolution of pension systems, such as, among others: i. the pending reforms to improve the scheme in Latin America; ii. new trends and investment options for retirement fund managers; 8 iii. how certain approaches to economic science, such as behavioral economics, can be leveraged to encourage voluntary savings in retirement systems; and iv. sustainable investments that more closely link financial decisions with their impact on the environment and society. This, by the way, is a fundamental topic that has gathered the attention of authorities and businessmen around the world and in which the Bank of Mexico has been actively participating, through the "Network of Central Banks and Supervisory Authorities to Green the Financial System" (NGFS), of which it is a founding member. Undoubtedly, from this exchange of experiences between pension administrators, public officials, representatives of international organizations and prestigious economists, including the 1997 Nobel Prize in Economics, Professor Robert C. Merton, many ideas can be extracted to face the challenges and take advantage of the opportunities of pension systems. This is crucial for the well-being of workers and for the economic development of the country. Thank you very much and congratulations. 9
text_original: Palabras del Lic. Alejandro Daz de Len, Gobernador del Banco de Mxico, durante la inauguracin de la Cuarta Convencin Nacional de AFORES. Arturo Herrera, Secretario de Hacienda y Crdito Pblico; Bernardo Gonzlez, Presidente de la Asociacin Mexicana de AFORES, (AMAFORE); Abraham Vela, Presidente de La Comisin Nacional del Sistema del Ahorro para el Retiro, (CONSAR); Zoe Robledo, Director General del Instituto Mexicano del Seguro Social; Seoras y seores Diputados y Senadores; Seores Presidentes de los rganos reguladores del sector financiero y lderes de gremios y asociaciones; Seores Directores de las Administradoras de Fondos para el Retiro; Seoras y seores: 1 Me da mucho gusto participar en esta Cuarta Convencin Nacional de Administradoras de Fondos para el Retiro (Afores). Los fondos de pensiones tienen una misin de justicia social en beneficio de quienes culminan su etapa laboral y, a su vez, contribuyen a una operacin eficaz de los mercados de trabajo y de la economa en su conjunto. En las ltimas dcadas, las tendencias demogrficas globales, la evolucin tecnolgica y los acelerados cambios en los mercados de trabajo han obligado a adecuar los sistemas de pensiones, a fin de asegurar su sustentabilidad financiera y el cumplimiento de sus objetivos sociales. En Mxico, hace ms de 20 aos se reform la Ley del Seguro Social y se estableci un sistema de pensiones que sustituy el esquema de beneficios definidos con uno de contribuciones definidas. Este cambio se extendi en 2007 para gran parte de los trabajadores del sector pblico. Si bien el sistema de pensiones de contribuciones definidas con un pleno control patrimonial de los trabajadores es el adecuado, dicho 2 sistema todava enfrenta importantes retos. En particular, es necesario avanzar con medidas que consoliden el empoderamiento de los trabajadores y que los coloquen en el centro del sistema. El amplio periodo de tiempo y la incertidumbre que rodea al retiro hacen necesario un sistema que acompae a los trabajadores durante toda su vida laboral, a fin de que puedan planear y ahorrar para su etapa de jubilacin. Para ello, la estrategia ms comn ha sido desarrollar sistemas para el retiro que contemplan el ahorro obligatorio tanto de los trabajadores, como de los empleadores y el Estado. Sin embargo, el reto no slo consiste en la aportacin de recursos, ya que la lejana con la que la mayora de los trabajadores percibe el retiro propicia falta de vigilancia y monitoreo hacia los intermediarios que administran sus recursos. De este modo, mientras en la administracin del ahorro voluntario, los ahorradores toman una actitud ms activa para elegir y vigilar el desempeo de las instituciones a las que confan sus recursos, en un esquema de ahorro obligatorio estos incentivos se reducen significativamente, lo que tiende a propiciar una menor calidad de los servicios y de la gestin fiduciaria que recibe el trabajador. As, en 3 mltiples ocasiones, en un sistema relativamente cerrado, las fuerzas de mercado y la innovacin operan de manera dbil e insuficiente. Por ello, la regulacin debe buscar la mejor manera de corregir estas distorsiones e introducir las medidas idneas para acercar los costos y la calidad de los servicios del ahorro obligatorio al del voluntario. Ms all de la regulacin, es imprescindible que el gremio de las administradoras asuma cabalmente la responsabilidad de servir de la mejor manera posible a los trabajadores. En este sentido, el gremio no slo debe cumplir con la regulacin y sus propias metas corporativas, sino actuar proactivamente y adoptar las mejores prcticas internacionales para realizar su misin fiduciaria y contribuir a mejorar las condiciones de retiro de millones de trabajadores. Permtanme referirme a algunos elementos clave que deben estar presentes en un sistema de ahorro para el retiro funcional, sostenible en el tiempo y que promueva el cabal empoderamiento de los trabajadores. 4 Uno: el sistema debe promover la movilidad y flexibilidad laboral en favor de la promocin de una mayor productividad y eficiencia en el uso de los recursos de la economa. Por ejemplo, es importante procurar que la migracin laboral entre distintos sectores no obre en perjuicio de las condiciones del retiro lo que apunta a la cabal universalidad del sistema. Dos: el sistema debe otorgar a los trabajadores derechos claros y bien definidos sobre sus recursos, a fin de que constituyan un incentivo a la formacin de un patrimonio a lo largo de su vida laboral. Al respecto, la tecnologa ofrece oportunidades inditas para fomentar la mayor proximidad de las administradoras y de la autoridad con el trabajador, ofrecindole informacin puntual y accesible sobre sus recursos y ampliando su abanico de opciones. Tres: el sistema debe propiciar que tanto trabajadores como empleadores contribuyan a consolidar el ahorro para el retiro. Esto fomenta la corresponsabilidad y genera estmulos para el ahorro voluntario. 5 Cuatro: el sistema debe proveer a los trabajadores de una gestin fiduciaria y de administracin de recursos de excelencia, equivalente con la que cuentan los mayores inversionistas privados. Ello implica aprovechar al mximo las opciones del rgimen de inversin y modernizarlo permanentemente para mantener portafolios que ofrezcan rendimientos atractivos de manera sostenible. Ello tambin implica superar rezagos y alcanzar mayor agilidad. A veces, las respuestas han sido lentas: por ejemplo, la adopcin de los portafolios de referencia tard varios aos, cuando sta constituye un elemento esencial de la administracin de fondos para el retiro actual. Cinco: el sistema debe buscar que los rubros de vivienda y retiro interacten con flexibilidad y ayuden al trabajador tanto a construir su patrimonio inmobiliario como a incrementar sus ingresos al retirarse, de acuerdo a sus necesidades y preferencias. Seis: el sistema debe propiciar que sus parmetros de contribucin en monto y frecuencia sean los necesarios para los requerimientos pensionarios del trabajador. Al respecto, es indispensable estimular las aportaciones voluntarias con incentivos adecuados y mayor flexibilidad 6 en su manejo, as como analizar la posibilidad de aumentar gradualmente las contribuciones, haciendo conciencia de que pequeos incrementos pueden traducirse en una mejor situacin de retiro. Siete: el sistema debe enfocarse en brindar una oferta integral y de primer orden en sus servicios financieros y de administracin de fondos, ms que enfocar esfuerzos en estrategias comerciales. Ocho: el sistema debe procurar que las opciones de renta vitalicia y retiro programado sean ms flexibles y le permitan al trabajador combinarlas de manera que pueda alcanzar el patrn de flujos pensionarios que mejor refleje sus necesidades en las distintas etapas de su retiro. Nueve: el sistema debe promover mayor competencia, ms informacin y mejores servicios, as como contribuir a superar sesgos conductuales, a fin de que los trabajadores cuenten con ms y mejores alternativas para construir su patrimonio y tengan un mayor control de las condiciones al momento del retiro. 7 Un sistema como el descrito, que empodera a los trabajadores, no slo redunda en beneficios para estos, sino que, al propiciar un ahorro creciente a lo largo del tiempo, provee mayores y mejores oportunidades de empleo y crecimiento econmico. Las Afores juegan un papel clave para alcanzar los elementos antes mencionados y, en general, para la viabilidad futura del sistema de pensiones. Estas entidades enfrentan el desafo permanente de mejorar su operacin y establecer estrategias financieras e incentivos idneos para intermediar ms eficientemente los recursos de los trabajadores, captar ms ahorro voluntario y ofrecer un balance adecuado entre rentabilidad y seguridad. Por eso, observo con inters que, en el programa de este ao, la Convencin contempla la discusin de temas torales en la evolucin de los sistemas de pensiones, como son, entre otros: i. las reformas pendientes para mejorar el esquema en Amrica Latina; ii. las nuevas tendencias y opciones de inversin para administradoras de fondos de retiro; 8 iii. la forma en que pueden aprovecharse ciertos enfoques de la ciencia econmica, como la economa conductual, para fomentar el ahorro voluntario en los sistemas para el retiro, y iv. las inversiones sustentables que vinculan ms estrechamente las decisiones financieras con su impacto en el medio ambiente y la sociedad. Este, por cierto, es un tpico fundamental que ha reunido la atencin de autoridades y empresarios de todo el mundo y en el cual el Banco de Mxico viene participando activamente, a travs de la Red de Bancos Centrales y Autoridades Supervisoras para Enverdecer el Sistema Financiero (NGFS por sus siglas en ingls), de la cual es miembro fundador. Sin duda, de este intercambio de experiencias entre administradores de pensiones, funcionarios pblicos, representantes de organismos internacionales y prestigiados economistas, entre ellos el Premio Nobel de Economa 1997, el profesor Robert C. Merton, podrn extraerse muchas ideas para afrontar los retos y aprovechar las oportunidades de los sistemas de pensiones. Ello es crucial para el bienestar de los trabajadores y para el desarrollo econmico del pas. Muchas gracias y felicidades. 9

Title: Panel: importance of price information systems in the agricultural sector, at the event commemorating the 60th anniversary of FIRA
text: WORDS OF MR. JAVIER GUZMaN CALAFELL, DEPUTY GOVERNOR OF THE BANK OF MEXICO, AS MODERATOR OF THE PANEL "IMPORTANCE OF PRICE INFORMATION SYSTEMS IN THE AGRICULTURAL SECTOR", AT THE COMMEMORATIVE EVENT OF THE 60TH ANNIVERSARY OF FIRA. Morelia, Michoacan, December 11, 2014.1 I would like first of all to extend my most sincere congratulations to all those who, throughout these 60 years, have contributed to making FIRA a fundamental institution for the development of the rural, agricultural, forestry and fishing sectors of our country. I am sure that through its valuable work of granting credits and guarantees, training, technical assistance and technology transfer, FIRA will continue to occupy a role of great importance in the Mexican economy for many years to come. I would also like to thank the panelists of this session for accepting the invitation to share with us their views and experiences on price information systems and their importance for the agricultural sector. The proper development of the agricultural sector of our country faces a great diversity of challenges. The availability of, and access to, information is undoubtedly one of the most important. Free and widespread access to relevant information is key to the proper functioning of any market. However, the evidence shows that the reality in which our agricultural producers and their communities operate is far from this ideal scenario. In fact, the 1 The opinions contained in this document are the sole responsibility of the author and do not necessarily coincide with those of the Governing Board of the Bank of Mexico. 1 marked asymmetries in access to information at different stages of the production chain represent an important source of inefficiencies throughout it. The problem is even more serious if one takes into account the sharp fluctuations to which the prices of agricultural and livestock products are subject. Although this high volatility is due to a wide range of factors, both internal and external, the fact is that the uncertainty that derives from it has important adverse effects not only on production, investment and resource allocation decisions in the sector, but also on the well-being of our producers and their families. The inefficiencies and distortions in the production process introduced by this greater uncertainty can be reflected in turn in a greater volatility of the prices of these products, thus generating a vicious circle that could be difficult to break. Given this scenario, the challenge for public policy and other actors in the sector is clearly posed: how to equip our producers with more and better information, in such a way that their decision-making contributes to greater efficiency and well-being? This is especially relevant for the agricultural sector, given its importance from an economic and social development perspective. In this regard, it is worth mentioning that, according to the World Bank, poverty reduction actions in the agricultural sector are effective in raising the income levels of poor families by about four times 2 superior to those implemented in other sectors.2 The case of Mexico illustrates very clearly the urgent need to find solutions to improve efficiency, productivity and well-being in this sector. Our country has a poverty rate of about 46 percent; in the case of rural areas, the corresponding figure is 62 per cent. Similarly, while the agricultural sector accounts for approximately 13 per cent of the country's employed population, this sector accounts for less than 3 per cent of GDP. Undoubtedly, the development of appropriate information systems is a fundamental pillar to address the inefficiencies that affect the agricultural sector. The availability of timely and relevant information, as well as adequate means of communicating it, has always played a crucial role for agriculture and livestock activities. However, the current context of highly interconnected markets, both nationally and globally, has increased its importance. Likewise, the high prevalence of small-scale producers, who must operate as part of production chains increasing in complexity, makes information systems an increasingly necessary tool for the orderly and efficient functioning of these markets. In addition, given the nature of agricultural activities, they are constantly subject to a variety of shocks, which can cause serious disturbances in their operation. It is clear that the 2 Ver World Bank (2011): "ICT in agriculture: Connecting smallholders to knowledge, networks, and institutions", Report No. 64605, November. 3 Availability of timely and accurate information is very useful for the planning and execution of public policies in the face of such contingencies. Although the prices of agricultural inputs and products are key pieces of information for decision-making by producers and other actors in this sector, it is important to emphasize that the development of comprehensive information systems must incorporate other elements. These include local and global trends in the supply of agricultural products, both on the production and inventory sides, as well as their demand, whether for consumption or storage. Likewise, the availability of statistics on the evolution of the financial derivatives markets of these products, such as options and futures, can provide valuable information on the expected trajectory of their spot prices. More extensive information systems could even incorporate projections on weather, water and demographic conditions.3 For an agricultural market information system to fully fulfill its purpose, it must have a number of characteristics. These include: 4 (1) that the information is timely, an element of particular relevance in a context of highly dynamic markets; (2) that the information is accurate, as the lack of this attribute results in information of zero or even negative value; (3) that the information is accessible and not only available, in the sense that 3 Ver Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations et al. (2011): "Price volatility in food and agricultural markets: Policy responses", Policy Report to the G-20, June. 4 Ver John J. VanSickle y Thomas J. Stevens (1989): "Market information systems: An online agricultural market news retrieval system", Southern Journal of Agricultural Economics, Vol. 21(2):195-201, December. 4 can be used by users with a wide variety of technical capabilities for proper interpretation; and (4) that their acquisition, allocation and use are efficient. Inevitably, this implies a series of challenges on a large scale and on multiple levels. On the one hand, an effort is needed at the national level, involving different actors from both the public and private sectors.5 On the other hand, the multidimensional nature of the problem of information in agriculture requires a comprehensive approach. This implies efforts that go beyond the mere availability of information, since its impact on the functioning of these markets depends on various factors, such as the educational level and technical capacity of the users of the information, as well as their access to, and aptitude for the use of, financial services.6 An illustrative case is the use of information technologies. The potential of mobile telephony and the Internet as a tool for disseminating information in the agricultural sector is enormous, but their usefulness is modest in the absence of the technical or economic capacity to use them. Simultaneously with these efforts at the national level, the global nature of agricultural markets calls for actions in the same direction at the multilateral and inter-institutional levels. In this regard, it highlights the recent initiative of the G-20 to operationalize the AMIS system 5 Ver Steven Wolf, David Just y David Zilberman (2001): "Between data and decisions: The organization of agricultural economic information systems", Research Policy Vol. 30(1):121-141, January. 6 Ver Jabir Ali y Sushil Kumar (2011): "Information and communication technologies (ICTs) and farmers' decision-making across the agricultural supply chain", International Journal of Information Management Vol. 31(2):149-159, April. 5 (Agricultural Market Information System),7 a collaborative information platform that seeks to improve transparency in the markets of some food products, as well as to promote the coordination of policy actions in response to periods of uncertainty in them. While AMIS represents an important step in the right direction, the still limited scope in its coverage, both in terms of products and regions, means that there is ample way forward in this area. Surely exchanges of ideas such as those that we are preparing to carry out today, will be very useful to set the tone to move forward. 7 Ver Agricultural Market Information System (2011): "Enhancing market transparency", November. 6

Inevitablemente, lo anterior implica una serie de retos a gran escala y en mltiples niveles. De manera simultnea a estos esfuerzos a nivel nacional, la naturaleza global de los mercados de productos agropecuarios, llama a acciones en el mismo sentido a escala multilateral e interinstitucional. Title: Opening of the exhibition: The money of the insurgents and revolutionaries; 800 coins, two revolutions and one nation
text: Remarks by the Governor of the Bank of Mexico, Dr. Agustin Carstens, during the inauguration of the exhibition "The money of the insurgents and revolutionaries; 800 coins, two revolutions and one nation" in the Interactive Museum of Economy (MIDE), within the framework of the Bicentennial of Independence and the Centennial of the Mexican Revolution. November 29, 2010. Good night. The Bank of Mexico is particularly honored by the presence of all of you here, in these beautiful and historic facilities of the Interactive Museum of Economy, on the occasion of the inauguration of the exhibition "The money of the insurgents and revolutionaries". I thank Mr. Jose Manuel Villalpando, national executive coordinator of the organizing committee of the 2010 commemorations, for his presence here tonight to formalize the opening of this vast exhibition of coins and banknotes that witnessed the two great transformative episodes in the history of our country. It is also an honor to have the presence of the president of the Association of Banks of Mexico, engineer Ignacio Deschamps. Welcome. I would also like to mention the collaboration of the Mint, which has been decisive in bringing together this rich and varied sample not only of numismatics but also of the issuance of dissimilar banknotes, which arose around Independence and the Mexican Revolution. Everyone is welcome. Ladies and gentlemen: Due to the incalculable historical interest and the great cultural value of the exhibition that in a few moments we will have the opportunity to visit and contemplate, it is amply justified that the Bank of Mexico has organized and made it possible. Throughout its 85 years of life, the Central Institute has constantly promoted and encouraged everything that contributes to spreading the richness of our history and to exalting our cultural values. For the Bank of Mexico, an exhibition of this nature also represents a very valuable opportunity to share with the public some reflections on the crucial importance of legal tender money in the life of nations and, specifically, in these 200 years of life of Mexico. The contemplation of these historical pieces will probably raise in many of the visitors a set of questions and concerns about the meaning and usefulness of legal tender money. Hence, the MIDE, a museum designed to make clearer and kinder the spread of economic and financial culture among the general public of all ages and conditions, is an unbeatable setting for this exhibition. The 800 coins and banknotes on display have in common that they revolve around the two central milestones of Mexico's history, Independence and Revolution. These are periods that were inevitably violent and abrupt, while being pregnant with ideals and hopes, which when served through constructive efforts managed to transcend to become permanent. The coins and banknotes of this exhibition show both contrasting faces: the violent face connatural to a rupture of the order hitherto established and the luminous face of the longings to build a better country for all. To the same extent that the struggle for Independence and the protracted revolutionary struggles sought to transform, once and for all, the existing legal and social order - because that and no other is the ultimate meaning that in the history of ideas has the word "revolution" - the first coins and banknotes that emerged from such crucibles were born condemned to be precarious money and ephemeral life. Take the case of the coins and banknotes that sprang from the forge of revolutionary struggles; the vast majority ended up being viewed by the public with justified suspicion and distrust. That abundant and multicolored sheet litter of paper money issued by various political leaders, military leaders, municipal and state authorities, and even by individuals clever in the scrambled river of the contests, ended up being baptized by popular ingenuity with the derogatory nickname of "bilimbiques". There were so many more banknote issues, the less value they reached as effective means of payment, because of the deep distrust that caused such excessive proliferation. It is not idle to notice, along with the artistic beauty of some of the pieces in this exhibition, the tragic character that some of these coinages and broadcasts suffered. The reason for this unfortunate fate was, in most cases, that behind such coins and banknotes there was no confidence-generating monetary authority that guaranteed their value in spite of all the vicissitudes. And there was no such monetary authority because the issuance and coinage, in those turbulent times, were seen as mere tools for this or that faction to become as soon as possible of resources to continue the fight or even so that the troops, some of them totally improvised and fortuitous, could drive away hunger. And there was no shortage of cases in which paper money was issued as a supposedly legal parapet to justify exactions or looting. Against the background of these considerations, the question of what is the meaning and raison d'etre of the issuance of legal tender money in a society that aspires to be free, prosperous and equitable is logical. Which leads us, almost inevitably, to reflect on what a modern central bank should be, how it should fulfill its mission of providing legal tender to a nation, in such a way that it fully complies with the mandates that that same Nation through the law has given it. The answer is clear: a modern central bank, at the service of a free and democratic nation that aspires to be ever more prosperous and equitable, must be a formidable generator of confidence in the present and in the future. Money is one of the great inventions of human ingenuity, an invention comparable perhaps to the invention of language, which must serve to unite, measure and preserve. These tasks can only be accomplished by money when it instills trust among its users. Economists usually list at least three primordial functions of money: it must be a means of exchange, which allows to unite to different wills, the will of the one who buys with the will of the one who sells; it must also be a unit of account that makes it possible to nominate under a single monetary sign the most varied goods, including intangible or non-material goods, count them and keep a specific record not only of their existence but of the value that we have agreed to give them in the markets who we buy and who sell; and in addition, and this is a crucial function for sustainable well-being, money must be a deposit or store of value, a safe and faithful safeguard of assets, which facilitates and encourages both savings and credit, which allows the formation of wealth to the extent that said money - expressed in a monetary sign worthy of universal trust - retains its purchasing power over time. To fully fulfill this mission of invariable generator of trust, and expectations of stability for the future, a modern central bank must be an example of transparent communication. Hence, increasingly, especially in an inflation targeting scheme that is according to which most central banks in the world operate, timely communication - aimed at founding and forming expectations among the public - is seen as an indispensable tool of monetary policy. Let us consider, to conclude, that the sometimes tragic history of some of the historical pieces that we are going to contemplate had, in the case of Mexico, and over the years, a venturous end in which the face of the foundation and construction of institutions prevailed, at last, with the creation in 1925 of the long-awaited Banco unico de Emision that is today the Bank of Mexico. The ideal proposed by the constituents of 1917 could thus be fulfilled. And today, at 85 years old from the founding of the Central Bank and one hundred years after the beginning of the revolutionary struggles, the Bank of Mexico aspires decisively to be that great generator of confidence. The bank's priority mandate, which is to ensure price stability, ultimately translates into a clear and inescapable mission: to contribute without hesitation to economic growth by sowing every day the indispensable ingredient for the sustained well-being of a nation. That ingredient is confidence in the present and in the future, based on the stability of the purchasing power of the money that the Central Bank puts into circulation. Thanks a lot.
text_original: Palabras del Gobernador del Banco de Mxico, doctor Agustn Carstens, durante la inauguracin de la exposicin El dinero de los insurgentes y revolucionarios; 800 monedas, dos revoluciones y una Nacin en el Museo Interactivo de Economa (MIDE), en el marco del Bicentenario de la Independencia y del Centenario de la Revolucin Mexicana. 29 de noviembre de 2010. Buenas noches. El Banco de Mxico se siente particularmente honrado con la presencia de todos ustedes aqu, en estas hermosas e histricas instalaciones del Museo Interactivo de Economa, con motivo de la inauguracin de la exposicin El dinero de los insurgentes y revolucionarios. Agradezco al licenciado Jos Manuel Villalpando, coordinador ejecutivo nacional de la comisin organizadora de las conmemoraciones de 2010, su presencia aqu esta noche para formalizar la apertura de esta vasta muestra de monedas y billetes que fueron testigos de los dos grandes episodios transformadores de la historia de nuestro pas. Tambin es un honor contar con la presencia del presidente de la Asociacin de Bancos de Mxico, ingeniero Ignacio Deschamps. Bienvenido. Deseo mencionar, tambin , la colaboracin de la Casa de Moneda que ha sido decisiva para conjuntar esta rica y variada muestra no slo de la numismtica sino tambin de la emisin de dismbolos billetes, surgidos alrededor de la Independencia y de la Revolucin Mexicana. Sean bienvenidos todos. Seoras y seores: Por el incalculable inters histrico y el gran valor cultural que tiene la exposicin que en unos momentos tendremos oportunidad de recorrer y contemplar, se justifica sobradamente que el Banco de Mxico la haya organizado y hecho posible. El Instituto Central a lo largo de sus 85 aos de vida constantemente ha promovido y alentado todo aquello que contribuya a difundir la riqueza de nuestra historia y a enaltecer nuestros valores culturales. Para el Banco de Mxico una exposicin de esta naturaleza representa, adems, una oportunidad valiossima para compartir con todo el pblico algunas reflexiones sobre la importancia crucial del dinero de curso legal en la vida de las naciones y, especficamente, en estos 200 aos de vida de Mxico. La contemplacin de estas piezas histricas probablemente suscitar en muchos de los visitantes un conjunto de preguntas e inquietudes acerca del significado y la utilidad del dinero de curso legal. De ah que el MIDE, un museo concebido para hacer ms clara y amable la propagacin de la cultura econmica y financiera entre el gran pblico de todas las edades y condiciones, sea un marco inmejorable para esta exposicin. Las 800 monedas y billetes exhibidos tienen en comn que giran alrededor de los dos hitos centrales de la historia de Mxico, la Independencia y la Revolucin. Se trata de periodos que fueron inevitablemente violentos y abruptos, a la vez que estuvieron preados de ideales y esperanzas, que cuando fueron servidos mediante afanes constructivos lograron trascender hasta volverse permanentes. Las monedas y billetes de esta exposicin muestran ambos rostros contrastantes: la faz violenta connatural a una ruptura del orden hasta entonces establecido y el rostro luminoso de los anhelos por edificar un mejor pas para todos. En la misma medida que la lucha por la Independencia y las prolongadas contiendas revolucionarias buscaron transformar, de una vez por todas, el orden jurdico y social existente  porque se y no otro es el significado ltimo que en la historia de las ideas tiene la palabra revolucin- , las primeras monedas y billetes que surgieron de tales crisoles nacieron condenadas a ser dinero precario y de vida efmera. Tomemos el caso de las monedas y billetes que brotaron de la fragua de las luchas revolucionarias; la gran mayora terminaron siendo vistos por el pblico con justificado recelo y desconfianza. Esa abundante y multicolor hojarasca de papel moneda emitida por diversos caudillos polticos, cabecillas militares, autoridades municipales y estatales, y hasta por particulares avispados en el ro revuelto de las contiendas, acab por ser bautizada por el ingenio popular con el despectivo mote de bilimbiques. Tantas ms emisiones de billetes haba, tanto menos valor alcanzaban como efectivos medios de pago, a causa de la profunda desconfianza que provocaba tan desmedida proliferacin. No es ocioso advertir, junto con la belleza artstica de algunas de las piezas de esta exhibicin, el carcter trgico que algunas de estas acuaciones y emisiones padecieron. La razn que explica ese destino desafortunado fue, en la mayora de los casos, que detrs de tales monedas y billetes no existi una autoridad monetaria generadora de confianza que garantizara su valor a despecho de todas las vicisitudes. Y no hubo tal autoridad monetaria porque la emisin y acuacin, en esos tiempos convulsos, fueron vistas como meras herramientas para que tal o cual faccin se hiciese lo ms pronto posible de recursos para proseguir la lucha o incluso para que las tropas, algunas de ellas totalmente improvisadas y fortuitas, pudiesen ahuyentar el hambre. Y no faltaron los casos en que el papel moneda se emiti como parapeto presuntamente legal para justificar exacciones o saqueos. Como trasfondo de estas consideraciones resulta lgica la pregunta sobre cul es el sentido y la razn de ser de la emisin de dinero de curso legal en una sociedad que aspira a ser libre, prspera y equitativa. Lo cual nos conduce, casi inevitablemente, a reflexionar sobre lo que debe ser un banco central moderno, cmo debe cumplir su misin de dotar de dinero de curso legal a una nacin, de forma tal que cumpla cabalmente con los mandatos que esa misma Nacin a travs de la ley le ha dado. La respuesta es clara: un banco central moderno, al servicio de una nacin libre y democrtica que aspira a ser cada vez ms prspera y equitativa, debe ser un formidable generador de confianza en el presente y en el porvenir. El dinero es uno de los grandes inventos del ingenio humano, invento equiparable tal vez a la invencin del lenguaje, que debe servir para unir, medir y conservar. Estas tareas slo puede lograrlas el dinero cuando infunde confianza entre sus usuarios. Los economistas solemos enumerar al menos tres funciones primordiales del dinero: debe ser medio de cambio, que permita unir a voluntades diversas, la voluntad de quien compra con la voluntad de quien vende; debe ser, tambin, unidad de cuenta que haga posible nominar bajo un solo signo monetario los ms variados bienes, incluso bienes intangibles o no materiales, contarlos y llevar un registro puntual no slo de su existencia sino del valor que hemos convenido darles en los mercados quienes compramos y quienes vendemos; y adems, y esta es una funcin crucial para el bienestar sostenible, el dinero debe ser depsito o almacn de valor, resguardo seguro y fiel de los haberes, que facilite y propicie tanto el ahorro como el crdito, que permita la formacin de riqueza en la medida que dicho dinero  expresado en un signo monetario merecedor de confianza universal- conserva su poder de compra a lo largo del tiempo. Para cumplir cabalmente con esta misin de generador invariable de confianza, y de expectativas de estabilidad para el futuro, un banco central moderno debe ser ejemplo de comunicacin transparente. De ah que cada vez ms, sobre todo en un esquema de objetivos de inflacin que es de acuerdo al cual funcionamos la mayora de los bancos centrales en el mundo, la comunicacin oportuna  destinada a fundar y formar expectativas entre el pblico- sea vista como herramienta indispensable de la poltica monetaria. Consideremos, para concluir, que la historia a veces trgica de algunas de las piezas histricas que vamos a contemplar tuvo, en el caso de Mxico, y con el paso de los aos, un final venturoso en el que prevaleci, al fin, el rostro de la fundacin y construccin de instituciones, con la creacin en 1925 del anhelado Banco nico de Emisin que es hoy el Banco de Mxico. El ideal propuesto por los constituyentes de 1917 pudo as verse cumplido. Y hoy, a 85 aos de distancia de la fundacin del Banco Central y cien aos despus del inicio de las luchas revolucionarias, el Banco de Mxico aspira decididamente a ser ese gran generador de confianza. El mandato prioritario del banco, que es procurar la estabilidad de precios, se traduce a la postre en una clara e ineludible misin: contribuir sin titubeos al crecimiento econmico sembrando todos los das el ingrediente indispensable para el bienestar sostenido de una Nacin. Title: Low and stable inflation, the success of structural reform
text: LOW AND STABLE INFLATION, THE SUCCESS OF STRUCTURAL REFORM (*) Augustine William Carstens Carstens . Governor of the Bank of Mexico. Agustin Carstens holds a PhD in Economics from the University of Chicago. During the first half of 2015 Mexico recorded annual inflations in the range of a low of 2.87 to a high of 3.14%. At the end of that semester, annual headline inflation was 2.87%, while core inflation - which excludes agricultural prices and those prices administered by the government - was 2.33% per year. It is the first time, since 1969, when the National Consumer Price Index began to be developed and used as a measure of inflation, that our country, for such a long period, has such consistently low inflations. In addition, the specialists in private sector economics that the Bank of Mexico surveys, month by month, about its economic expectations predict that at the end of 2015 annual inflation will be less than 3%: 2.91% is the average of their forecasts. Indeed, it would be to fall into a very dangerous complacency to consider that a goal of this importance, once achieved, will perpetuate itself. Nothing more boastful and wrong. Maintaining low and stable inflation - with the multitude of benefits that this entails for economic well-being, for the long-term planning of the country's growth and development, of investments and of the formation of assets of individuals, families and companies - requires a constant and meticulous monitoring of economic indicators and the internal and external environment, as well as timely and assertive monetary policy decisions that respond without delay to any factor that jeopardizes general price stability. Consolidating what has been achieved, that is the immense challenge that the Bank of Mexico now faces. This essay aims to show that the fundamental cause behind the long-awaited achievement of low and stable inflation lies in one of the most profound structural reforms carried out by our country in the final decades of the twentieth century: the granting of full autonomy to the Bank of Mexico in 1994. This statement does not disdain some factors of a conjunctural nature, such as the relative weakness that still prevails in economic activity, or non-recurrent factors, such as the beneficial effect that structural reforms in telecommunications and energy have had on prices in the first months of 2015. Undoubtedly, these factors, especially those derived from the aforementioned structural reforms, have contributed to the decline in inflation becoming more noticeable and accelerated since the beginning of the year, but it is clear that without a monetary policy consistent with the objective of price stability, product of an autonomous central bank, such benefits in terms of 2 "1995 "1996 "1997 "1998 "1999"2000 "2001"2002"2003 "2004"2005"2006 "2007"2008"2009 "2010"2011"2012 "2013"2014 "Jun 2015 Prices would have been ephemeral or would not have materialized if expectations of low and stable inflation were not well anchored, as they effectively are. Figure 2. Annual inflation in December of each year (1995-2014) and June 2015 ANNUAL INFLATION IN DECEMBER OF EACH YEAR (1995-2014) AND JUNE 2015 60 50 40 30 20 10 0 Source: Own elaboration based on Inegi and Banxico The transcendent structural reform that gave autonomy to the Bank of Mexico was embodied both in the General Constitution of the Republic (Articles 28, 73 and 123), and in the Law of the Bank of Mexico, and the core of it is that no authority may order the Bank of Mexico to grant credit, which, in functional terms, means that the Central Bank will be able to have all the tools of monetary policy to achieve the priority objective ordered by the Constitution: to ensure the stability of the purchasing power of the currency. There is no doubt that without this institutional framework - the full autonomy of the issuing bank - it would have been practically impossible to achieve the low and stable inflation that we enjoy today and, even less, we could realistically propose today, in the Governing Board of the Bank of Mexico, to consolidate this achievement to make it a permanent condition of the Mexican economy; for this it has been essential that our Central Institute had the tools of 3 monetary policy that gives it its character as an autonomous institution of the Mexican State. To illustrate the importance of the autonomy of the Central Bank, an analysis is proposed, first, on the nature of money and its importance as a facilitator and catalyst of the economy in all its aspects, that is: in the generation of wealth through investment, in the conservation and increase of it through savings or in the multiplicity of exchanges of goods and services through trade. Once the immense importance of money has been established, the great power that, for better or worse, the exclusive power of central banks to issue legal tender will be understood more clearly and broadly, and hence the importance of issuing institutions acting in accordance with a carefully designed legal framework that prevents such power from being exercised abusively or perversely causing serious harm to society. Equally relevant is that such a legal framework grants autonomy to central banks by protecting them from pressures, either from the government or from individuals, that by pretending to use the tools of monetary policy for purposes other than price stability, could pervert the nature of money and, ultimately, strip the currency of its ability to facilitate and catalyze economic well-being. In this sense, the autonomy of the Central Bank must be understood above all as a guarantee for the users of the currency, an inalienable right of society to enjoy the benefits of a reliable and stable medium of exchange, unit of account and store of value. Likewise, it is argued in this essay that the autonomy of the Central Bank, which must be translated into a responsible monetary policy, works optimally - to the benefit of the country - when it is twinned with an equally responsible fiscal policy, as has been the case in Mexico for more than 20 years. Indeed, the combination of a sound fiscal policy - which has as its permanent objective a structural balance of public finances - with a responsible monetary policy, and both complemented by a system 4 A soundly capitalized and well-regulated financial institution is the only ideal framework for an economy to achieve sustained high growth. In this regard, just as a reference, it is worth recalling the unfortunate experiences, in other latitudes, of the failure of monetary arrangements designed to achieve price stability, which, however, were not accompanied by a fiscal policy consistent with the same objective. Such was the case, for example, of the one-to-one convertibility of the Argentine currency with the US dollar in force in the final decade of the last century, which a few years later succumbed and was reversed, overwhelmed by an overwhelming fiscal deficit. Likewise, the severe crisis that Greece's economy is currently experiencing has shown that a so-called optimal monetary area - as the euro area seeks to be - is extremely vulnerable if it does not contemplate, at the same time, what we could call an optimal fiscal and financial zone, in which the countries that share a common currency also share effective institutional arrangements that guarantee the soundness of public finances and financial systems. of each of them. 1. Money, one of the greatest inventions in history. Its immense creative potential... and destructive Money must be considered, along with language, one of the most important findings in the history of humanity, in view of the immense benefits it has brought to the human being in terms of progress, poverty reduction, intergenerational well-being, stability and confidence in the future. It is well known that the invention of money allowed the human being to overcome the painful limitations of the barter of material goods, opening an immense range of exchange options, while allowing homogenizing the accounting of goods and, at the same time, providing stability to the same goods allowing the formation of patrimony and capital; since these goods expressed in units of money or, strictly speaking, in monetary units, retain and even increase their value over time. 5 It is no coincidence that the turning point in the history of the economy of the human being and of nations, in which it went from stagnation to progress, coincides with the generalization of the use of money. With this generalization would appear the first stock markets in which the mediation of money, as a sign of the value of physical goods, facilitated and enhanced the multiplication of commercial exchanges, the hoarding of goods, their insurance over time and until the concretion in the present of operations to be consummated in the future, which brought certainty and stability to productive activities, such as agriculture, subject to the unforeseeable contingencies of climate variations and natural disasters. It is worth reflecting on the character of sign that money has. Indeed, money is not the good in itself that that money buys, the money of the wage is not the work itself that that money remunerates, but money means all those goods and services: labor, land, the fruits of the earth. And it does so by transcending the limitation of present time, so that money can be the translation - the sign - of a work already done as well as the sign of a work to be done in the future. The same money can be the result of what has already been harvested as the instrument to acquire a harvest that at the present time is only a project, seed arranged for sowing. In this sense, money shares the same nature as language. The philosopher John Locke pointed out in his Essay on Human Understanding that in language everything is material-the ink on paper, the vibrations of the sound of words in the air-except for the meaning which, however, is the most important thing, is the essence of language and what makes communication possible. In this way, language allows us to dematerialize objects -to make them abstract to turn them into signs- in order to communicate without having to resort to the constant and tiring material marking of each object to which we wish to refer: a tree, the sky, the ground, a house. The same intermediation that, through the signs of language, de-materializes objects and transforms them into meanings in order to dispose of them and exchange them, is carried out by money and performed more efficiently when it is transformed into currency, 6 through the minting and issuance of signs whose meaning lies not in themselves but in what we have agreed to signify, as is the case with banknotes and coins. As it is a conventional sign - the meaning of which was agreed between the users of the sign - its effectiveness as a sign, and until its permanence, lies in the respect of that convention. This applies the same to language, as to money and currency. In both cases, trust is essential. The confidence that the word I use means the same to me as it does to the one who reads or hears it. Confidence that the monetary sign has the same meaning, and retains it over time, for all who use it. From this reflection, the immense creative potential of money and its most generalized expression, which is the monetary sign, is obvious. Whoever issues currency, then, has a gigantic power that, however, vanishes sooner rather than later if he abuses that power and degrades the sign by stripping it of its genuine meaning. Again, the same thing happens with language: the abuse of words, degrading or distorting their meaning, ends up - sooner rather than later - by stripping language of its creative potential to communicate. Whoever misuses language ends up incommunicado. Whoever misuses the ability to issue currency ends up stripping the currency of value. Bearing in mind these considerations about the immense power, for better or for worse as the case may be, that entails the ability to issue currency, it will be understood the great importance, for the well-being of a nation, which has to create an ideal institutional framework for the task of issuing currency, which is entrusted to a central bank, is delimited with precision and scruples, so that such power is not degraded, not misused and is always for the benefit of the users of said currency. That, and no other, is the ultimate reason, from a philosophical perspective, why a central bank should be autonomous. 7 2. Central Bank autonomy: the essence of a notoriously successful structural reform 90 years ago the then president of the Republic Plutarco Elias Calles sent to the Congress of the Union the Initiative of Law to create the Bank of Mexico. As is known, this proposal fulfilled the purpose expressed by the constituents of 1917 to create a Single Bank of Issuance. In the first instance, this bank, according to what was expressed by the same constituents, should end the plurality of private institutions authorized to issue banknotes and grant exclusively this power of issuance to a state bank. When the Constitution of 1917 was drafted, only the purpose of the single issuing bank being controlled by the State was embodied, but the specific legal nature of the same was not defined, since there were two options on which there was no final decision at that time: that of a bank controlled by the State but in which there was private participation or that of a State bank. In this way, such a definition was left pending to be determined in the secondary legislation. The law that created the Bank of Mexico in 1925 chose to contemplate private participation in the single bank of issue, paying in favor of this option a particularly significant argument: the need for the issuing bank to be safe from subordinating itself to the political interest of the government, and this was expressed by President Calles in the explanatory statement of his initiative: "There is indeed, in a bank controlled by the government, the very serious danger that political interest may at any given time predominate over the public interest." The importance of President Calles making this warning in the explanatory statement of the aforementioned initiative lies in the fact that it is a clear recognition that the nascent single bank of issuance should enjoy the greatest autonomy with respect to the governments in turn to fully fulfill its mission. Of course, such autonomy should not be detrimental to the State's control over the central bank. 8 For his part, another of the founders of the Bank of Mexico and first president of its Board of Directors, Manuel Gomez Morin would write with frank pride, shortly after the Institution was born, to his friend Jose Vasconcelos: "So you have me at this moment as a banker and not just any banker, but a bank that because I am Mexican has been and will be on many occasions tragic, made in the midst of the hostility of many people (...) The bank has been a complete success and entered, as they say, on the right foot. The Council is absolutely independent and we hope it stays that way for the good of all." Three years later, in 1928, it was specified- through an addition to the original law of the Bank of Mexico - that the bank was not obliged to provide the federal government with more services than those established by the law itself, specifying that neither could local laws impose on the Central Bank the obligation to lend to the states. In the same way of guaranteeing its autonomy in 1936 the new Organic Law of the Bank of Mexico, which replaced the first, made the requirements for the issuance of banknotes more severe and prohibited - explicitly and absolutely - that the Central Bank grant credits to the federal government. However, this path towards full autonomy of the Bank of Mexico was not without hesitation and frank setbacks. Thus, in 1938 its organic law was reformed, relaxing the prohibition on giving financial support to the Government. This orientation, which opened the door to a dangerous subordination of the power of issuance to the financing needs of the Government or even to interests of a political nature, remained in the new Organic Law of the Bank promulgated in 1941. It is worth mentioning here the assessment that, several decades later, in 1993 - in the explanatory statement of the presidential _Iniciativa to reform Articles 28, 73 and 123 of the Constitution - was made of the risks implicit in the Organic Law of 1941: "Unfortunately, the indirect limitation that was established in this last order for the issuance of currency was susceptible to circumvention. The limitation was that the sum of the banknotes in circulation plus the 9 demand and national currency obligations of the institution should not exceed four times the value of its gold, silver and foreign exchange reserves. However, when a depreciation of the peso occurred, such a restriction became nugatory, since such action made it possible to increase the value in national currency of the aforementioned reserve". So it was. The defect of origin of this legal design was translated, in later times, into some episodes of abuse of financing from the Bank of Mexico to the federal government that, as expected, encouraged fiscal deficits, produced crises in the balance of payments, inflation and, ultimately, the impoverishment of millions of Mexicans. To fully understand how the lack of effective autonomy of the Central Bank led to these regrettable results, it is necessary to recall that the Government fully controlled the Bank by having the power to appoint and remove at its discretion the majority of the members of its board of directors, and also its Director General through agreements of the board itself. That is: even if some of the directors of the Bank of Mexico and its general director opposed meeting the government's financing demands, the government could remove them without further requirement or procedure. So far I have followed the historical review that is made in the explanatory statement of the constitutional reform that would give full autonomy to the Bank of Mexico because, in a very correct way, it shows two key points that are the essence of the success of that structural reform: I- That from the origin of the Bank of Mexico there was a serious concern to prevent the exclusive power of issuance from being perverted by becoming a source of financing for deficit public spending, and II- That, in fact, when a defective institutional design relaxed the prohibition on the Central Bank financing the federal government, this gave rise to serious economic crises - all characterized by high inflation, which in turn is the most regressive tax of all, which affects more those who have less - which had their origin in the fact that the lack of effective autonomy prevented the Bank of Mexico from carrying 10 carry out a responsible monetary policy that would preserve the purchasing power of the currency issued by the same institution. On the second point, it should be noted that, despite the fact that a deficient institutional arrangement made it possible to abuse the power to broadcast, this was not the rule, but rather the exception. Fortunately, Mexico had officials and technical cadres, both in the Bank of Mexico and in the Ministry of Finance, who by conviction, and with a high sense of public service, maintained responsible fiscal and monetary policies. Obviously, these public servants had the support of presidents of the Republic who shared that same conviction. This was the case of the period known as the stabilizing development (1954-1970) in which the Bank of Mexico certainly did not enjoy institutional autonomy, but a margin of action conducive to a responsible monetary policy, granted by public administrations, in the federal Government, convinced of the great social benefits derived from maintaining healthy public finances and a solid currency with stable purchasing power. Having made this precision, I return to describe what the structural reform that granted autonomy to the Bank of Mexico in 1994 consisted of. Based on a clear diagnosis of the defects and risks evident in the legal framework that regulated the existence of the Central Bank and its relationship with the federal government, the reform removed the biggest obstacle that the Bank of Mexico had to fully use the tools of monetary policy with the priority objective of protecting the purchasing value of the currency. Such an obstacle was, as the brief historical review of the lines back showed us, the possibility of the Central Bank financing the Government. In this way, it can be said that the essence of the autonomy of the Bank of Mexico lies in the explicit prohibition to grant credit to the federal government; prohibition thoroughly explained in the current Articles 9, 11 and 12 of the Bank of Mexico Law. For obvious reasons, and in light of the historical experience of both Mexico and other countries, making that ban effective requires that they be put in place. 11 mechanisms and safeguards in the law that prevent the subordination of the Central Bank to the federal government and political power. Thus, the reform carefully established the procedure for appointing the members of the Governing Board of the Bank of Mexico, closing any possibility that this collegiate body - responsible for monetary policy decisions - would be subordinate to the Executive Power. I mention the two main characteristics of this procedure aimed at guaranteeing the effective autonomy of the Bank of Mexico: to. The members of the Governing Board are appointed by the President of the Republic with the approval of the Senate of the Republic or, in its recesses, of the Permanent Commission of the Congress of the Union. This characteristic is aimed at making the Legislative Power work, in the appointment of those who have to govern the Central Bank, as a counterweight to the Executive. b. The terms for which they are appointed are not only long (eight years for the sub-governors and six years for the governor, in both cases with the possibility of being ratified for subsequent periods, provided that they have not reached, at the time of such ratification, 65 years of age), but staggered, so that the Executive is not in a position to appoint within a short period the whole or the majority of the members of that governing body. This feature, in addition, promotes that the horizon according to which the members of the Governing Board deliberate and make their decisions, transcends in time the period of a government administration. It should be noted that, in the institutional design of the autonomy of the Bank of Mexico, it is not understood in any way as a will to oppose or oppose the federal government, but as a healthy limitation to the power of the latter, for the benefit of society. In fact, the same Law of the Bank of Mexico states that the Central Institute will be "advisor to the Federal Government in matters 12 economic and, particularly, financial", in addition to providing treasury services and acting as your financial agent. 3. Sound public finances, the correlate of the autonomy of the Central Bank The spirit that animated the structural reform that gave autonomy to the Bank of Mexico was born from the conviction that it is not convenient that those who have the power to exercise public spending also have the power to issue currency to get resources. Thus, by restricting sources of government resources to tax collection, to the income of state enterprises and to the placement of debt instruments in the markets, the autonomy of the Bank of Mexico represents a clear definition of the Mexican State in favor of a fiscal balance that structurally remains in balance. Hence, the Federal Law on Budget and Financial Responsibility enacted in March 2006 - and whose most recent reform dates from August 2014, to include, among other matters, that of transfers from the Mexican Petroleum Fund from 2015 - constitutes, together with the Bank of Mexico Law, the legal basis of a consistent macroeconomic policy that generates confidence in economic agents. For the achievement of low and stable inflation, it has been fundamental during the last decades the contest of a responsible fiscal policy, based on the principle that a healthy public finance is one that limits its indebtedness to a proportion of the Gross Domestic Product that makes it sustainable over time, and that permanently seeks that most of the public expenditure be covered with tax revenues and with those coming from the profits obtained by state enterprises, such as oil production and exports. Given that the Bank of Mexico maintains an inflation targeting scheme in its monetary policy, and since January 2008 it adopted as a target 13 In the operational overnight interbank interest rate, consistency between fiscal policy and monetary policy is of particular importance. This is because in a hypothetical scenario of chronically deficit public finances, the Central Bank should - in congruence with its priority objective - raise the reference interest rate considerably, generating serious difficulties for the Government to obtain financing in the market for its fiscal deficit and imposing a high cost on credit for the rest of society. Additionally, in an environment of chronic fiscal imbalance, pressures are rising sharply for the central bank to abandon its priority objective, under the fallacious assumption that accepting higher inflation could stimulate economic growth. This is not the case: higher inflation, instead of promoting the dynamism of the economy, generates stagnation and greater poverty, as the historical experience of both Mexico and many countries has shown. In the case of Mexico, the periods of higher inflation in the last three decades of the last century coincided with stages of decline in growth, which meant an increase in poverty and a regression in the distribution of income. 14 Figure 3. GDP Growth and Inflation (1970-2000) GDP GROWTH AND INFLATION (1970-2000) left axis: GDP growth right axis: annual inflation GDP growth: inflation bars: line 10 180 8 160 6 140 4 120 2 100 0 80 -2 60 -4 40 -6 20 -8 0 Source: Own elaboration, based in Banxico That is why the most important contribution made by the Bank of Mexico to economic growth and a better distribution of income is precisely to ensure price stability, as a necessary, although not sufficient, condition for the dynamism of the economy. On the other hand, given that economic agents - especially those that affect the formation of financial markets - have rightly identified persistent fiscal imbalances as a factor that generates higher inflation and, eventually, balance of payments crises, they maintain monitoring. 15 constant on the balance of income and expenditure of governments, so that healthy public finances have become, together with a responsible and transparent monetary policy, key factors in keeping inflation expectations anchored. Hence, structurally balanced public finances, together with a healthy financial system - capitalized and well regulated - are the best allies of monetary policy to consolidate an environment of low and stable inflation, as is currently the case in Mexico.
