Title: Conference on macroprudential policies organized by the Center for Latin American Monetary Studies (CEMLA), the World Bank and Banca dItalia
text: REMARKS BY JAVIER GUZMAN CALAFELL, DEPUTY GOVERNOR AT THE BANCO DE MeXICO, DURING THE CONFERENCE ON MACROPRUDENTIAL POLICIES ORGANIZED BY THE CENTER FOR LATIN AMERICAN MONETARY STUDIES (CEMLA), THE WORLD BANK AND BANCA DITALIA.Mexico City, June 20, 2013.1 1. Introduction First of all, I would like to thank CEMLA, the World Bank, and Banca DItalia for the invitation to participate in this important conference. For me this is an especially significant opportunity, not only because I had the privilege of working at CEMLA until recently, but also because after having helped in the initial stages of organizing the seminar, it is very gratifying to see such a successful outcome. In addition, it is a pleasure to be able to greet old friends and of course, exchange points of view on such a timely and important subject. I would like to divide my remarks into two parts. First, I will focus on some of the challenges that the design and implementation of macroprudential policy currently face, and afterwards on the policy framework and the concrete actions that have been put in place in Mexico in this area. 1. Challenges for macroprudential policy Until relatively recently, and particularly until before the global economic crisis in which we are still immersed, the predominant view was that the combination of price stability along with adequate regimes for regulating and supervising individual financial institutions would be sufficient to maintain financial stability. In this context, it was frequently argued that monetary policy should not be oriented towards counteracting possible excessive increases in financial market or real estate prices, but rather, contribute to repairing the damage once the bubbles burst. As you know, this view changed after the crisis. On the one hand, it has become clear that price stability is a necessary but insufficient condition for maintaining financial stability. On the other, it has also become evident that the impact of the bursting of a bubble can be of such a magnitude that monetary policy instruments are insufficient or inadequate to face them. Thus, the conclusion has been reached that it is indispensable for central banks as well as other authorities to seek other mechanisms to contribute in a more effective way to the preservation of financial stability. One option is to use the policy interest rate to reach this aim. However, this carries with it the risk of assigning too many tasks to monetary policys most important instrument. In addition, the use of the interest rate could be too aggressive in view of the fact that its impact goes beyond the financial system, and there could even be times in which adjustments to the interest rate have opposing implications for price and financial stability. 1 Opinions in this document are strictly personal and do not necessarily coincide with Banco de Mexicos positions. 1 Given this situation, there is a need of complementing available instruments with other more direct ones, and with a systemic view of the financial system. This is how macro-prudential policy has gained increasing importance at the global level. In general terms, this policy has been identified with the use of prudential instruments to face financial weaknesses of a systemic nature, although as we shall see later on, different interpretations exist. The merits of seeking financial stability through a complementary focus that includes macroprudential tools, as well as traditional monetary, fiscal, and microprudential instruments, are clear in theory. However, it is also true that the situation is more complex in practice. This is mainly due to the challenges that macroprudential policy faces in its design and implementation, as well as in its interaction with other policies and in the allocation of responsibilities among different authorities. What are these challenges? I would like to highlight some of those which from my point of view are particularly important, without of course attempting to make an exhaustive list. First, there is no consensus on the precise meaning of the term macroprudential. Notably, the origin of the term is not recent. Various authors trace its birth at the end of the 1960s, in documents associated with discussions of the so-called Cook Committee, the precursor to the current Basel Banking Supervision Committee.2 From the start, the concept was focused on the need for financial regulation and supervision to adopt a systemic focus in the search for financial stability. However, until now it has not been possible to arrive at a generally accepted definition, despite the prominence the instrument has gained due to the crisis. On the basis of what are perceived to be the key points of agreement, the Financial Stability Board (FSB), the International Monetary Fund, and the Bank for International Settlements consider that the main elements of macroprudential policy are the following: the objective of containing systemic risk, its concentration on the financial system as a whole, and the use of prudential tools (or non-prudential tools as long as they are focused on systemic risk).3 Obviously, the search for elements of agreement on the concept of macroprudential policy carried out by these institutions is of great value. However, it is clear that even with this definition numerous ambiguities persist. For example, the possibility of including prudential or other tools opens considerable space for measures that could be considered macroprudential. In a similar way, there is the possibility that some authorities justify the implementation of measures (such as capital controls) on the basis of systemic risk, when in reality the ultimate objective is of a macroeconomic nature. Even the above-cited organizations recognize the existence of gray areas in the definition, e.g., with respect to where to place policies focused on strengthening financial infrastructure, since even though a broad concept would consider them to be macroprudential, these organizations exclude them from the definition. In this context, it is not surprising that the 2 See Piet Clement, The Term Macroprudential: Origins and Evolution, BIS Quarterly Review, March 2010. 3Financial Stability Board, International Monetary Fund and Bank for International Settlements, Macroprudential Policy Tools and Frameworks, Progress Report to the G20, October 27, 2011. 2 range of policies considered to be macroprudential is inconveniently wide. This generates, among other risks, the possibility of distortionary effects and a lack of transparency in implementation. Second, the concept of systemic risk, a central component of any definition of macroprudential policy, gives rise to considerable challenges. On the one hand, it is well known that systemic risk has various dimensions. Specifically, the literature highlights the time dimension, that is, the amplification of risk with time through interaction between the financial system and the real economy, or through pro-cyclical factors from microprudential regulation; the transversal dimension, resulting from the common exposure of financial institutions to risk and the contagion of problems in some of them to the rest of the sector; and the structural dimension, associated with regulations and policy actions that limit risk-taking and strengthen financial-system infrastructure.4 The multidimensional character of systemic risk, combined with our still modest understanding of interactions between the financial sector and the real economy, complicate measurement considerably. Currently there are no reliable, generally accepted measures of systemic risk. The absence of precise and complete indicators to evaluate risk is not exclusive to the macroprudential area. However, for the reasons stated, the problem is particularly acute in this case. Thus, it is hard to identify the situations that give rise to systemic risk. Specifically, it is frequent to see possible sources of risk which at the end of the day do not materialize, or as in the current crisis, events with systemic consequences that are not adequately anticipated. In other words, the margin of error is high. The foregoing highlights the need to improve not only the quality and timeliness of financialmarket information and indicators, but also the capacity to analyze them, detect weaknesses, and propose courses of action to alleviate them. Third, until relatively recently, the analytical support for decision making in macro-prudential policy was very limited. As a result of the interest that the crisis has generated in the topic, research on the subject has rapidly proliferated.5 Nevertheless, the theoretical and empirical backing for macro-prudential policy is still at a preliminary stage and far from capable of providing the basis required for the design of integrated policy frameworks in this area. This is explained partly by the fact that recognition of the important role that macroprudential policy could play in financial stability surfaced only a short time ago. In addition to becoming a recent incentive for research in the area, the above implies that very little empirical evidence exists on the effects of macroprudential instruments used to date which could serve as a guide for the design of new tools of this kind. 4 See Stefan Ingves, et. al., Central Bank Governance and Financial Stability - A Report by a Study Group, Bank for International Settlements, May 2011. 5 See Gabriele Galati and Richard Moessner, Macroprudential Policy - A Literature Review, BIS Working Papers, No. 337, February 2011. 3 On the other hand, the crisis has made clear the limitations of current economic analysis, the impact of which affects not only the design of macroprudential policy, but also monetary policy. I am referring to the need for a better understanding of the relation of the financial system with the macro-economy, and the importance of building models that capture this relationship in an adequate way. Until recently, most macroeconomic and monetary models did not explicitly take the financial system into consideration. Today, there are some who believe that in the future the analysis and modeling of cycles and crises should start with imbalances in the financial markets.6 In the absence of generally accepted theoretical and empirical models for the implementation of macro-prudential policy, the evaluation of a possible role for these instruments in the containment of systemic risk and the possible costs involved becomes much more complex. In general, evidence suggests that these instruments have been of greater use in strengthening financial systems against the risk of shocks than in moderating financial cycles. However, the reality is that the basis for a deep evaluation of the effectiveness of macroprudential policy is weak. Fourth, interactions exist between macro-prudential policy and other policies that should be taken carefully into consideration, and which to date have not been adequately analyzed. This is given the fact that the use of these instruments can enter into conflict with or amplify the effects of other policy tools. In the macroprudential context, the clearest interaction occurs with monetary policy. In general, it is to be expected that monetary and macroprudential policies work in a complementary way and thus mutually reinforce one another. Actions oriented towards underpinning the financial system allow monetary policy to work better, by improving transmission mechanisms and protecting the economy from abrupt fluctuations in financial markets. In a similar way, macroeconomic stability lessens the vulnerability of the financial system. However, the possibility for conflict exists. Thus, for example, evidence shows that a relaxed monetary policy can stimulate the search for risk and excessive leverage, accentuating the fragility of the financial system. In addition, the introduction of macroprudential measures can affect domestic demand in a direction other than that sought by monetary policy. Thus, at times, the performance of variables in the real and financial sectors can lead to opposite recommendations from these policies. Additionally, we should not lose sight of the risk that financial institutions find ways to evade certain macroprudential measures. In cases in which this is not possible, frequently a displacement of activities beyond the regulatory perimeter will be observed. The conclusion is obvious: mechanisms are needed that allow for an adequate coordination of monetary and macro-prudential policies. In this context, there is growing acceptance of the idea 6 See Summers, Lawrence, Learning From and Responding to Financial Crises II, Lectures in Honor of Arthur Okun, Yale University, 2008. 4 that monetary policy should maintain inflation control as its priority objective, and macroprudential policy should adopt a more important role in smoothing pro-cyclical and transversal risks in the financial system.7 In addition, it is crucial to take into account that the need for coordination goes beyond monetary policy. Microprudential and fiscal policies also have a high degree of complementarity and potential short-term conflict with macroprudential policy. Thus, here too a continue exchange of information and adequate mechanisms for resolving conflicts are necessary. This leads me to the fifth and last challenge I would like to mention: the creation of optimal institutional arrangements for designing and implementing macroprudential policies. I would like first to emphasize that no single recipe exists that fits all cases. In reality, the choice of an adequate arrangement depends on the specific characteristics of each country, including its laws and political context. Thus, in some cases, such as the United States, the euro zone and as we shall see, Mexico, financial stability councils have been formed, without decision-making powers but with faculties for recommending courses of action oriented towards coordinating the work of agencies such as the central bank, supervisory entities, the agency responsible for insuring bank deposits, and the finance ministry. In other cases, such as the United Kingdom, the central bank has been assigned macro- and microprudential responsibilities. Naturally, these are only examples. In fact, the range of possible options is wide. In addition, all of them have advantages and disadvantages. Given the above, more than the specific characteristics of each institutional arrangement, I would like to highlight some of the principles which from my point of view are essential to making these types of arrangements work. a) The agencies responsible for macroprudential policies should be given an adequate mandate to comply with the responsibility. b) These authorities should have the information and analytical capabilities necessary to rapidly identify the surfacing of systemic risks, and the tools necessary to confront them. c) The decision-making process should be transparent and isolated from political pressure and from the influence of interested parties. d) Adequate accountability mechanisms should exist, among them strict requirements for the supply of information to the public. I believe that it is widely accepted that central banks should play a fundamental role in these efforts.8 The reasons are clear. These institutions have wide analytical and operational experience in macroeconomic and financial matters. In addition, as mentioned above, there is a tight 7 See Stijn Claessens et al., The Interaction of Monetary and Macroprudential Policies, International Monetary Fund, January 29, 2013. 8 See Committee on the Global Financial System, Operationalizing the Selection and Application of Macroprudential Instruments, CGFS Papers, No. 48, the Bank for International Settlements, December 2012. 5 relationship, which yields synergies but also conflicts, between monetary and macroprudential policies. Neither should we forget that as lenders of last resort, central banks, in addition to playing a crucial role in the preservation of financial stability, are exposed to considerable risks if the latter is not maintained. It is clear from the above observations that the design and implementation of macroprudential policy has a high degree of complexity. It is true that various countries, especially but not only in Asia, have used these kinds of instruments for many years. However, it is important to bear in mind that under the current circumstances, what is contemplated is not only the possibility of a more generalized use of macroprudential policy, but also assigning it a much more important role in the attainment of financial stability, both at the domestic and at the global levels. This underlines the importance of carefully considering the challenges to which I have referred. I have the impression that the discussion of these subjects will be clearer if it is illustrated with a concrete case, and thus I will refer briefly to the Mexican experience. 2. The Mexican case The bankruptcy of Lehman Brothers and its repercussions at a global level had a severe impact on the Mexican economy. The transmission channels were similar to those seen in other emerging markets. However, because the crisis started in the United States, and in view of the tight links between the two economies, in the case of Mexico, contagion was particularly acute through the real sector. Nevertheless, the impact through financial channels was also significant. The increase in the cost of financing resulting from uncertainty in the international financial markets and the problems faced by global banks significantly affected firms as well as families. Uncertainty became worse when it became known that some Mexican firms faced heavy losses due to derivatives operations, since it was not known with certainty which companies were involved or the size of losses. In this context, GDP dropped 6% in 2009 (See Graph 1). Financial markets saw significant volatility in the months following Lehmans failure: the exchange rate depreciated more than 50% from the beginning of August 2008 to the early March 2009; long-term government interest rates spiked (at the moment of greatest pressure rising almost 400 basis points) and remained high with respect to the monetary policy target; rates on corporate bonds rose almost 240 basis points above the reference rate, and country risk as measured by the EMBI increased more than 600 basis points (Graphs 2 to 4). Financial markets stabilized gradually, and toward the end of 2009, exchange rate depreciation had been reduced to around 30% vs. the level before the crisis, while country risk and the interest rate spread for corporate debt returned to pre-crisis levels. 6 Graph 1 Mexico: GDP Growth Real annual % change 10% 2009 change: -6% 8% 6% 4% 2% 0% -2% -4% -6% -8% -10% 2005 2006 2007 2008 2009 2010 2011 2012 2013 Data up to March 2013 Source: Banco de Mexico Graph 2 Peso  Dollar Exchange Rate Aug.-1-08 100 160 Aug-08100 150 140 130 120 110 100 2008 2009 2010 Data up to June 19, 2013 Source: Banco de Mexico 2011 2012 2013 Graph 3 Mexico: Yield on 10-year Bonds and Target Rate % Policy interest rate Yield on 10 year bonds 12 11 10 9 8 7 6 5 4 2005 2006 2007 2008 2009 2010 2011 2012 2013 Data up to June 19, 2013 Source: Banco de Mexico. Graph 4 Mexico: Spread between Corporate Debt Yields and the TIIE 1/ Basis points 250 Diferential / TIIE 200 150 100 50 0 -50 2005 2006 2007 2008 2009 2010 2011 2012 2013 1/ Equilibrium interbank interest rate Data up to June 19, 2013 Source: Banco de Mexico 7 Despite the magnitude of these shocks, and the fact that the crisis provoked substantial losses for various financial entities in advanced economies that are parent banks of Mexican banks, the nations financial system showed great resilience. What factors allowed the financial system to maintain its strength in the face of such a severe crisis? I would highlight the following: The implementation of prudent monetary and fiscal policies, which, combined with a flexible exchange-rate regime and high levels of international reserves, strengthened the nations economic fundamentals considerably. The efforts undertaken as a result of the 1995 crisis to improve the legal framework and the regulatory and financial supervisory processes. This allowed Mexico to have an efficient and modern payment system, with profitable and well-capitalized financial intermediaries, and deep financial markets. Suffice to point out in this respect that in August 2008, a few days before Lehmans bankruptcy, the Mexican banking system had a capitalization ratio of 15%, a non-performing loan ratio of 3%, and a loan-loss reserve ratio of 156%. Mexican banks modest direct exposure to assets linked to the U.S. mortgage market as well as to governments, financial intermediaries and corporations in the euro zone, which contained the risk of contagion through this channel. Mexican law requires financial institutions that offer services in Mexico to operate through branches or subsidiaries, so that even if foreign entities have a participation in them, they are separate legal entities and have their own capital. In addition to lowering the risks of direct contagion between the parent bank and the entity established in Mexico, this law subjects all banks established in the country to the same rules and supervisory processes regardless of the nationality or other characteristics of shareholders. This is particularly important in Mexico, since a little more than 70% of assets in the banking systems are in the hands of foreign institutions. Retail deposits in the domestic market are the main source of financing of Mexican banks. In August 2008, the ratio of deposits to loans was above 100 percent. This allowed the financial system to respond more flexibly to liquidity problems in international markets. Did macroprudential policies play an important role in these efforts? The answer is definitely so, since macroprudential policies implemented before and in response to the crisis contributed to maintaining a solid financial system. Table 1 includes the key macroprudential measures implemented in Mexico from 1992 to date, on the basis of the previously mentioned definition of the Financial Stability Council, the International Monetary Fund, and the Bank for International Settlements. As is evident, as far as implementation and impact are concerned, macroprudential measures in Mexico can be classified into three groups. The first is comprised by measures introduced years ago and which have been of significant help in containing the effect of shocks on the financial system in different periods. This group includes regulations for banks foreign-currency operations 8 (structural and short-term liquidity and exchange rate risk positions). These regulations allow banks not to be exposed to: A structural imbalance due to funding long-term foreign-currency assets (e.g., mortgages) with short-term liabilities. Insufficient liquid assets to face short-term obligations. An imbalance between assets and liabilities in the face of significant foreign-exchange moves. These regulations, among other factors, were important in preventing a situation similar to that which occurred in some countries in Eastern Europe, in which banks depended on market financing in foreign currency to grant mortgages both in local and foreign currency, which exposed them to significant exchange-rate and credit risk when the crisis hit and their domestic currencies depreciated. 9 Table 1 MAIN MACROPRUDENTIAL POLICY INSTRUMENTS IN MEXICO Year Responsible Institution Measure Impact 1997 Banco de Mexico Prior to the 1994-95 crisis, a regulation was in place which together with other regulations on foreign-currency operations, limited imbalances in banks foreign-exchange positions. In 1997 a regulation was established stipulating a requirement for liquid assets with respect to short-term liabilities (up to 2 months). This was modified successively both to introduce stricter requirements for the eligibility of liquid assets and to limit structural gaps between banks assets and liabilities in foreign currency. The last change was made in 2000. The rule on exchange-rate positions prevented an impact on the equilibrium of bank balance sheets from the 1994 peso devaluation. However, banks faced dollar liquidity needs, because of which Banco de Mexico granted loans to them in foreign currency. As a result, foreign-currency liquidity rules were introduced. Together, the rule on positions and that on liquidity limited structural currency gaps and kept abrupt FX movements in 2008 from having an effect on the banking system through this channel. 1994 2011 National Banking and Securities Commission (CNBV) In 1994 a cap was established of 50% on Tier-1 capital for an exposure to a related counterparty. In 2011 the rules on capital were changed with the aim of requiring banks to deduct from capital exposures greater than 25% of capital. The key aim of these measures was to prevent possible contagion of problems from related counterparties, including difficulties in foreign parent banks passed to subsidiaries, which is of key importance to Mexico given the proportion of assets in the hands of foreign banks. During the recent crisis, this measure prevented the exposure of subsidiaries to their parent banks from rising significantly. However, an exposure of 50% of capital was considered to be too high in the face of stress, and therefore the cap was lowered. 10 2012 Banco de Mexico In October 2012, Banco de Mexico established the requirement to seek authorization from the central bank to make transfers of assets and implement other operations among banks operating in Mexico and related counterparties, when in one year these operations exceed 25% of Tier-1 capital. The objective is to ensure that these operations are carried out under market conditions. This is a recent measure, and thus its impact cannot yet be analyzed. 2001 CNBV Caps on interbank exposures, including among other instruments, caps on net positions in derivatives and repurchase agreements, with the aim of reducing exposure to the risk of interbank contagion. The financing cap among banks is equivalent to one time the Tier-1 capital of the lending institution. In the future, these caps could vary according to the size of the institution. This rule has reduced the risk of interbank contagion. 2009 2010 National Retirement Savings Commission (CONSAR) Higher limits on VaRs for pension fund portfolios at times of high volatility. The aim is to prevent massive sales by Firms Specialized in Retirement Investment Funds (SIEFORES) during periods of higher volatility in financial markets. First the number of scenarios was increased from 500 to 1,000 to calculate the VaR, and in February 2010 a methodology was developed that automatically establishes higher limits on VaRs at times of significantly higher market volatility. When a pension fund reaches its risk limit according to the VaR, it is required to unwind positions to reduce risk. When market volatility increases, it is easier for these funds to surpass these limits. During 2009-2010, taking into account the magnitude of the financial crisis, the size of these funds positions and the effect a massive sale of assets would have had at a time of great turmoil, the authorities decided to allow funds to surpass the VaR limits. This prevented a precipitous recomposition of portfolios through asset sales, which would have triggered a vicious cycle. With the adjustments introduced to the VaR methodolgy, this adverse effect on pension funds and its consequences for market volatility are eliminated. 11 2009 CNBV 2011 Loan loss provisioning depending on expected losses rather than on those observed for revolving consumer lending starting in 2009, and for mortgage and non-revolving consumer lending portfolios, as well as for loans to federal and municipal entities, in 2011. Also, in 2013 the corresponding methodologies were published for commercial lending. The aim is to diminish the cyclicality of provisioning and thus of losses. Diminishes the pro-cyclicality of lending and bank revenue, by requiring intermediaries to recognize that they will face losses on some loans which at the time of provisioning are current. This allows for past-due loan provisions to be built up in a gradual way and as the quality of loans deteriorate according to statistical models, and not at the moment losses materialize due to non-payment. 12 The regulation for the building up of reserves based on the methodology of expected losses for consumer lending (credit cards) is another of the measures implemented before the global crisis struck. This allowed banks to build reserves that were sufficient to face losses from these portfolios, and thus reduced their vulnerability during the crisis. At the same time, the regulation that limited exposures to related counterparties was important in protecting the Mexican financial system from a case in which a Mexican banks parent bank faced difficulties. On the basis of experience during the crisis, the limit was lowered even further. Also, adjustments to the methodology for calculating VaRs for the SIEFORES 9 has prevented massive asset sales during periods of higher market volatility, and the limits on interbank exposures have reduced contagion risk among banks. The second group is comprised of measures that have been implemented, but given the fact implementation is relatively recent, their impact cannot be analyzed with precision. This group includes the introduction of the requirement for authorization to carry out buy-sell operations, asset transfers, and other operations among banks in Mexico and related counterparties. Finally, the third group of macroprudential measures includes those under considerations at an international level and which could be implemented in Mexico with some variations. Among these measures are counter-cyclical capital requirements, and the identification of systemically important financial institutions and the introduction of regulatory requirements for them. The Mexican authorities are also working to implement other measures which, in principle, are considered to be microprudential, such as the Basel III short-term liquidity ratio. In the view of some authorities, this rule could be used as a macroprudential tool by adjusting the level of the required ratio under different circumstances. This should be evaluated once the requirement is put into effect, and the desired level of the indicator is analyzed in different situations and according to the way markets react to the adjustments banks make. Despite the resilience shown by the Mexican financial system to the effects of the global crisis, the crisis highlighted the need to continuously evaluate possible sources of risk that could affect the functioning of the financial system as a whole and the real sector. At the same time, the crisis demonstrated the importance of establishing mechanisms for coordination among different authorities, with the aim of preventing or facing this type of crises. In this context, in mid-2009 the authorities decided to create the Financial System Stability Council (CESF). This is an entity of evaluation, analysis and coordination among financial authorities, oriented toward identifying risks to financial stability and proposing preventive policies or if needed minimize their impact. The Council is not a decision-making body, but rather a forum for cooperation and recommendation of courses of action, in which each participating authority is 9 Sociedades de Inversion Especializadas en Fondos para el Retiro (firms specialized in retirement investment funds). 13 committed to promoting, in the context of its faculties and subject to the laws that govern it, the implementation of the recommendations formulated in accordance with the applicable laws. The Council is comprised of the Finance Minister, who presides over it, the Governor of the Banco de Mexico, the Deputy Finance Minister, two central bank deputy governors, the President of the National Banking and Securities Commission (CNBV), the President of the Insurance and Surety National Commission (CNSF), the President of the National Commission for Retirement Savings (CONSAR), and the Executive Secretary of the Bank Savings Protection Institute (IPAB). The Councils statutes, in addition to considering the need for coordination, stipulate that the entity should hold sessions at least every three months and publish an annual report. The CESF has five working groups oriented towards covering all aspects of risk detection and systemic risk mitigation: Standardization and data collection. Responsible for identifying the relevant information to monitor financial stability, as well as validate, process, and make available this information to all Council members. Design of metrics and methodologies to measure systemic risk. Detection of risks and weaknesses. In charge of designing a framework for analyzing weaknesses in the financial system, the rapid evaluation of which allows for a timely detection of risks. Information transparency. Responsible for ensuring that market participants have adequate and timely information for decision making. Financial markets. Focuses on evaluating risks originating in the financial markets. Naturally, the creation of the Council strengthens significantly the framework for the implementation of macroprudential policy. Indeed, the CESF is the ideal forum for analyzing and recommending the introduction of macroprudential measures. In addition, the Council complies with or is oriented toward complying with the four principles I mentioned that are essential for these kinds of arrangements to work: the CESF has a clear mandate for performing its duties in this area, stated in the statutes of each of the institutions that comprise it and in its own statutes; the CESF works in a transparent way and with complete respect for the responsibilities and, if applicable, autonomy of the institutions involved; and the CESF operates on the basis of a mechanism of accountability, based mainly on the abovementioned periodic reports to the general public. Finally, the composition of the Council has served as a basis for underpinning the availability of information and the analytical foundation for evaluating the risks that could affect the financial system as a whole as well as the mechanisms needed for facing them, although much remains to be done in this respect. 14 Importantly, the CESFs sphere of action goes beyond macroprudential matters, since it includes microprudential issues as well, and in general compliance with commitments under the international financial regulatory agenda. In addition, the Council includes authorities responsible for monetary and fiscal policy which, as already mentioned, play a key role in attaining financial stability. Thus, the CESF allows the consideration of a great diversity of approaches while widening the perspective on financial stability matters that the authorities could have individually. Given the importance of this entity, in May 2013 the executive branch submitted a series of financial reform initiatives to Congress that include among other measures the incorporation in law of the Council. 3. Conclusion The global economic crisis has made clear that under current conditions, the attainment of financial stability requires a new policy focus, in which macroprudential measures have a more prominent role than in the past. It has also evidenced that financial stability is so complex that its attainment implies the coordination of macroprudential policies with monetary, fiscal and microprudential policies, and that under no circumstances should macroprudential policy be considered a substitute for monetary and fiscal discipline. In addition, though many countries, among them Mexico, have successfully used macroprudential measures for many years, what is currently on the horizon is a greater role for this instrument: both a more generalized adoption by different economies and more responsibility attributed to it in attaining financial stability. Here it is important to note that we are still in an experimental stage that requires us to face various risks. Meeting these risks implies putting into place a combination of measures at both the domestic and international levels. Clearly, more research efforts are needed to understand the complexities that surround the preservation of financial stability, a wider and more sophisticated set of statistics, the establishment of an adequate international infrastructure, etc. Additionally, the existence of highly integrated financial systems at a global level and the resulting risk of contagion and regulatory arbitrage, among other risks, underscore the need for cooperation from the international community in this respect. Finally, I would just like to emphasize that even though macroprudential policy can be of great use to the attainment of financial stability, it is necessary to evaluate its reach pragmatically. In this sense, it is important that the use of these instruments be focused on realistic aims. Naturally, as we gain experience and build a better analytical foundation, we wil be in a better position to evaluate the potential contribution of macroprudential policy to financial stability. 15

Title: Inauguration of the Mexico Strategy Forum 2013
text: Remarks by the Governor of the Bank of Mexico, Agustin Carstens, at the opening of the Forum "Mexico Strategy 2013" organized by Grupo Financiero Banorte. August 27, 2013 Good evening. Welcome to the Interactive Museum of Economy, a splendid setting for the inauguration of this Forum convened by the Banorte Financial Group. I would like to thank Guillermo Ortiz, President of Grupo Financiero Banorte, as well as the General Director of the same financial group, Alejandro Valenzuela, for the great honor of inviting me to the inauguration of the work of this Forum "Mexico Strategy 2013". The holding of this forum is very opportune because, without a doubt, Mexico is experiencing one of those crucial moments that arise in the life of nations, during which the conjunction of various factors creates the conditions conducive to provoking a long-awaited transformation. Of course, the fact that the conditions are particularly propitious does not mean that change will occur as a fatality, it requires talent, effort and a clear awareness that we are facing an opportunity that, it is most likely, will be very difficult to repeat in the foreseeable future. 1 On several occasions, and already for two or three years, I have allowed myself to affirm that the solid macroeconomic bases that we have achieved in Mexico, both in the monetary field and in the fiscal field and in the environment of financial institutions and markets, are a splendid platform for our country to grow at significantly higher rates, in a sustained way and, with this, we manage to reduce the undeniable lags we suffer in terms of poverty, job creation and competitiveness. It has been no small thing to maintain and increase these conditions of macroeconomic strength in the midst of the deepest global economic crisis of the last 80 years. Of course, and this has been talked about to the point of exhaustion, from that platform of stability, an essential task to achieve the qualitative leap that Mexico requires in terms of productivity is to carry out a new round of structural reforms, some of which have already been approved and are about to be implemented through secondary laws and regulations and others, Broad and profound, such as the energy reform, have been raised and are being debated today with intensity. 2 But the landing of this reform drive is not limited to secondary rules and regulations, it requires that we go into the details and analysis of both what is happening in the global economy, as well as the peculiar opportunities, advantages and risks that the challenge of global economic development poses to each region. We must, so to speak, translate the major proposals of the reforms that are written in a language of general principles and postulates into the specific language of the strategies of action indispensable for these reforms to produce the desired fruits of economic growth, job creation and poverty reduction. In this sense, I congratulate Grupo Financiero Banorte for the design it has given to this forum, since it will allow us to go from the lessons learned in other countries of the continent and globally, related by its protagonists, to the specific responses, even of a local nature, in three decisive aspects: first, the attraction of investments; secondly, the construction and operation of infrastructure and, last but not least, how we should prepare our cities for a future in which both 3 Competition as opportunities and challenges will be global. Given the variety and richness of the participations planned in this Forum, I will limit myself in this speech to conveying the vision of the Bank of Mexico about the global economic environment, the perspectives that we can glimpse for the short and medium term, as well as the challenges that, we foresee, we will face in the coming months and years, both in terms of inflation and growth. The structural reforms to be undertaken by Mexico are necessary in themselves; if we add to this the fact that the global economic environment shows a great weakness and that this sluggishness will most likely extend for several more years, making structural reforms acquires a sense of urgent and unpostponable task. Indeed, the outlook for the short and medium term is that we will continue to experience a noticeable weakness in external demand, which makes it imperative to search for more stable and strong domestic growth engines. So far in 2013, world trade has shown a progressive decline, which, in turn, has an impact on lower production and lower economic growth. The 4 The recovery of the dynamism of world trade to pre-crisis levels is by no means imminent. This fragility of the external environment is not uniform; important differences prevail. As we know, the weakness of growth is most noticeable in Europe, where although there was finally a quarter of positive growth in output, it is lean and it is an average of the entire region, which disguises the great weakness of some individual economies of that continent that are relevant by themselves. In addition, the countries of monetary union remain unresolved the great problem of making a single parity for all the countries of the Union compatible with the glaring differences in their fiscal balance sheets, in their productivity and in the health or weakness of their banking systems. Until this dilemma is resolved, it is highly unlikely that Europe as a whole will grow at rates sufficient to boost, through trade, the growth of emerging economies. In turn, the decline in international prices of primary products is affecting, with greater or lesser intensity, several emerging economies. To this is added the 5 relative weakness that the Chinese economy is experiencing after several years of accelerated growth based on a model focused on exports; China has entered a process of readjustment of its growth model to give greater emphasis to the advance of its domestic economy. This will mean a slower pace of growth over a more or less prolonged period, regardless of the relative success or failure of such a transition. On the other hand, where the recovery of growth has begun, but in an incipient and gradual way, is in the United States. Due to the strong integration of the Mexican economy, especially the manufacturing industry, with the dynamism of production in the United States, this recovery is undoubtedly good news for Mexico. That is why, together with the normalization in the pace of execution of public spending and with the expectation of the first effects of structural reforms, that the Bank of Mexico maintained its forecast of GDP growth in our country for 2014 in the range of 3.2 to 4.2 percent, despite the fact that we have adjusted downwards the growth expectation for 2013. 6 The recovery of dynamism in the United States economy is, as we all know, being much slower than on previous occasions. In large part, this weakness is explained by the persistence of a large fiscal deficit and, even more, because there is no early political agreement between the Executive and Congress in that country, to address this fiscal imbalance. To be sure, the severe fiscal problem in the United States gravitates as a burden against growth, even though families and businesses have already adjusted their respective balance sheets. The perception by the Federal Reserve bank system of a recovery, even moderate, in growth and employment has resulted in the forecast that, in this second half of the year, the Federal Reserve itself could begin to reduce the pace of asset purchases, that is: it could gradually temper its extraordinarily loose monetary policy. This perception recently generated in the financial markets increases in risk premiums and, therefore, in medium- and long-term interest rates, which, in turn, caused great volatility in international financial markets and a reversal of capital flows that were reaching emerging markets, what in the end is 7 it also resulted in noticeable adjustments in the exchange rates of these economies against the dollar. The paradox regarding this episode of intense volatility, in the case of Mexico, is that the forecast of a relatively close recovery of dynamism in the US economy is good news for us if we consider the close link between our economy and that of the United States. In addition, while all emerging markets were affected by the volatility episode, the impact in Mexico has been relatively minor, as in other economies that also have strong macroeconomic fundamentals. In fact, adjustments in the domestic foreign exchange and bond markets have taken place in an orderly manner. This resilience of the Mexican economy in the face of episodes of turbulence and volatility in international markets is explained by the persistence of responsible fiscal and monetary policies, as well as by the particular strength and solidity of the banking system in Mexico. In fact, and specifically with regard to monetary policy, so far in the twenty-first century the virtuous circle between the process of price formation and the 8 anchoring of inflation expectations, which are increasingly less affected by adjustments in relative prices, as is the case of transitory increases in the prices of some agricultural goods, caused by alterations in their supply. This was demonstrated once again by the rapid return of the headline inflation figure to the range of 3 to 4 percent, after the increases recorded at the end of the first quarter of this year. This panorama of the world economy confirms that, unfortunately, during the coming years it is very unlikely that the international economic situation will improve to such a degree that it will lead the Mexican economy to grow above 4.2 percent per year (upper limit of the growth forecast for 2014), unless structural reforms in the country are successfully consolidated. Without reforms, there is no factor on the horizon that will boost the Mexican economy above that 4.2 percent growth. And that level of growth, as we know, is clearly insufficient to reduce the unemployment rate to levels comparable to those before the global crisis, to create better-paying jobs, to 9 encourage the incorporation of more Mexicans into the formal economy and to reduce poverty in an accelerated and sustainable way. Only with structural reforms will Mexico be able to bring its potential GDP growth above 5 percent in the medium term. For all this, an event like the Forum that we are inaugurating is particularly relevant. The window of opportunity for Mexico to achieve this qualitative leap in its development will be open for a short time and everyone, in the field that corresponds to us, must get down to work so that this unique opportunity is exploited to its full potential. Thanks a lot. 10
text_original: Palabras del Gobernador del Banco de Mxico, Agustn Carstens, al inaugurar el Foro Estrategia Mxico 2013 organizado por el Grupo Financiero Banorte. 27 de agosto de 2013 Muy buenas noches. Bienvenidos al Museo Interactivo de Economa, esplndido marco para la inauguracin de este Foro convocado por el Grupo Financiero Banorte. Deseo agradecer el gran honor que me han hecho Guillermo Ortiz, presidente del Grupo Financiero Banorte, as como el Director General del mismo grupo financiero, Alejandro Valenzuela, al invitarme a la inauguracin los trabajos de este Foro Estrategia Mxico 2013. Es muy oportuna la realizacin de este foro porque, sin duda, Mxico vive uno de esos momentos cruciales que se presentan en la vida de las naciones, durante los cuales la conjuncin de diversos factores crea las condiciones propicias para provocar una transformacin largamente anhelada. Por supuesto, el hecho de que las condiciones sean particularmente propicias no significa que el cambio se dar como una fatalidad, se requiere de talento, de esfuerzo y de una clara conciencia de que estamos frente a una oportunidad que, es lo ms probable, ser muy difcil que se repita en el futuro previsible. 1 En diversas ocasiones, y ya desde hace dos o tres aos, me he permitido afirmar que las slidas bases macroeconmicas que hemos logrado en Mxico, tanto en el mbito monetario como en el terreno fiscal y en el entorno de las instituciones y los mercados financieros, son una plataforma esplndida para que nuestro pas crezca a tasas sensiblemente mayores, de forma sostenida y, con ello, logremos abatir los innegables rezagos que padecemos en materia de pobreza, de generacin de empleos y de competitividad. No ha sido poca cosa mantener y acrecentar estas condiciones de fortaleza macroeconmica en medio de la ms profunda crisis econmica global de los ltimos 80 aos. Por supuesto, y de esto se ha hablado hasta el hartazgo, a partir de esa plataforma de estabilidad, una tarea esencial para lograr el salto cualitativo que requiere Mxico en materia de productividad es realizar una nueva ronda de reformas estructurales, algunas de las cuales ya se han aprobado y estn por instrumentarse mediante leyes secundarias y reglamentos y otras ms, amplias y profundas, como la reforma energtica, se han planteado y se debaten hoy mismo con intensidad. 2 Pero el aterrizaje de este impulso reformador no se limita a las normas secundarias y a los reglamentos, requiere que entremos a los detalles y al anlisis tanto de lo que est sucediendo en la economa global, como de las oportunidades, ventajas y riesgos peculiares que el desafo del desarrollo econmico global plantea a cada regin. Tenemos, por decirlo as, que traducir los grandes planteamientos de las reformas que estn escritos en un idioma de principios y postulados generales al lenguaje especfico de las estrategias de accin indispensables para que esas reformas produzcan los frutos deseados de crecimiento econmico, generacin de empleos y abatimiento de la pobreza. En este sentido, felicito al Grupo Financiero Banorte por el diseo que le ha dado a este foro, ya que permitir ir de las lecciones aprendidas en otros pases del continente y de forma global, relatadas por sus protagonistas, a las respuestas especficas, incluso de carcter local, en tres vertientes decisivas: primero, la atraccin de las inversiones; segundo, la construccin y operacin de infraestructura y, por ltimo pero no menos importante, cmo debemos preparar a nuestras ciudades para un futuro en el cual tanto la 3 competencia como las oportunidades y los retos sern globales. Dada la variedad y riqueza de las participaciones previstas en este Foro, me limitar en esta intervencin a trasmitir la visin del Banco de Mxico acerca del entorno econmico mundial, las perspectivas que podemos vislumbrar para el corto y mediano plazos, as como los desafos que, prevemos, enfrentaremos en los prximos meses y aos, tanto en materia de inflacin como de crecimiento. Las reformas estructurales que debe emprender Mxico son necesarias por s mismas; si a ello le sumamos que el entorno econmico mundial muestra una gran debilidad y que esa atona se extender, muy probablemente, varios aos ms, hacer las reformas estructurales adquiere un sentido de tarea urgente e inaplazable. En efecto, el panorama para el corto y mediano plazo es que seguiremos experimentando una notoria debilidad de la demanda externa, lo que hace imperativa la bsqueda de ms motores de crecimiento interno, estables y fuertes. En lo que va de 2013 el comercio mundial ha mostrado una progresiva disminucin lo que, a su vez, incide en una menor produccin y un menor crecimiento econmico. La 4 recuperacin del dinamismo del comercio mundial a los niveles previos a la crisis no es, ni mucho menos, inminente. Esta fragilidad del entorno externo no es uniforme; prevalecen diferencias importantes. Como sabemos, la debilidad del crecimiento es ms notoria en Europa, donde si bien por fin se registr un trimestre de crecimiento positivo en el producto, ste es magro y se trata de un promedio de toda la regin, lo que disfraza la gran debilidad de algunas economas individuales de ese continente que son relevantes por s mismas. Adicionalmente, los pases de la Unin Monetaria continan sin resolver el gran problema de compatibilizar una paridad nica para todos los pases de la Unin con las palmarias diferencias que se registran en sus balances fiscales, en su productividad y en la salud o debilidad de sus sistemas bancarios. Mientras este dilema no se resuelva es muy poco probable que Europa en su conjunto crezca a tasas suficientes como para impulsar, a travs del comercio, el crecimiento de las economas emergentes. A su vez, la disminucin de los precios internacionales de los productos primarios est afectando, con mayor o menor intensidad, a varias economas emergentes. A ello se suma la 5 debilidad relativa que est experimentando la economa china despus de varios aos de un crecimiento acelerado en base a un modelo volcado a las exportaciones; China ha entrado a un proceso de reajuste de su modelo de crecimiento para darle mayor nfasis al avance de su economa interna. Ello significar un menor ritmo de crecimiento durante un periodo ms o menos prolongado, independientemente del xito o del fracaso relativos de dicha transicin. Por su parte, donde s se ha iniciado la recuperacin del crecimiento, pero de forma por dems incipiente y gradual, es en los Estados Unidos. Por la fuerte integracin de la economa mexicana, especialmente de la industria manufacturera, con el dinamismo de la produccin en los Estados Unidos esta recuperacin sin duda es una buena noticia para Mxico. Es por esto, junto con la normalizacin en el ritmo de ejecucin del gasto pblico y con la expectativa de los primeros efectos de las reformas estructurales, que el Banco de Mxico mantuvo su previsin de crecimiento del PIB de nuestro pas para 2014 en el intervalo de 3.2 a 4.2 por ciento, a pesar de que hemos ajustado a la baja la expectativa de crecimiento para 2013. 6 La recuperacin del dinamismo en la economa de los Estados Unidos est siendo, como todos sabemos, mucho ms lenta que en ocasiones anteriores. En gran parte esta debilidad se explica por la persistencia de un abultado dficit fiscal y, ms an, porque no se vislumbra un pronto acuerdo poltico entre el Ejecutivo y el Congreso en aqul pas, para hacerle frente a ese desequilibrio fiscal. Sin duda, el severo problema fiscal en Estados Unidos gravita como una carga en contra del crecimiento, a pesar de que las familias y las empresas ya han ajustado sus respectivos balances. La percepcin por parte del sistema de bancos de la Reserva Federal de una recuperacin, as sea moderada, del crecimiento y del empleo se ha traducido en la previsin de que, en este segundo semestre, la propia Reserva Federal podra empezar a reducir el ritmo de compra de activos, es decir: podra atemperar de forma gradual su poltica monetaria extraordinariamente laxa. Esta percepcin gener recientemente en los mercados financieros incrementos en las primas de riesgo y, por ende, en las tasas de inters de mediano y largo plazos, lo que, a su vez, provoc una gran volatilidad en los mercados financieros internacionales y un conato de reversin de los flujos de capitales que estaban llegando a los mercados emergentes, lo que a la postre se 7 tradujo tambin en ajustes notorios en los tipos de cambio de dichas economas frente al dlar. La paradoja respecto de este episodio de intensa volatilidad, para el caso de Mxico, es que la previsin de una relativamente cercana recuperacin del dinamismo en la economa estadounidense es para nosotros una buena noticia si consideramos la estrecha vinculacin entre nuestra economa y la de los Estados Unidos. Adems, si bien todos los mercados emergentes se vieron afectados por el episodio de volatilidad, el impacto en Mxico ha sido relativamente menor, al igual que en otras economas que tambin tienen slidos fundamentos macroeconmicos. De hecho, los ajustes en los mercados cambiarios y de renta fija nacionales se han dado de manera ordenada. Esta resistencia de la economa mexicana frente a los episodios de turbulencia y volatilidad en los mercados internacionales se explica por la persistencia de polticas fiscales y monetarias responsables, as como por la particular fortaleza y solidez del sistema bancario en Mxico. De hecho, y especficamente en lo que se refiere a la poltica monetaria, en lo que va del siglo XXI se ha fortalecido el crculo virtuoso entre el proceso de formacin de precios y el 8 anclaje de expectativas de inflacin, las cuales cada vez se ven menos afectadas por los ajustes en precios relativos, como es el caso de las alzas transitorias en los precios de algunos bienes agropecuarios, ocasionadas por alteraciones en la oferta de los mismos. Esto qued demostrado una vez ms con el rpido regreso de la cifra de inflacin general al intervalo de 3 a 4 por ciento, despus de las alzas registradas a fines del primer trimestre de este ao. Este panorama de la economa mundial nos confirma que, lamentablemente, durante los prximos aos es muy poco probable que la situacin econmica internacional mejore a tal grado que lleve a la economa mexicana a crecer por arriba del 4.2 por ciento anual (lmite superior de la previsin de crecimiento para 2014), a menos que se consoliden exitosamente las reformas estructurales en el pas. Sin reformas no hay en el horizonte ningn factor que dinamice a la economa mexicana por arriba de ese 4.2 por ciento de crecimiento. Y ese nivel de crecimiento, ya lo sabemos, es insuficiente a todas luces para reducir la tasa de desempleo a niveles comparables a los previos a la crisis global, para crear empleos mejor remunerados, para 9 incentivar la incorporacin de ms mexicanos a la economa formal y para abatir la pobreza de forma acelerada y sostenible. Slo con las reformas estructurales Mxico podr llevar el crecimiento de su PIB potencial por arriba del 5 por ciento en el mediano plazo. Por todo esto un evento como el Foro que estamos inaugurando resulta particularmente relevante. La ventana de oportunidad para que Mxico logre ese salto cualitativo en su desarrollo estar abierta poco tiempo y todos, en el mbito que nos corresponde, debemos poner manos a la obra para que esta oportunidad nica sea aprovechada en todo su potencial. Muchas gracias. 10

Title: Ceremony of promulgation, by the President of the Republic, of the Financial Reform
text: Remarks by the Governor of the Bank of Mexico, Agustin Carstens, during the ceremony of promulgation, by the President of the Republic, of the Financial Reform. January 9, 2014 ? Mr. President of the Republic, Mr. Enrique Pena Nieto. ? Mr. President of the Board of Directors of the Permanent Commission of the Congress of the Union, Mr. Ricardo Anaya Cortes. ? Mr. Senator President of the Board of Directors of the Chamber of Senators, Mr. Raul Cervantes Andrade. ? Mr. Secretary of Finance and Public Credit, Dr. Luis Videgaray Caso. ? Mr. Secretary of Economy, Mr. Idelfonso Guajardo Villarreal. 1 ? Mr. President of the Finance and Public Credit Commission of the Chamber of Deputies, Mr. Jose Isabel Trejo Reyes. ? Mr. President of the Finance and Public Credit Committee of the Senate Chamber, Maestro Jose Francisco Yunez Zorrilla. ? Mr. President of the Business Coordinating Council, Mr. Gerardo Gutierrez Canadiani. ? Mr. President of the Association of Banks of Mexico, Mr. Javier Arrigunaga Gomez del Campo. ? Mr. President of the Board of Directors of the Mexican Association of Stock Exchange Intermediaries, Mr. Jose Mendez Fabre. ? Mr. President of the Confederation of National Chambers of Commerce, Service and Tourism, teacher Jorge Enrique Davila Flores. 2 ? Madam President of the National Concentrator of Ornamental Plants, Silvia Rosario Figueroa Sotelo. ? Madam Commissioner President of the Federal Economic Competition Commission, Alejandra Palacios Prieto. ? Mr. Legal Advisor of the Federal Executive, Mr. Humberto Castillejos Cervantes ? Mr. Head of the Office of the Presidency, Teacher Aurelio Nuno Mayer. ? Ladies and gentlemen legislators, ? Ladies and gentlemen It represents for the Bank of Mexico, and for me personally, a great honor to have been invited to participate in this transcendent ceremony during which the President of the Republic will promulgate the vast set of modifications to several laws that make up one of the most 3 ambitious and promising financial reforms that have been made in Mexico in recent decades. It must be recognized that this reform, an initiative of President Pena Nieto and enriched by the valuable and productive contributions of the members of the Honorable Congress of the Union, is particularly successful because it lays the foundations to make it more feasible for the Mexican financial system to develop in an accelerated, inclusive, but also sustainable way. That is, the reform that summons us today responds opportunely, and based on abundant empirical evidence, to an undeniable need of Mexico that is to promote the increase of credit, given that clearly the contribution of the same to the economic growth of the country is still very low compared to what happens in economies similar in size to ours. This contribution is also lower if we compare it with some economies of smaller size or lower degree of development. 4 On the other hand, the need for this reform is also evident if we consider that the few episodes of accelerated credit growth that Mexico has experienced in recent decades have not been sustainable because, among other factors, its expansion was not accompanied by a similar increase in domestic savings. Worse, sometimes, in addition to being ephemeral, these episodes have led to crises of a systemic nature, in real setbacks that generated a loss of confidence in the financial system, as well as a loss of the capacity of the Mexican financial system itself to grow steadily at the rate demanded by the national economy. It should be remembered that between the seventies and mid-nineties Mexico suffered a devastating sequence of recurring financial crises. These crises have since been averted, as a result of state policies clearly. 5 aimed at strengthening the country's macroeconomic framework and, in particular, thanks to a gradual adaptation of the regulatory and supervisory framework of the financial system. It is fair to mention that thanks to these efforts we have for more than a decade with solid, well-capitalized, stable financial institutions, capable of facing with solvency especially adverse situations such as the global crisis that erupted in 2008. But it is also a reality that this evolutionary and constant process of reconstruction that has followed the Mexican financial system in the last two decades, has not finished giving all the fruits that were expected of it, To solve that lack points to a large extent the great reform that the President of the Republic will promulgate today. If I may use the simile, this reform is required so that the great financial vehicle that Mexico has, 6 laboriously and meticulously built for years, which has been cared for and tuned with great scruple and prudence, it finally marches at a higher speed, without frights. Solid certainly but also agile and flexible to put at the service of economic growth, and ultimately of all Mexicans, the immense potential of catalyst of well-being of which the financial system must be capable. In fact, financial reform is a very important step towards increasing the growth rate of the country's potential Gross Domestic Product. This, for the following reasons. First, greater availability of credit to households will allow consumption levels to soften as the economy moves down the business cycle. This fact alone already implies a gain in terms of well-being, but it also implies a significant increase in consumption and with it an increase in GDP. 7 Second, financial reform can increase the country's potential growth through a greater supply of credit for small and medium-sized enterprises that today have insufficient capital to consolidate, despite offering innovative products and operating in markets with dynamic growth. Crucial to this is the role that the reform gives to development banks, which will have the ideal tools to ensure that financing reaches small companies with innovative projects that have the capacity to increase the country's productivity and, therefore, Mexico's potential GDP. Third, the financial reform will impose a higher opportunity cost on the permanence in informality, since only by joining the formal economy, small innovative enterprises will have access to the capital they require to deploy their full productive potential. 8 Likewise, the reform will tend to generate a virtuous circle with the rest of the structural reforms, since it will allow financing the investment and growth opportunities that have opened up and that these reforms will open. What does all this mean in numbers? There is a clear positive correlation between economic growth and penetration of the financial system, as measured by the ratio "financing to the private sector in relation to GDP". Our estimate, based on the experience of a large number of countries over the past 50 years, is that to the extent that in Mexico we manage to raise the level of financial penetration from the current 26 percent of GDP to 52 percent of GDP, this could be associated with a permanent increase of 0.5 percentage points in the growth rate of potential GDP. Domestic financing to the private sector is currently growing in real terms at a rate of between 6 and 7 per cent per annum; 9 if that growth rate were to double, for example over the next eight years, it would also be feasible to double the level of financial penetration and achieve that estimated impact of 0.5 percentage points on the potential GDP growth rate I mentioned earlier. It is pertinent to note that multiple countries have been able to achieve similar results in recent decades. In addition, a key feature of the architecture of the reform has been the search, and I would say the achievement, of four essential balances: First, the balance between boosting credit growth, but subject to greater capitalization, liquidity requirements, a regime of bank resolutions adhering to new international standards and an expansion of the regulatory perimeter to other financial intermediaries. 10 Second, the balance between the soundness of financial institutions and greater mobility of users between them. This balance must arise from healthy competition in the financial system, between intermediaries and in the payment system. Third, the balance between the imperative need to protect users of financial services, as well as to give them greater access to such services, with the requirement to avoid practices that weaken financial intermediation in its essence, such as those derived from breaches of obligations. Fourth, and finally, in this reform there is also a balance between the greater flexibility that is being granted to development banks with the obligation it will have to facilitate access to financial services for those who currently lack them. In addition, it must be ensured that the banks of 11 Development clearly delineates its complementary, not substitute, role for private intermediation. Mr. President, ladies and gentlemen, this reform lays the foundations for a more efficient financial intermediation that will ultimately lead, without a doubt, to an acceleration of sustained economic growth, in a greater generation of better paid jobs, in short: in greater well-being for all Mexicans. As I have already pointed out, the key to the success of this reform lies in its architecture that emphasizes, in each case, the balance between opportunities and responsibilities. This essential balance between a wider range of options 12 Development and a narrower network of obligations applies to authorities, intermediaries and users of financial services. This balance sheet will allow not only that the financial reform functions as the adequate complement to the rest of the structural reforms that are being carried out, but also that the financial sector is increasingly a prominent protagonist in the progress of the country. Thanks a lot. 13

Seoras y seores legisladores,  Seoras y seores Representa para el Banco de Mxico, y para m en lo personal, un gran honor haber sido invitado a participar en esta trascendente ceremonia durante la cual el Seor Presidente de la Repblica promulgar el vasto conjunto de modificaciones a varias leyes que configuran una de las ms 3 ambiciosas y promisorias reformas financieras que se han hecho en Mxico en las ltimas dcadas. Debe reconocerse que esta reforma, iniciativa del Presidente Pea Nieto y enriquecida por las valiosas y productivas aportaciones de los miembros del Honorable Congreso de la Unin, es particularmente acertada porque sienta las bases para hacer ms factible que el sistema financiero mexicano se desarrolle de forma acelerada, incluyente, pero tambin de forma sostenible. Es decir, la reforma que nos convoca el da de hoy responde oportunamente, y a partir de abundante evidencia emprica, a una necesidad innegable de Mxico que es impulsar el incremento del crdito, dado que a todas luces la contribucin del mismo al crecimiento econmico del pas sigue siendo muy baja en comparacin a lo que sucede en economas similares en tamao a la nuestra. Incluso tambin es menor este aporte si lo comparamos con algunas economas de menor tamao o menor grado de desarrollo. 4 Por otro lado, la necesidad de esta reforma tambin es evidente si consideramos que los contados episodios de crecimiento acelerado del crdito que ha experimentado Mxico en dcadas recientes, no han sido sostenibles debido a que, entre otros factores, su expansin no estuvo acompaada por un aumento similar del ahorro interno. Peor an, en ocasiones, adems de ser efmeros, esos episodios han desembocado en crisis de carcter sistmico, en autnticos retrocesos que generaron una prdida de confianza en el sistema financiero, as como una prdida de la capacidad del propio sistema financiero mexicano para crecer sostenidamente al ritmo que demanda la economa nacional. Hay que recordar que entre los aos setenta y mediados de los noventa Mxico sufri una secuencia devastadora de crisis financieras recurrentes. Estas crisis se han evitado desde entonces, a raz de polticas de Estado claramente 5 orientadas a fortalecer el marco macroeconmico del pas y, en particular, gracias a una adecuacin gradual del marco regulatorio y de supervisin del sistema financiero. Es de justicia mencionar que gracias a esos esfuerzos contamos desde hace ms de una dcada con instituciones financieras slidas, bien capitalizadas, estables, capaces de enfrentar con solvencia situaciones especialmente adversas como fue la crisis global que estall en 2008. Pero tambin es una realidad que este proceso evolutivo y constante de reconstruccin que ha seguido el sistema financiero mexicano en las ltimas dos dcadas, no ha terminado de dar todos los frutos que de l se esperaban, A resolver esa carencia apunta en buena medida la gran reforma que promulgar hoy el Seor Presidente de la Repblica. Si se me permite el smil, se requiere esta reforma para que el gran vehculo financiero con el que cuenta Mxico, 6 construido laboriosa y minuciosamente durante aos, que se ha cuidado y afinado con gran escrpulo y prudencia, marche por fin a una velocidad mayor, sin sobresaltos. Slido ciertamente pero tambin gil y flexible para poner al servicio del crecimiento econmico, y en ltima instancia de todos los mexicanos, el inmenso potencial de catalizador del bienestar del que el sistema financiero debe ser capaz. De hecho, la reforma financiera constituye un paso muy importante para incrementar la tasa de crecimiento del Producto Interno Bruto potencial del pas. Ello, por las siguientes razones. Primero, una mayor disponibilidad de crdito a los hogares permitir suavizar los niveles de consumo cuando la economa transite por la parte baja del ciclo econmico. Este solo hecho ya implica una ganancia en trminos de bienestar, pero adems supone un aumento importante en el consumo y con ello un incremento en el PIB. 7 Segundo, la reforma financiera puede incrementar el crecimiento potencial del pas por la va de una mayor oferta de crdito para empresas pequeas y medianas que hoy en da tienen insuficiente capital para consolidarse, a pesar de ofrecer productos innovadores y actuar en mercados con crecimientos dinmicos. Para esto es determinante el papel que la reforma otorga a la banca de desarrollo, la cual tendr las herramientas idneas para asegurarse de que el financiamiento llegue a empresas pequeas con proyectos innovadores que tienen la capacidad para incrementar la productividad del pas y, por lo tanto, el PIB potencial de Mxico. Tercero, la reforma financiera impondr un mayor costo de oportunidad a la permanencia en la informalidad, ya que slo incorporndose a la economa formal, los pequeos emprendimientos innovadores tendrn acceso al capital que requieren para desplegar todo su potencial productivo. 8 Asimismo, la reforma tender a generar un crculo virtuoso con el resto de las reformas estructurales, ya que permitir financiar las oportunidades de inversin y crecimiento que han abierto y que abrirn dichas reformas. Qu quiere decir todo esto en nmeros? Hay una clara correlacin positiva entre crecimiento econmico y penetracin del sistema financiero, medida a travs de la razn financiamiento al sector privado en relacin con el PIB. Nuestra estimacin, a partir de la experiencia de un gran nmero de pases durante los ltimos 50 aos, es que en la medida que en Mxico logremos elevar el nivel de penetracin financiera del 26 por ciento actual respecto del PIB para llevarlo a 52 por ciento del PIB, esto podra asociarse con un incremento permanente de 0.5 puntos porcentuales en la tasa de crecimiento del PIB potencial. Actualmente el financiamiento interno al sector privado crece en trminos reales a una tasa de entre 6 y 7 por ciento anual; 9 con que esa tasa de crecimiento se duplicara, por ejemplo durante los siguientes ocho aos, sera factible duplicar tambin el nivel de penetracin financiera y lograr ese impacto estimado de 0.5 puntos porcentuales en la tasa de crecimiento del PIB potencial que mencion antes. Es pertinente sealar que mltiples pases han podido conseguir resultados similares en dcadas recientes. Adems, una caracterstica clave de la arquitectura de la reforma ha sido la bsqueda, y yo dira la consecucin, de cuatro balances esenciales: Primero, el balance entre potenciar el crecimiento del crdito, pero sujeto a una mayor capitalizacin, requerimientos de liquidez, un rgimen de resoluciones de bancos apegado a los nuevos estndares internacionales y una ampliacin del permetro regulatorio a otros intermediarios financieros. 10 Segundo, el balance entre la solidez de las instituciones financieras y una mayor movilidad de los usuarios entre las mismas. Este balance debe surgir a partir de una competencia sana en el sistema financiero, entre intermediarios y en el sistema de pagos. Tercero, el balance entre la necesidad imperiosa de proteger a los usuarios de los servicios financieros, as como darles un mayor acceso a dichos servicios, con la exigencia de evitar prcticas que debiliten en su esencia a la intermediacin financiera, como son aquellas derivadas de los incumplimientos de obligaciones. Cuarto, y por ltimo, en esta reforma hay tambin un balance entre la mayor flexibilidad que se le est otorgando a la banca de desarrollo con la obligacin que tendr de facilitar al acceso a los servicios financieros a quienes hoy carecen de ellos. Adems, deber velarse porque la banca de 11 desarrollo delimite claramente su papel complementario, no sustitutivo, de la intermediacin privada. Seor Presidente: Seoras y seores: Con esta reforma se sientan las bases para una intermediacin financiera ms eficiente que derivar a la postre, sin duda, en una aceleracin del crecimiento econmico sostenido, en una mayor generacin de empleos mejor remunerados, en suma: en mayor bienestar para todos los mexicanos. Como ya he sealado la clave del xito de esta reforma radica en su arquitectura que enfatiza, en cada caso, el balance entre oportunidades y responsabilidades. Este balance esencial entre un mayor abanico de opciones de 12 desarrollo y un entramado ms estrecho de obligaciones se aplica tanto para las autoridades, como para los intermediarios y para los usuarios de los servicios financieros. Este balance permitir no slo que la reforma financiera funcione como el adecuado complemento del resto de las reformas estructurales que se estn llevando a cabo, sino tambin que el sector financiero sea cada vez un protagonista ms destacado en el progreso del pas. Muchas gracias. 13

Title: Yellow Corn Futures Market Launch Ceremony at Mex Der
text: Remarks by the Governor of the Bank of Mexico, Agustin Carstens, during the launch ceremony of the yellow corn futures market in the Mex Der. October 24, 2012 ? Francisco Javier Mayorga Castaneda, Secretary of Agriculture, Livestock, Rural Development, Fisheries and Food ? Mr. Gerardo Rodriguez Regordosa, Undersecretary of Finance and Credit and Public ? Doctor Luis Tellez Kuenzler, President of the Mexican Stock Exchange ? Jaime Ruiz Sacristan, President of the Association of Banks of Mexico ? Mr. Jorge Alegria Formoso, General Director of MexDer ? Mr. John Pietrowicz, Managing Director of CME Group ? Ladies and gentlemen The launch of this first corn futures contract in the Mexican derivatives market can only be welcomed. It shall contribute, in the specific case of maize 1 yellow, to a better formation of prices for the benefit of producers, intermediaries and consumers. Also, it would be expected to lead to greater stability in the price of that product that today is extremely volatile. I congratulate MexDer, the Chicago Mercantile Exchange Group, the Mexican Stock Exchange and, in particular, the Ministry of Agriculture for bringing this initiative to fruition. Hopefully soon we will also welcome more derivatives of products whose international prices are highly volatile.
