Title: Opening remarks
text: Network models, stress testing, and other tools for financial stability monitoring and macroprudential policy design and implementation November 11 and 12, 2015. Mexico City Manuel Ramos-Francia1 Opening Remarks Good morning. It is my pleasure to give everyone a warm welcome to our conference: Network models, stress testing, and other tools for financial stability monitoring and macroprudential policy design and implementation. I would like to thank all, and in particular those researchers and policy makers that have come from abroad, for sharing your knowledge and insights with us. I would also like to express my gratitude to the organizers: CEMLA, the University of Zurich, the Journal of Financial Stability and, the host, the Banco de Mexico, more specifically, its Financial Stability Division. At least since the times of Walter Bagehot, the importance of financial systems was well understood.2 Mr. Bagehot knew the advantage the English economy had over other ones due to its financial system. Englands unprecedented economic growth at the time was possible due to its advanced financial system, which gathered capital and allocated it where it had the best investment opportunities. In effect, financial systems bring about enormous benefits. For instance, their participants have significant gains as they are able to smooth their incomes through time and states of nature in ways they would have been but only a remote possibility under the absence of such systems. Notwithstanding their benefits, financial systems link us in ways that can lead to significant costs under certain contingencies. 1 I would like to thank Santiago Garcia-Verdu for his insightful comments and suggestions. 2 Walter Bagehot lived from 1826 to 1877 in England. In 1860, he became editor-in-chief of The Economist. He is the author of Lombard Street: A Description of the Money Market, among other books. 1 Such contingencies can come about for a plethora of reasons. Perhaps, at a basic level, while we are wired for languages, as has been underscored, for example, by Chomsky, we are not so for numbers, let alone for probability, as we have been reminded, for instance, by Taleb.3 At a more general level, and being part of our concern today, we seek to understand how, when, and why financial systems can go wrong, in short, about their stability, and what can be done to avoid, and to deal with such contingencies, possibly through the implementation of macro-prudential policies. The conference features as two of its main tools 1) Networks Models and Stress Testing, and 2) Macro-prudential Policy, as its main subject matter. These tools have become the workhorses for researchers and policy makers to gain a deeper understanding of the referred contingencies. Of course, macro-prudential policy has gained unprecedented impetus in the aftermath of the global financial crisis. One could argue that the study of networks started with the Konigsberg bridge problem solved by Euler in 1736, all the way to the more recent and, until a few years ago, elusive four-color map theorem.4,5,6 Naturally, today there are many notable researchers studying networks. Networks allow us to better understand how different entities, be them, for example, financial institutions or economies, interact in a financial system with each other. Also, they shed light upon what has been called the crosssectional dimension of systemic risk. 3 See, respectively, Chomsky, N. (1965). Aspects of the Theory of Syntax. MIT Press, and Taleb, N.N. (2005). Fooled by randomness: the hidden role of chance in life and in the markets. New York. Random House. 4 The city of Konigsberg in Prussia (presently Kaliningrad, Russia) was crossed by the Pregel River. The river had two islands that were connected to each other and to the rest of the city by seven bridges. The problem at hand was to find a path walking through the city such that: it would cross each bridge only once; the islands could only be reached by the bridges; once a bridge was entered it had to be crossed; and, the starting and finishing points could be different. Euler proved that the problem had no solution. Euler, L. (1736) Solutio problematis ad geometriam situs pertinentis. Comment. Acad. Sci. U. Petrop. 8, 128-140. Reprinted in Opera Omnia Series Prima, Vol. 7. pp. 1-10, 1766. 5 The four color map problem can be stated as follows. Given any separation of a plane into contiguous regions (i.e., what one could call a map), it takes no more than four colors to color the regions of the map so that no two neighboring regions have the same color. 6 See for example, Appel, K and W. Haken (1977). Solution of the Four Color Map Problem. Scientific American 237 (4): pp. 108121 2 Stress Testing has proved to be a very powerful tool as well. One could argue that it started with simulation.7 Three years before Eulers paper was published, the Count of Buffon posited his needle problem, which conceivably was the predecessor to simulation as a subject.8 Yet, it was not until Ulam and Metropolis published their 1949 paper that simulation was formally introduced.9 Certainly, it has come a long way since then. Simulation, and more generally Stress Testing, one could argue, have given us the closest to an experiment in finance as one could have.10 Moreover, the use of Stress Testing has increased and, in tandem, has been adopted or endorsed by institutions like the Prudential Regulatory Authority (PRA), the European Banking Authority (EBA), central banks, including the Bank of Mexico, and various Councils of Financial Stability, where many financial authorities intersect.11,12 Macro-prudential policy is, in a sense, a young subject. Let me quote Xavier Freixas and co-authors (2015) on the subject. there is much confusion about what constitutes macro-prudential policy and little agreement about how to operationalize it, in part because its objective is not clearly defined, and in part because there is scarce historical experience about the use of macro-prudential tools to gauge their effectiveness and calibration.13 7 Models such as Ramsi from the Bank of Englands, and the Systemic Risk Monitor from the Central Bank of Austria are based on simulation. Of course, stress testing has relied on other methodologies as well. 8 Buffons needle problem was originally conceived as a geometric probability problem. Yet, it allows one to estimate  by simulation. Buffon, G. (1733). Editors note concerning a lecture given 1733 by Mr. Le Clerc de Buffon to the Royal Academy of Sciences in Paris. Histoire de lAcad. Roy. des Sci., pp. 43-45. 9 Metropolis, N. and S. Ulam (1949). The Monte Carlo Method. Journal of the American Statistical Association, Vol. 33, No. 247, pp. 335-341. 10 Of course, this might be up to a debate. On the one hand, e.g., Campbell, Lo and MacKinlay (1996) characterize finance as a non-experimental subject (Campbell, Lo and MacKinlay (1996). The Econometrics of Financial Markets. Princeton University Press.) On the other, one could argue that this has changed with the development of experimental economics and finance as subjects. See, e.g., Chamberlin, E. H. (1948). An Experimental Imperfect Market. Journal of Political Economy, 56(2), 95-108. 11 The Prudential Regulation Authority (PRA) was created as a part of the Bank of England. It is responsible for the prudential regulation and supervision of banks, credit unions, insurers and major investment firms. 12 For example, the Financial Stability Board endorses the use of Stress Testing. See, e.g., FSB (2015) Press release of the Meeting of the Financial Stability Board in London. September 25. 13 Freixas, X., L. Laeven and J.L. Peydro (2015). Systemic Risk, Crises and Macroprudential Policy. MIT Press. 3 This quote, I think, highlights one of the reasons why we are gathered here today: that is, is to learn from each other so as to substitute for the scarce historical experience. By the same token, we as policy makers need the best possible theoretical support for the decisions we take. Of course, this also underscores the need for financial institutions, including central banks, to maintain close links with researchers as yourselves. It is worthwhile to consider a more general context. Previous to the global financial crisis, the perception existed that the micro-prudential approach was sufficient to deal with the market failures prevalent in the financial sector which were then recognized. Three of the most prominent ones are: Adverse selection; Moral hazard; and, Limited liability. Most importantly, though, was the perception that supervising and regulating financial institutions at an individual level was sufficient to achieve financial stability. Next, let me point out the following episodes from the economic profession which I think reflect the general feeling prior to the global financial crisis. First, Lucas in his 2003 presidential address to the American Economic Association, declared that the central problem of depressionprevention has been solved, for all practical purposes, [] Second, Bernanke, in a speech in 2004 explaining the possible factors behind the Great Moderation, stated: The increased depth and sophistication of financial markets, deregulation in many industries, [], and increased openness to trade and international capital flows are [] examples of structural changes that may have increased macroeconomic flexibility and stability.14 Third, the response to Rajans speech at the Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City in August 2005. His answer to the question Has Financial 14 The term was coined in Stock, J. and M. Watson (2002). Has the business cycle changed and why? NBER Macroeconomics Annual. The cited speech is: Bernanke, B. (2004). "The Great Moderation". February 20: Source: federalreserve.gov. 4 Development Made the World Riskier? was essentially yes. Back then, he was severely criticized.15 Fourth, Blanchard stated in an interview Before I came to the Fund, I thought of the financial system as a set of arbitrage equations. Basically the Federal Reserve would choose one interest rate, and then the expectations hypothesis would give all the rates everywhere else, with premia which might vary, but not very much. It was really easy.16 Moreover, let me draw the following analogy. As known, individual monetary policies interact on what is known as the International Monetary System, in which countries are expected to follow a set of rules.17 Prior to the crisis, many had the perception that if each country maintained an adequate and orderly set of economic policies, then the rest of the world economy would take care of itself. [] At most, only a continuous exchange of information was really needed in order to maintain economic and financial stability [].18 Thinking that the micro-prudential approach will be sufficient to procure financial stability is somewhat analogous to think that if each country [in this case a bank] maintained an adequate and orderly set of economic policies, then the rest of the world economy [the banking system in this case] would take care of itself. Needless to say, the global financial crisis shattered these perceptions. Indeed, the importance of other market failures has been recognized, as well as the market failures mentioned above. Let me underscore some of the most prominent issues: 15 Rajan, R. (2005) Has Financial Development Made the World Riskier? Paper presented at the Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City Economic Symposium on The Greenspan Era: Lessons for the Future. 16 Blanchard joined the Fund in September 2008, just before the Lehman collapse. Reference: Wesel (2015). Olivier Blanchards Five Lessons for Economists from the Financial Crisis, WSJ, April 1. 17 Needless to say, there is no authority which could strictly enforce these rules. 18 This concept was called the house-in-order doctrine by Padoa-Schioppa. For example, see RamosFrancia and Garcia-Verdu (2012). Cooperation among Central Banks during Crises: Lessons from the Recent Experience. Conference Volume: Conferencia Conmemorativa del 60 Aniversario del CEMLA: La Cooperacion entre Bancos Centrales a Principios del Siglo XXI. 5 a. The originate to distribute credit scheme; b. The too big to fail, Systemically Important Financial Institutions (SIFIs), and Global Systemically Important Banks (G-SIBs) concepts. c. The incentives to increase leverage in some institutions, e.g. investment banks, certainly beyond what is socially optimal. d. The structure of executive compensation, which in some cases leads them to take on too much risk.19 e. The huge atomization and inefficient reporting and information disclosing in some financial markets, which in case of a shock leads to insufficient knowledge about where risks lie and of their magnitude. f. The pro-cyclicality of capital. g. An overreliance on credit agencies which, as has been argued, do not have the proper incentives to act efficiently. Given enough time and some triggering shock to one or various of the factors above in the case of one or more financial institutions, what can make this a systemic issue are the interconnections in the financial system. It could come through different channels, e.g., depending on the institutions size, and specialization, among others.20 Moreover, there are also some macroeconomic issues. For instance, the search-for-yield phenomenon, in which global asset management companies face significant pressure to obtain returns under an environment of very low interest rates in AEs. This has contributed to significant capital flows in and out of EMEs, which may very well turn to be a systemic risk factor. Accordingly, some macro-prudential policy tools and regulations have emerged, while others have regained their luster. Allow me to mention some of the most noteworthy ones, which can be classified in the following groups (Claessens, 2014).21 19 In effect, in Rajan (2005, p. 315) argues that changes in the financial sector altered managerial incentives, which in turn have altered the nature of risks undertaken by the system, []. 20 At a firm level, it makes a potential liquidation process too slowly to be efficient. At a more general level, it makes risk harder to understand and thus to supervise and regulate. 21 Claessens, S. (2014). An overview of macroprudential Policy Tools. IMF Working paper. 6 1. Restrictions on borrowers; e.g., loan to income, debt to income, and loan to value ratios, lending to sectors, and credit growth. 2. Restrictions on financial sector balance sheets; e.g., reserve requirements, liquidity coverage ratio, and total loss absorbing capacity.22 3. Capital provisions and surcharges; e.g., countercyclical capital requirements, leverage restrictions, and capital surcharges associated with systemic risk. 4. Taxation/Levies; e.g., taxation on specific assets and or/liabilities, and as a function of externalities. 5. Others; e.g., accounting practices, executive compensation, corporate governance, information depositories, central counterparties clearing houses, and resolutions.23 As a result, the macro-prudential approach to risk management has gained a central role. Yet, it is crucial to acknowledge that we are in its initial stages. Naturally, some essential questions arise: a. How effective are macro-prudential regulations? b. How do macro-prudential regulations interact with each other and with other policies? c. Have we moved the regulation pendulum too far? d. What are the unintended consequences of the new regulations, for both AEs and EMEs? among other pertinent questions. In this context, this conference will touch upon some of the specific tools that have been developed to try measuring systemic risk such as Networks and Stress Testing, and other tools to monitor financial stability, as well as particular aspects of Macro-prudential policy and design. Against this backdrop, let me then briefly comment on some of the papers that will be presented at the conference. I apologize in advance to those authors which I will not mention for the benefit of time. The conference includes two keynote sessions, and eight ordinary ones. I am sure Professor Sanjeev Goyal and Professor Xavier Freixas will have much to say about the key issues at the frontier of knowledge on these 22 These increase their risk absorption capacity. 23 These improve risk distribution and its monitoring. 7 subjects, and I believe everyone is very much looking forward to their respective keynote sessions. As a general overview, it is useful to group the ordinary sessions as follows: In terms of policy: the first and sixth sessions assess Macro-prudential Policy design and evaluation, respectively, In terms of methodological tools: the third, fourth and fifth sessions cover Financial Networks and Stress Testing; In terms of subjects: the second and seventh sessions examine Systemic Risks, while the eighth session takes a look at Financial Stability. In my comments next, I will follow this order. In terms of policy: The first session is titled: Macro-prudential Policy Design. In one of its papers, Christoph Aymans and co-authors propose Macroprudential policies for controlling the Basel cycle. While we commonly think about the trade-off between economic growth and systemic risk, or between excess returns and volatility, they explore the trade-off between micro-prudential and macro-prudential risks, giving some clues about their interaction. The sixth session covers Macro-prudential policy evaluation with two papers. My friend and grad schoolmate Dimitrios Tsomocos and coauthors ask How does macro-prudential regulation change bank credit supply? They examine an extension of the celebrated Diamond-Dybvig (1983) model, in which savers can use a bank to invest in a risky project operated by an entrepreneur.24 As they explain, in their model, the bank and the entrepreneur face limited liability and there is a possibility of a run which depends on the banks leverage, and the mix of safe and risky assets. The possibility of the run reduces the incentive to lend and take risk, while limited liability pushes for excessive lending and risk-taking. The authors explore how several regulations interact to affect the frictions in their 24 Diamond and Dybvig (1983). Bank runs, deposit insurance, and liquidity. Journal of Political Economy 91 (3): 401419. 8 model, providing some answers to the question on how macroprudential regulations interact.25 Srobona Mitra and co-authors contribute by: Evaluating the net benefits of macro-prudential policy: A cookbook. In their paper, they propose a framework for assessing the net benefits of macro-prudential policies in terms of the following: the probability of a crisis, the loss in output given a crisis, policy effectiveness in bringing down both the probability and damage during a crisis, and the output-cost of a policy decision. These elements are relevant to be able to rank different policies. In terms of methodological tools: The third session explores Contagion Risk in Financial Networks. The paper by Marco dErrico and co-authors titled passing the hot potato: how does credit risk flow in the CDS market? describes how credit risk flows by exploring the network structure of the CDS market. They analyze the flow of risk in the network in terms of fundamental credit risk and counterparty credit risk.26 This facilitates to monitor risk and its distribution more reliably, in a network in which risks do not flow in a simple way. The fourth session is called Structural Properties of Financial Networks. In one of its papers, titled Measures of financial network complexity, a topological approach Mark Flood and co-authors present a definition of complexity in financial networks, and argue about its relevance. Measuring complexity consistently through time and across financial networks is no small feat, yet it is relevant for both monitoring and regulation purposes. The fifth session covers Stress Testing with two papers. First, Kartik Anand and co-authors propose Quantifying contagion risk in funding 25 The regulations they consider are: capital regulation, liquidity regulation, deposit insurance, loan to value limits, and dividend taxes. 26 As one of their main results, the authors explain that they find that the CDS network structure displays a bow-tie topology. As they describe: in it a set of ultimate risk sellers sell credit risk only to a set of strongly connected dealers. The dealers then pass on the risk to one another in a dense subnetwork. Eventually, dealers sell risk to a set of ultimate risk buyers consisting mainly of asset managers and banks. Graphically, they explain, this network resembles a bow-tie. 9 markets: A model-based stress testing approach. They put forward a model-based stress-testing framework in which banks solvency risk, funding liquidity risks, and market risks are interweaved. Such an approach is central to understanding the cross-effects of risk factors in banks. Mark Paddrik and co-authors present A system-wide stress testing of the CDS market. They argue that supervisory stress testing typically focuses on the resilience of large banks to tolerate the direct effects of a credit shock. Nonetheless, for example, they find that the indirect effect of the largest counterpartys failure on the banks other counterparties could be significant in many cases, highlighting the importance of second round effects when performing stress testing. In terms of subjects: The second session is named Financial Interconnectedness and Systemic Risk. It includes the following two papers: Rodney Garratt and coauthors seek The missing links: A global study on uncovering financial network structure from partial data by performing a horse race between different methods that reconstruct networks based on partial data. They use a rich cross-sectional database. Their study sheds light on the performance of different methodologies to estimate a financial network structure, and thus measure systemic risk more efficiently. Stefano Battiston and co-authors explore the Interconnectedness as a source of uncertainty in systemic risk. They study how the structure of networks can impair the capacity of regulators to assess the level of systemic risk. Thus, interconnectedness, while having well-known benefits, in this context, it is seen as a drawback when monitoring systemic risk. The seventh session reviews Systemic risk and SIFIs. In one of the papers: Doyne Farmer and co-authors study The intra-firm complexity of systemically important financial institutions. While the SIFIs designation is based on size, complexity, and systemic interconnectedness, less attention has been paid to a firms complexity. They measure the complexity of a financial institution by using the 10 structure of an individual firms control hierarchy as a proxy.27 They explore an aspect of financial institutions that was overlooked in the past, and is now deemed relevant, for example, in terms of a possible resolution. The eighth session closes with Financial Stability and includes the paper: Is trouble brewing for EMEs? written by Santiago GarciaVerdu and myself, in which we study the possible presence of run-like dynamics in bond flows to and from EMEs. These dynamics are motivated by the existence of an agency problem in global asset management companies, their consequent aversion to being ranked last, and the size of the assets under their management relative to EMEs financial markets. This type of incentives for capital managers could have financial stability implications. All in all, this is one of the main policy dilemmas presently being faced by EMEs. Finally, Juan Sole and co-authors use the Financial Accounts of the US to obtain time series of bank and nonbank credit to different sectors, and to examine the cyclical behavior of these series in relation to (i) the longterm business cycle, (ii) recessions and recoveries, and (iii) systemic financial crises. Among other things, they describe that bank and nonbank credit display different dynamics throughout the business cycle. Such characterization could ease the implementation of credit growth restrictions at a more granular level. To conclude, let me add one final comment. Let us not forget that these are all means to an end. Research is important to society not only for the sake of knowledge per se, but also to the extent to which such research allows us to have more stable financial systems which will promote economic growth, and let our societies flourish. Without further ado, let me congratulate all for your laudable efforts, and cede the floor to Professor Sanjeev Goyal. 27 The control hierarchy the authors used is a network representation of the institution and its subsidiaries. 11

Title: Strengthening cybersecurity for the stability of the Mexican financial system
text: Remarks by Mr. Alejandro Diaz de Leon, Deputy Governor of the Bank of Mexico, during the forum "Strengthening cybersecurity for the stability of the Mexican financial system". October 23, 20017, Mexico City Highly esteemed Dr. Jose Antonio Meade Kuribrena, Secretary of Finance and Public Credit; Jaime Gonzalez Aguade, President of the National Banking and Securities Commission; Ladies and gentlemen: It is an honor to participate in the Forum "Strengthening cybersecurity for the stability of the Mexican Financial System", organized by the National Banking and Securities Commission. New technologies provide a unique opportunity to expand the coverage of the financial system, streamline operations and design new products. Thanks to technology, extraordinary progress has been made in terms of financial inclusion, thereby promoting greater equity of opportunity and better development conditions for millions of people. However, these technologies carry intrinsic risks and pose challenges in ensuring the safety of users, institutions and the system as a whole. 1 Cyber risks are changing in nature and their increasing sophistication, frequency and persistence can significantly disrupt the financial system both because of their direct effect on institutions and because of the high degree of interconnection between them. Thus, cybercrimes and attacks on the technological infrastructures of the financial system would not only generate losses of information or assets for customers and institutions, they could also cause effects on the financial system as a whole. Hence the importance, as this Forum does, of analyzing the different dimensions of the cybersecurity challenge, exchanging experiences among various members of the system and coordinating efforts at all levels for the prevention and mitigation of risks. Below, I will highlight some of the challenges we face in cybersecurity and the need for a comprehensive strategy to overcome them. The magnitude of the challenges Threats to the cybersecurity of the financial system have multiplied in recent years. These are of different kinds and involve considerable damage to both corporations and individuals in their assets and in the use of their information. 2 These incidents transcend borders and constitute a global challenge. To mention a few examples, in 2016, after an incubation period, cyber criminals managed to breach the computer systems of the central bank of Bangladesh and extracted 81 million dollars from their accounts at the Federal Reserve in New York. While this was an isolated event, it demonstrated the ability to affect all kinds of institutions. Similarly, in May 2017, a hijacking of information was presented to institutions in several countries, using the virus known as WannaCry, which affected computers by encrypting their information and requesting a ransom to release it. This attack stands out for its international dimension, the wide range of affected users and the sophistication of the method used to penetrate security filters. In these and other cases of cyberattacks, common denominators can be found, one of them is that they can originate in seemingly minor oversights, such as that of an employee who opens an email without identifying the source properly, another lies in the fact that attacks can incubate for a long time within the systems of the institution to study how to cause the most damage. In addition to these high-impact events, common crimes, such as phishing or identity theft, threaten the assets of users and could generate distrust in the most modern processes of the financial system. 3 A comprehensive strategy For all of the above, it is imperative to adopt a comprehensive strategy that strengthens our ability to detect, contain, and mitigate cyberattacks. Especially if we consider that cybersecurity not only entails a technological challenge, but for the entire corporate organization and its staff, as well as awareness and information to consumers. In addition, special care must be taken in networks and interconnection between institutions. Therefore, to promote the security of the financial system and its full development, it is necessary to work on the entire ecosystem, at three levels: 1. in the institutions, 2. in interconnection networks and, 3. in favour of users or consumers. At the institutional level, best practices should be adopted in areas such as: 1. the governance of the security system, which should provide for responsibility at the highest corporate level, 2. data protection on all drives, 3. identity, access and segregation of duties controls, 4. coordination with related third parties (suppliers), 5. the protection of computer equipment and data centres, 4 6. the safeguarding of the communication network, 7. a proactive safety culture that improves responsiveness to possible incidents, and 8. very important, the awareness and training of both the operators of critical processes as well as personnel in general. At the level of interconnection networks, and considering the potential systemic risks, strict security criteria and in accordance with best practices must prevail. At this level, the participation of regulators is key. For example, in the payment system, the Bank of Mexico has issued precise guidelines to mitigate cyber-risk. These guidelines consider aspects such as: 1. Dedicated and encrypted communication channels, 2. the obligation to have computer equipment for the exclusive use of the payment system, 3. the prohibition of internet connectivity, and 4. the use of electronic signatures in operations, among others. Finally, at the level of the user, who is usually the weakest link in the chain and the most susceptible and sensitive to damage to their assets, it must be actively incorporated into the comprehensive protection strategy. About that 5 in addition to consumer protection measures, authorities and institutions should facilitate processes and provide the public with the training and information necessary to safeguard their cybersecurity and prevent the most common crimes. Ladies and gentlemen: It is important to reiterate that new technologies, applied to the financial system, provide a unique opportunity, especially for emerging nations, to reduce lags and incorporate a greater number of people into the benefits of modern financial intermediation and thus contribute to raising their development opportunities and improving their quality of life. For this, it is essential to give confidence to all participants in the financial system and face the challenges of cybersecurity through comprehensive solutions. This Forum is significant for this purpose, as it brings together authorities, representatives of financial institutions and national and international experts in the field. Additionally, the signing of the "Declaration of Principles for the Strengthening of Cybersecurity and stability of the Mexican Financial System" is a pioneering effort that allows drawing up an agenda and coordinating efforts between authorities and the private sector. 6 I believe that only in this way, with joint work, will it be possible to root both within the institutions and in the general public, a culture of cybersecurity that helps to fully deploy the potential of the current technological evolution in favor of inclusion and development. Thank you very much and congratulations 7

Si bien esto fue un evento aislado, demostr la capacidad de afectar todo tipo de instituciones. De igual manera, en mayo de 2017, se present un secuestro de informacin a instituciones de varios pases, mediante el virus conocido como WannaCry, que afect a las computadoras encriptando su informacin y solicitando un rescate para liberarla. Este ataque destaca por su dimensin internacional, el amplio rango de usuarios afectados y la sofisticacin del mtodo utilizado para penetrar los filtros de seguridad. En estos y otros casos de ciberataques pueden encontrase denominadores comunes, uno de ellos es que pueden originarse en descuidos aparentemente menores, como el de un empleado que abre un correo sin identificar la fuente adecuadamente, otro radica en el hecho de que los ataques pueden incubar por largo tiempo dentro de los sistemas de la institucin para estudiar cmo ocasionar el mayor dao. Adems de estos sucesos de alto impacto, los delitos comunes, como el phishing o la suplantacin de identidad, amenazan el patrimonio de usuarios y podran generar desconfianza en los procesos ms modernos del sistema financiero. 3 Una estrategia integral Por todo lo anterior, es imprescindible adoptar una estrategia integral que fortalezca nuestra capacidad para detectar, contener y mitigar los ciberataques. Especialmente si consideramos que la ciberseguridad no slo entraa un reto tecnolgico, sino para toda la organizacin corporativa y su personal, as como de concientizacin e informacin a los consumidores. Adems, se debe tener especial cuidado en las redes y la interconexin entre instituciones. Por tanto, para promover la seguridad del sistema financiero y su pleno desarrollo se requiere trabajar en la totalidad del ecosistema, a tres niveles: 1. en las instituciones, 2. en las redes de interconexin y, 3. en favor de los usuarios o consumidores. A nivel institucional, deben adoptarse las mejores prcticas en aspectos como: 1. la gobernanza del sistema de seguridad, que debe contemplar la responsabilidad al ms alto nivel corporativo, 2. la proteccin de datos en todas las unidades, 3. los controles de identidad, acceso y la segregacin de funciones, 4. la coordinacin con terceros relacionados (proveedores), 5. la proteccin de equipos de cmputo y centros de datos, 4 6. el resguardo de la red de comunicacin, 7. una cultura de seguridad proactiva que mejore la capacidad de respuesta ante eventuales incidentes, y 8. muy importante, la concientizacin y capacitacin tanto de los operadores de procesos crticos como del personal en general. A nivel de redes de interconexin, y considerando los potenciales riesgos sistmicos, deben prevalecer criterios de seguridad estrictos y acordes a las mejores prcticas. En este nivel la participacin de las entidades reguladoras resulta clave. Por ejemplo, en el sistema de pagos, el Banco de Mxico ha emitido lineamientos precisos para mitigar el ciber-riesgo. Dichos lineamientos consideran aspectos como: 1. canales de comunicacin dedicados y encriptados, 2. la obligacin de contar con equipos de cmputo de uso exclusivo para el sistema de pagos, 3. la prohibicin de conectividad a internet, y 4. el uso de la firma electrnica en las operaciones, entre otros. Finalmente, a nivel del usuario, quien suele ser el eslabn ms dbil de la cadena y el ms susceptible y sensible de afectaciones a su patrimonio, ste debe ser incorporado de manera activa a la estrategia integral de proteccin. Al respecto, 5 adems de las medidas de proteccin al consumidor, las autoridades e instituciones deben facilitar procesos y proporcionar al pblico la formacin e informacin necesaria para resguardar su ciberseguridad y prevenir los delitos ms comunes. Seoras y seores: Es importante reiterar que las nuevas tecnologas, aplicadas al sistema financiero, brindan una oportunidad nica, especialmente para las naciones emergentes, para abatir rezagos e incorporar a un mayor nmero de personas a los beneficios de la intermediacin financiera moderna y coadyuvar, con ello, a elevar sus oportunidades de desarrollo y mejorar su calidad de vida. Para ello, es imprescindible dar confianza a todos los participantes del sistema financiero y hacer frente a los retos de la ciberseguridad a travs de soluciones integrales. Este Foro resulta significativo para este propsito, pues rene autoridades, representantes de instituciones financieras y expertos nacionales e internacionales en la materia. Adicionalmente, la firma de la Declaracin de principios para el fortalecimiento de la ciberseguridad y la estabilidad del Sistema Financiero Mexicano es un esfuerzo pionero que permite trazar una agenda y coordinar esfuerzos entre autoridades y sector privado. 6 Considero que solo as, con el trabajo conjunto, ser posible arraigar tanto al interior de las instituciones, como en el pblico en general, una cultura de ciberseguridad que ayude a desplegar cabalmente el potencial de la actual evolucin tecnolgica en favor de la inclusin y el desarrollo. Muchas gracias y felicidades 7

Title: Two great institutions of excellence
text: Two great institutions of excellence: ITESM and BANXICO Remarks by the Governor of the Bank of Mexico, Agustin Carstens, during the presentation of the recognition of his career by the Instituto Tecnologico y de Estudios Superiores de Monterrey, in the Auditorium of the EGADE Business School, ITESM, Campus Monterrey. August 31, 2017, Monterrey, Nuevo Leon Good afternoon, everyone. ? Juan Pablo Murria, Dean of the School of Business, Instituto Tecnologico y de Estudios Superiores de Monterrey, ? Ignacio de la Vega, Dean of the EGADE Business School, Instituto Tecnologico y de Estudios Superiores de Monterrey, ? Jose Antonio Fernandez Carbajal, Chairman of the Board of Directors of Tecnologico de Monterrey, 1 ? Jose Antonio Quesada, Director of the EGADE Business School, Mexico City, ? Dear members of the academic and student community of Tecnologico de Monterrey, ? Ladies and gentlemen, It is a great honor for me to receive this distinction today from an educational institution of great prestige in Mexico and in the world such as Tecnologico de Monterrey. I am grateful with emotion for this recognition of my professional career in public service, but this trajectory would not have been possible without all that I have received, over almost four decades, from another institution of excellence that has been, for 92 years, a solid pillar of the development of Mexico and the well-being of millions of Mexicans. I am referring, of course, to the Bank of Mexico. There are deep and significant parallels between our Central Bank and Tecnologico de Monterrey. Similarities in the origins, in the generosity that the specific mission of each of these institutions entails, in the values that are lived and promoted in both, in the deep appreciation that both give to the integral development of human capital, in their 2 vocation of autonomy and intellectual honesty and, finally, in the indeclinable will that prevails, both in the Tecnologico de Monterrey and in the Bank of Mexico, to serve our country. It is no coincidence that both institutions have that air of family, which we also find in the mood and prestige of outstanding Mexicans who, over many decades, have passed through them, who have dedicated the best of their talent and knowledge to them, and who have received - in a fruitful exchange - invaluable teachings and experiences. It is no coincidence, I repeat, because in its origins the will to consolidate a modern country was decisive, whose prosperity and equity were based on values and permanent agreements, that is: on institutions that could not only overcome, but transcend the conjunctural vicissitudes. It was the will and vision of a few exceptional Mexicans that made it possible. I will refer briefly to three of them that, it is also no coincidence, belonged to the generation of those born between 1890 and 1905 and that the historian Luis Gonzalez y Gonzalez called, with justice, the constructive generation of Mexico. 3 The first of these is Eugenio Garza Sada, born here in Monterrey in 1892, the main founder of Tecnologico and its permanent guide, inspirer and promoter until his tragic death in 1973. The second character was also born in Nuevo Leon, in Linares, five years later, in 1897. It is Rodrigo Gomez Gomez, who made a long career at the Bank of Mexico and who was general director of the Central Bank from 1952 until his death in 1970; most of those years were those of the so-called "stabilizing development" in which our country grew at accelerated and sustained rates with great price stability, which resulted in the generation of millions of jobs and a notable rise in the standard of living of Mexicans. And there is a third character who coincides in the origins of both the Bank of Mexico, in 1925, and the Tecnologico de Monterrey, in 1943. He is the one who brings his brilliant intelligence in the conceptual and legal design of both institutions. Norteno too, but from Batopilas, Chihuahua, where he was born in 1897. This is Manuel Gomez Morin, whose role as one of the founders and first Chairman of the Board of Directors of the Bank of Mexico is widely known, but who is perhaps less known to have been a key advisor. 4 of the group of businessmen from Monterrey, Mr. Eugenio Garza Sada included, who since the second half of the 30s had the concern to create an institution of higher education of excellence in Monterrey, which would be the seedbed of future managers and administrators of industries and financial and commercial companies not only from here, from Monterrey, but of all of Mexico. In fact, since the second half of the decade of the 30s Manuel Gomez Morin, who was then the main advisor of the so-called Monterrey Industrial Group, was enthusiastic about the project of establishing an institution of higher education in this city, with the determined impulse of private initiative, which had avant-garde pedagogical methods and proposed that instead of directly creating a university a civil association without ends be formed. of profit, which would be the one that promoted the creation of the new educational institution. The project had to be suspended by the political situation of the late 30s, but finally in June 1943 it was founded, according to the model proposed by Gomez Morin, Ensenanza e Investigacion Superior Asociacion Civil (EISAC) which, in turn, created the ITESM and was awarded the capacity to administer it. 5 I have mentioned these three admirable characters who, each in their field and according to their respective temperament and specific skills, built or consolidated at the time great institutions of excellence that have been and will continue to be crucial for the development of Mexico and the well-being of Mexicans. A singular engineer and businessman, as was Mr. Eugenio Garza Sada. A private accountant with a formidable self-taught vocation and great gift of people, Don Rodrigo Gomez. A brilliant lawyer, public servant, full of social and political concerns, as was Manuel Gomez Morin. The three forgers of institutions, the three aware that this constructive will must be reflected in solid, lasting agreements that transcend people and temporal circumstances, however dramatic or ominous they may seem at the time. The fruit of their constructive efforts is in sight, both in the great system of higher education, avant-garde, which has consolidated the Tecnologico de Monterrey throughout the country, and in the Bank of Mexico in the reduction of inflation. With regard to the latter, I would like to comment on the following: 6 ? That we are on track to convergence of inflation to 3% in 2018; and ? That the Bank of Mexico is prepared to be an element of certainty, during this and next year, a period in which the country could suffer an increase in uncertainty, both due to external and internal causes. Finally, I return to the example left to us by those three admirable Mexicans that I have mentioned. Their constructive eagerness is a legacy that commits us to preserve these institutions of excellence and keep them at the forefront, according to the challenges of this twenty-first century. I receive this recognition gratefully, but aware that it also represents that great legacy and an immense, almost overwhelming, responsibility. Thanks a lot. 7
text_original: Dos grandes instituciones de excelencia: ITESM y BANXICO Palabras del Gobernador del Banco de Mxico, Agustn Carstens, durante la entrega del reconocimiento a su trayectoria por parte del Instituto Tecnolgico y de Estudios Superiores de Monterrey, en el Auditorio de la EGADE Business School, ITESM, Campus Monterrey. 31 de agosto de 2017, Monterrey, Nuevo Len Buenas tardes a todos.  Juan Pablo Murria, Decano de la Escuela de Negocios, Instituto Tecnolgico y de Estudios Superiores de Monterrey,  Ignacio de la Vega, Decano de la EGADE Business School, Instituto Tecnolgico y de Estudios Superiores de Monterrey,  Jos Antonio Fernndez Carbajal, Presidente del Consejo de Administracin del Tecnolgico de Monterrey, 1  Jos Antonio Quesada, Director de la EGADE Business School, Ciudad de Mxico,  Estimados miembros de la comunidad acadmica y estudiantil del Tecnolgico de Monterrey,  Seoras y seores: Representa para m un gran honor recibir hoy esta distincin de parte de una institucin educativa de gran prestigio en Mxico y en el mundo como lo es el Tecnolgico de Monterrey. Fue la voluntad y la visin de unos cuantos mexicanos de excepcin la que lo hizo posible. Me referir brevemente a tres de ellos que, tampoco es casual, pertenecieron a la generacin de los nacidos entre 1890 y 1905 y que el historiador Luis Gonzlez y Gonzlez llam, con justicia, la generacin constructiva de Mxico. 3 El primero de ellos es Eugenio Garza Sada, nacido aqu en Monterrey en 1892, principal fundador del Tecnolgico y su permanente gua, inspirador y promotor hasta su trgica muerte en 1973. El segundo personaje tambin naci en Nuevo Len, en Linares, cinco aos despus, en 1897. Es Rodrigo Gmez Gmez, quien hizo una larga carrera en el Banco de Mxico y quien fue director general del Banco Central desde 1952 hasta su fallecimiento en 1970; la mayor parte de esos aos fueron los del llamado desarrollo estabilizador en los que nuestro pas creci a tasas aceleradas y sostenidas con una gran estabilidad de precios, lo que se tradujo en la generacin de millones de empleos y en una notable elevacin del nivel de vida de los mexicanos. Y hay un tercer personaje que coincide en los orgenes tanto del Banco de Mxico, en 1925, como del Tecnolgico de Monterrey, en 1943. Es quien aporta su brillante inteligencia en el diseo conceptual y jurdico de ambas instituciones. Norteo tambin, pero de Batopilas, Chihuahua, donde naci en 1897. El proyecto debi quedar en suspenso por la coyuntura poltica de fines de los aos 30, pero finalmente en junio de 1943 se fund, de acuerdo con el modelo propuesto por Gmez Morn, Enseanza e Investigacin Superior Asociacin Civil (EISAC) que, a su vez, cre el ITESM y se adjudic la capacidad de administrarlo. 5 He mencionado a estos tres personajes admirables que, cada cual en su terreno y de acuerdo a su respectivo temperamento y destrezas especficas, construyeron o consolidaron en su momento grandes instituciones de excelencia que han sido y seguirn siendo cruciales para el desarrollo de Mxico y el bienestar de los mexicanos. Un ingeniero y empresario singular, como fue don Eugenio Garza Sada. Un contador privado con una formidable vocacin autodidacta y gran don de gentes, don Rodrigo Gmez. Un abogado brillante, servidor pblico, pletrico de inquietudes sociales y polticas, como fue Manuel Gmez Morn. Los tres forjadores de instituciones, los tres conscientes de que esa voluntad constructiva deba plasmarse en acuerdos slidos, perdurables, que trascendieran a las personas y a las circunstancias temporales, por dramticas u ominosas que en su momento pudieran parecer. Title: Inauguration of the interactive module of Cetes Directo
text: 1 Remarks by the Governor of the Bank of Mexico, Dr. Agustin Carstens, during the inauguration of the interactive module of Cetes Directo in the Interactive Museum of Economics. May 23, 2011. ? Mr. Secretary of Finance and Public Credit, Maestro Ernesto Cordero Arroyo ? Mr. Undersecretary of Finance, Dr. Gerardo Rodriguez Regordosa ? Mr. President of the Condusef, Doctor Luis Pazos de la Torre ? Mr. General Director of Nacional Financiera, Engineer Hector Rangel Domene ? Madam Director General of MIDE, Dr. Silvia Singer Sochet ? Mr. General Fernando Millan Venegas, General Director of Banjercito ? Mr. Alejandro Rios, Representative of Bansefi ? Ladies and gentlemen Good afternoon. First of all, I would like to congratulate Secretary Cordero and the team of the Ministry of Finance for the Cetes Directo Program. 2 For the Central Bank, whose priority objective is to ensure the stability of the purchasing power of the currency, the Cetes program Directo represents an ally and an incentive of inestimable value for the best fulfilment of the mandate we have received. Behind Cetes Directo, as you all know, there is a great creative effort to encourage and democratize savings and investment backed by a solid and impeccable financial design. When the first issue of Cetes was placed in January 1978, they were seen, above all, as a financing mechanism of the Federal Government that would also contribute, over time, to the formation of a deeper and more stable money market. But at that time it seemed of very secondary importance, and perhaps for some it was even illusory, to think of the Cetes as an instrument to make available to the general public, and at the most competitive costs of the market, a solid tool for savings and investment. At that time, 1978, the Cetes allowed the Federal Government to add, and I quote the Report of the Bank of Mexico corresponding to that year, "a new element to the process of administration and management of the public debt. The Treasury of the Federation adopted the strategy of penetrating the short-term debt sector, without creating serious repercussions on the credit markets." End the appointment. It could be striking that at that time the appearance of the Cetes was not associated with its potential as a tool of 3 savings, but rather the interest of analysts and above all of the federal government as an issuer focused on the Cetes they would allow the government itself to get more resources and accelerate the public spending in the short term. But don't be surprised, if we consider that in such years the situation of public finances in Mexico was precarious, while the effort to stimulate the Economy through deficit public spending had set its real in the government's development strategy, even in spite of of the serious inflationary risks that this entailed. Today, in sharp contrast to that time, Cetes are already seen as a popular savings and investment tool, available to everyone through the Cetes Directo program, which allows access to highly competitive interest rates in the money market, both to housewives and to modest employees and workers, without major intermediation and without onerous charges or commissions. This, I have no doubt, will have a decisive impact so that Mexico, in the medium term, is a country of increasingly prosperous savers. Hence my sincere and enthusiastic congratulations to Secretary Ernesto Cordero and his team for launching this successful Program. The Cetes Directo Program would be unthinkable in an environment of high inflation and economic instability, nor would it have been viable or attractive to the general public if we suffered threatening fiscal deficits or if the Central Bank did not exercise a responsible monetary policy. 4 To achieve that the current and the new generations of Mexicans acquire in the most vivid and immediate way a solid culture of savings and investment will bring incalculable benefits to Mexico and for Mexicans. And, incidentally, also for the Central Bank because there are no more demanding watchdogs of price stability than those who save and invest. Those savers, whose number is will undoubtedly multiply with this program Cetes Directo, they are the best allies of the Bank of Mexico in its priority task of ensure the stability of purchasing power. And I say that a program of this nature propagates that solid culture of saving vividly and immediately because there is no more persuasive argument in favor of saving and stability - which is the condition that makes saving possible and attractive --, to feel in the pocket and assets of the family patrimony its tangible and forceful presence. The interactive module of Cetes Directo that opens today at MIDE will be a clear example of the potential that, to multiply the economic well-being of millions of people, offers the intelligent dissemination of financial education. It will be the best introduction to this practical pedagogy of saving and investing, which encourages the Cetes Directo program. Such a teaching of the power of saving to generate well-being is a constant that appears in the history of all prosperous nations, which see the future with optimism and confidence. Finally, I must thank and recognize the professional work and enthusiasm of Dr. Singer, Director General of MIDE, and 5 your team to make this interactive module possible. The MIDE is and, quite rightly, the first and obligatory reference in the field of financial education in Mexico. Mide is in fact another example of the fruitfulness of good ideas put into practice with talent and dedication. The idea of this museum arose some years ago in the Governing Board of the Bank of Mexico and the satisfaction of seeing it crystallized and alive is similar to the well-deserved joy that the saver experiences when he sees the fruit of his effort materialized. Thanks a lot.
text_original: 1 Palabras del Gobernador del Banco de Mxico, doctor Agustn Carstens, durante la inauguracin del mdulo interactivo de Cetes Directo en el Museo Interactivo de Economa. 23 de mayo de 2011.  Seor Secretario de Hacienda y Crdito Pblico, Maestro Ernesto Cordero Arroyo  Seor Subsecretario de Hacienda, Doctor Gerardo Rodrguez Regordosa  Seor Presidente de la Condusef, Doctor Luis Pazos de la Torre  Seor Director General de Nacional Financiera, Ingeniero Hctor Rangel Domene  Seora Directora General del MIDE, Doctora Silvia Singer Sochet  Seor General Fernando Milln Venegas, Director General de Banjrcito  Seor Licenciado Alejandro Ros, Representante de Bansefi  Seoras y seores Muy buenas tardes. Antes que nada, deseo felicitar al Secretario Cordero y al equipo de la Secretara de Hacienda por el Programa Cetes Directo. 2 Para el Banco Central, cuyo objetivo prioritario es procurar la estabilidad del poder adquisitivo de la moneda, el programa Cetes Directo representa un aliado y un acicate de valor inestimable para el mejor cumplimiento del mandato que hemos recibido. Detrs de Cetes Directo, como todos ustedes saben, hay un esfuerzo de gran creatividad para fomentar y democratizar el ahorro y la inversin respaldado por un diseo financiero slido e impecable. Cuando se coloc la primera emisin de Cetes en enero de 1978 stos fueron vistos, ante todo, como un mecanismo de financiamiento del Gobierno Federal que contribuira tambin, con el paso del tiempo, a la formacin de un mercado de dinero ms profundo y estable. Pero en esos momentos pareca de importancia muy secundaria, y quiz para algunos era hasta ilusorio, pensar en los Cetes como en un instrumento para poner al alcance del gran pblico, y a los costos ms competitivos del mercado, una slida herramienta de ahorro e inversin. En ese entonces, 1978, los Cetes permitieron que el Gobierno Federal aadiera, y cito el Informe del Banco de Mxico correspondiente a dicho ao, un nuevo elemento al proceso de administracin y manejo de la deuda pblica. La Tesorera de la Federacin adopt la estrategia de penetrar al sector de deuda a corto plazo, sin que creara repercusiones serias en los mercados de crdito. Termina la cita. Podra llamar la atencin que en ese entonces no se asociara la aparicin de los Cetes con su potencial como herramienta de 3 ahorro, sino que ms bien el inters de los analistas y sobre todo del gobierno federal como emisor se centrase en que los Cetes le permitiran al propio gobierno allegarse ms recursos y acelerar el gasto pblico en el corto plazo. Pero no hay que sorprenderse, si consideramos que en tales aos la situacin de las finanzas pblicas en Mxico era precaria, en tanto que el empeo por estimular la economa mediante el gasto pblico deficitario haba sentado sus reales en la estrategia de desarrollo del gobierno, an a despecho de los serios riesgos inflacionarios que ello implicaba. Hoy, en agudo contraste con aquella poca, los Cetes ya son vistos como una herramienta de ahorro e inversin popular, al alcance de todos mediante el programa Cetes Directo, que permite acceder a tasas de inters altamente competitivas en el mercado de dinero lo mismo a amas de casa que a empleados y trabajadores modestos, sin mayor intermediacin y sin cargos o comisiones onerosas. Esto, no me cabe duda, tendr un impacto decisivo para que Mxico, en el mediano plazo, sea un pas de ahorradores crecientemente prsperos. De ah mi sincera y entusiasta felicitacin al Secretario Ernesto Cordero y a su equipo por haber puesto en marcha este exitoso Programa. El Programa Cetes Directo sera impensable en un entorno de elevada inflacin y de inestabilidad econmica, tampoco habra sido viable ni atractivo para el gran pblico si padecisemos amenazantes dficit fiscales o si el Banco Central no ejerciese una poltica monetaria responsable. 4 Lograr que las actuales y las nuevas generaciones de mexicanos adquieran de la forma ms vvida e inmediata una slida cultura de ahorro e inversin traer incalculables beneficios para Mxico y para los mexicanos. Y, de paso, tambin para el Banco Central porque no hay vigilantes ms exigentes de la estabilidad de precios que quienes ahorran e invierten. Esos ahorradores, cuyo nmero se multiplicar indudablemente con este programa Cetes Directo, son los mejores aliados del Banco de Mxico en su tarea prioritaria de procurar la estabilidad del poder adquisitivo. Y digo que un programa de esta naturaleza propaga esa slida cultura de ahorro de manera vvida e inmediata porque no hay argumento ms persuasivo a favor del ahorro y de la estabilidad - que es la condicin que hace posible y atractivo el ahorro --, que sentir en el bolsillo y en los haberes del patrimonio familiar su presencia tangible y contundente. El modulo interactivo de Cetes Directo que hoy se inaugura en el MIDE ser una muestra clara del potencial que, para multiplicar el bienestar econmico de millones de personas, ofrece la divulgacin inteligente de la educacin financiera. Title: Axes of growth: institutions, education, banking and business
text: WORDS OF MR. JAVIER GUZMaN CALAFELL, DEPUTY GOVERNOR OF THE BANK OF MEXICO, IN THE WORKSHOP "AXES OF GROWTH: INSTITUTIONS, EDUCATION, BANKING AND BUSINESS". BANORTE STRATEGY FORUM 2016: "A STRONG MEXICO AND OPPORTUNITIES", Mexico City, August 23, 2016. 1 I wish first of all to express my gratitude to Grupo Financiero Banorte, for the invitation to participate in this interesting Workshop of the Banorte Strategy Forum 2016. As requested by the organizers, I will concentrate my presentation on the interaction between the institutional framework and economic development, emphasizing in this context the role that the Bank of Mexico has had to play in the case of our country. The study of the role of institutions within the process of development of nations began a long time ago. Since the writings of intellectuals such as John Locke, Adam Smith and John Stuart Mill in the seventeenth, eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, the importance of the institutional framework and its evolution as fundamental elements for economic progress has been emphasized. However, as research by academics such as Ronald Coase, Douglass North, Mancur Olson, and Daron Acemoglu, among others, shows, interest in this topic has been accentuated in more recent years.2 This is mainly explained by the marked and persistent divergences between countries and regions of the world in terms of the level, growth and distribution of 1 Las opiniones expresadas en este documento son estrictamente personales. 2 Ver, por ejemplo, Coase, R. (1960): "The Problem of Social Cost", Journal of Law and Economics, Vol. 3, pp. 1-44; North, D. (1981): "Structure and Change in Economic History", W.W. Norton & Company; Olson, M. (1982): "The Rise and Decline of Nations: Economic Growth, Stagflation and Social Rigidities", Yale University Press; y Acemoglu, D. et al. (2005): "Institutions as a Fundamental Cause of Long-Run Growth", en Aghion, Philippe y Steven Durlauf (eds.) Handbook of Economic Growth, Vol. 1A, Cap. 6. 1 income, and for the possibility of finding an explanation for this phenomenon in aspects of an institutional nature. As is well known, traditional analyses of economic growth have emphasized as their main determinants the accumulation of the factors of production, i.e. labour and physical and human capital, as well as technological change and, in general, the efficiency with which these factors are used, that is, their productivity. However, some authors have pointed out that these types of models concentrate on the analysis of the immediate causes, not on the fundamental ones of economic growth, and that there is invariably an institutional framework that precedes them and, to a large extent, determines them.3 Although it is difficult to define them in a unique way, it is convenient to highlight some notions that allow us to better understand the concept of "institutions". In a relatively broad sense, institutions are the "rules of the game", that is, the set of rules and restrictions, whether formal or informal, that structure the interactions (not only economic, but also social and political) between the various agents, in order to provide them with order and certainty.4 In a somewhat more specific sense, it has been pointed out that the institutional context of an economy is 3 Ver Acemoglu, Daron y James Robinson (2008): "The Role of Institutions in Growth and Development", Commission on Growth and Development Working Paper No. 10. 4 North, Douglass (1991): "Institutions", Journal of Economic Perspectives, Vol. 5, No. 1, pp. 97-112. 2 it is integrated by the set of entities, procedures and regulatory frameworks with which it operates.5 Although the concrete impact of institutions on economic development is a matter of debate, it is clear that they have an impact on it through various mechanisms. Institutions fundamentally influence the incentive structure prevailing in an economy. It should be noted, by way of example, the importance of adequate property rights schemes to stimulate private investment in a country. Additionally, institutions represent a central determinant of resource allocation. This can be illustrated by the costs that result from the absence of rules that allow efficient operation of market mechanisms (such as asymmetries in access to information or barriers that inhibit competition). In addition, as the experience with central bank autonomy schemes or fiscal responsibility rules shows, institutions can also have a decisive impact on economic policy decision-making. On the other hand, it should be noted that the importance of the institutional framework goes beyond its impact on the growth potential of an economy. It is also fundamental to define the distribution of the benefits of such growth among different groups in society, which explains the resistances that reforms often face in this field. 5 Ver International Monetary Fund (2003): "Growth and Institutions", Capitulo 3 en World Economic Outlook, April. 3 It should come as no surprise, then, that empirical evidence shows a close and robust correlation between the degree of institutional development and economic performance. Thus, it has been found that higher quality in institutions is associated with higher levels and rates of growth of national income, as well as with lower volatility of national income, and that improvements in institutional quality have a positive and significant effect on the level of GDP per capita.6 Several studies have also concluded that the effects of institutional change on the level and/or growth rates of income tend to be higher in low-development economies than in advanced economies.7 This highlights the importance of institutional change for emerging and developing economies. On the other hand, it is also true that the causal relationship between institutional progress and higher levels or rates of growth in income is bidirectional.8 In this context, it has been observed that, in general, those countries with high levels of income tend to have relatively strong institutions. This may give rise to doubts about the extent to which economic development is influenced by the institutional framework. However, seen from another angle, the possibility of a virtuous circle can be pointed out, in which higher quality institutions stimulate growth. 6 Ver, por ejemplo, Knack, Steven y Philip Keefer (1995): "Institutions and Economic Performance: CrossCountry Tests using Alternative Measures", Economics and Politics 7:207-27; Rodrik, Dani et al. (2002): "Institutions Rule: The Primacy of Institutions Over Geography and Integration in Economic Development", IMF Working Paper No. 02/189, November; y Jutting, Johannes (2003): "Institutions and Development: A Critical Review", OECD Development Centre Working Paper No. 210, July. 7 Ver International Monetary Fund (2003): "Growth and Institutions", Capitulo 3 en World Economic Outlook, April; y Goes, Carlos (2015): "Institutions and Growth: a GMM/IV Panel VAR Approach", IMF Working Paper No. 15/174, July. 8 Goes, Carlos, Op. Cit. 4 Economic, and higher income levels in turn underpin institutional development. What is the relevance of central banks within the institutional framework? Although their functions may vary from one country to another, and even over time within the same country, in general central banks have as a priority mandate to combat inflation. In addition, many of them are assigned the task, increasingly in recent years, of promoting financial stability. Central banks are also responsible for the management of liquidity in the economy and the role of lenders of last resort. In this context, as the global financial crisis shows, central banks have a crucial responsibility in preventing, managing and resolving financial crises. To this can be added his assignment in the administration of international reserves, in the development and supervision of payment systems, and in the surveillance and development of the financial system. In other words, central banks constitute one of the key organizations of any economy, although as we will see later, their performance is closely linked to the rules of the game that govern them. The entity itself, and the rules to which it must adhere in accordance with the laws governing it, constitute the institutional framework of a central bank. Central banks play a particularly significant role in emerging and developing economies. This is because in countries with 5 these characteristics, their experience, resources and prestige often make them a suitable vehicle for the design and implementation of initiatives in a wide range of activities. The case of the Bank of Mexico is undoubtedly a clear example of the importance of the institutional framework for economic development. Throughout its history, our Central Institute has evolved to adapt to the changing needs of the country over time.9 Let me briefly describe some of the main features of such evolution and its implications. The most important challenge faced by the Bank of Mexico at the time of its foundation, in September 1925, was to end the prolonged period of monetary instability that, although it had been accentuated during the revolutionary stage, had already manifested itself before due to the multiplicity of issuing banks. In this way, at the beginning of its operations, the central bank had to face a rejection of the population to the use of paper money. His first great achievement was to endow the nation with a monetary system based on the use of fiat currency. Thus, in the early 1930s, banknotes issued by the Bank of Mexico were already entrenched as the main means of payment in the country. In its initial stages, the Bank of Mexico fulfilled a dual function, that of commercial bank and central institute simultaneously. This was due to the 9 Turrent, Eduardo (2008): "Banco de Mexico: Su historia en capsules". 6 the need to increase the availability of credit, while allowing the Institution to strengthen its financial situation. In addition, this contributed to a significant decrease in interest rates and to the gradual consolidation of the Bank's position in the financial system. As economic circumstances evolved, the need to support credit expansion was diluted. Consequently, in 1932 the decision was made to concentrate the Bank of Mexico on central banking activities, ending its functions as a lending institution. At a later stage, the Bank of Mexico was given a dual function of a different nature. In addition to its traditional central bank objectives, it was assigned a number of tasks aimed at supporting economic development. One of the most widely used instruments for this purpose was the selective channelling of credit to sectors, such as agriculture, insufficiently served by commercial banks. It was also in these years that various development trusts were created in the Bank of Mexico aimed at promoting activities considered priorities, including the Guarantee and Promotion Fund for Agriculture, Livestock and Poultry (part of the current FIRA), the Housing Bank Operation and Discount Fund (FOVI), the Fund for the Promotion of Exports of Manufactured Products (FOMEX) and the Fund for the Promotion of Tourism Infrastructure (INFRATUR). Throughout its history, the Bank of Mexico has played a central role in the development of the country's financial system. In addition to your contribution to the 7 In the creation of conditions of economic stability, our Central Institute has been carrying out another series of tasks conducive to this purpose. These include its role in shaping fundamental pieces of our financial system, such as multiple banking, the scheme for the protection of bank deposits and the bond and securities market. In addition, the Bank has striven to design a regulatory framework that is not only appropriate to the needs of the financial system, but also seeks its stability in the face of adverse scenarios. Likewise, beyond providing the national economy with such a basic instrument for facilitating the transactions that take place in it as money, the Bank of Mexico has promoted the development of infrastructure, rules and means that allow the transfer of resources through an efficient and reliable payment system. I also think it is important to highlight the contributions of the Bank of Mexico to the development of human capital and research in our country. Faced with the lack of qualified labor in monetary and financial matters, taking advantage of the training programs of the Central Institute, in 1928 the Banking and Commercial School was founded in the Bank, which at a later stage passed into private hands. Some years later, these efforts were complemented by the creation of the Scholarship Program of the Bank of Mexico, in force until today. The contribution of the central bank to the training of high-level personnel in our country is evident when considering the high number of cadres trained in the Institution who have occupied prominent positions in both the public and private sectors. Also, the 8 Banco has given high priority to promoting research from an early stage in its existence. This has not been limited to economic and financial research, as for several years the Bank served as one of the most important centers of industrial research in Mexico. The Bank's importance in establishing conditions of economic stability has become clear since its inception. Indeed, the need to have an institution to ensure the stability of the value of our currency was present even during the period in which it functioned as a commercial bank, since at that time the Bank could only issue banknotes in exchange for gold or through rediscount with its associated banks. Subsequently, with the Bank concentrated exclusively on its functions as a central bank, the Organic Law of 1936 focused on giving the Institution an operational framework "free of any inflationary note", for which several precautionary locks were created.10 However, from a very short time later, political interests predominated, so that the legal framework of operation of the Bank was adjusted, turning it at various stages of its existence into a financing mechanism for government spending. These episodes were inevitably characterized by high levels of inflation and low, or even negative, rates of economic growth. The obtaining of autonomy since 1994 marks a watershed in the history of the Bank of Mexico. This reform gave the Bank both de jure and de facto autonomy, based on solid foundations: 10 Turrent, Eduardo (2015): "Historia del Banco de Mexico", Volume II, Chapter 7. 9 1. The priority objective, established at the level of the Constitution, of ensuring the stability of the purchasing power of the currency, that is, of combating inflation. The reasons for this constitutional mandate are based on solid empirical evidence at the national and international levels, which has demonstrated the harmful effects of inflation on economic growth, employment and income distribution. 2. The safeguard, also at the constitutional level, that no authority may order the Bank to grant financing. This focuses on avoiding the possibility that for political reasons the monetary authorities will implement measures that may result in a rebound in inflation. 3. A collegiate decision-making body, the Governing Board, whose members are free from political pressure and must comply with strict requirements. Although his appointment corresponds to the President of the Republic, the independence in his action is guaranteed through mechanisms provided for in the Law, such as the approval of his appointment by the Senate of the Republic, the staggering in the rotation of its members, and their irremovability except for serious reasons specified in the law. 4. Administrative independence, which eliminates the possibility of coercion by other entities through indirect budgetary pressures. 10 It is important to highlight that this fundamental change in the legal framework of the Bank of Mexico was supported by the widespread awareness of society about the harmful effects of inflation and the need to have an institution that would allow this problem to be addressed. Naturally, the autonomy of the Bank of Mexico is accompanied by responsibilities of transparency and accountability for the Central Institute. For this purpose, the Bank has a variety of channels and tools to inform society, in a clear and timely manner, about its decisions, actions and results. Thus, through the publication of communiques of monetary policy decisions and the minutes corresponding to each discussion, quarterly reports on inflation and periodic appearances before Congress, among other mechanisms, the Bank's actions are placed under public scrutiny. In addition, the Institution is legally obliged to comply with different audit processes, as far as the exercise of its budget and administrative practices are concerned. The trajectory of inflation in recent years highlights the merits of a monetary policy conducted by an autonomous central bank. During a long period prior to the entry into force of the autonomy of the Bank of Mexico, our country registered inflationary indices of two and up to three digits. In contrast, over the past 16 years, the inflation rate in Mexico has been in the single digits. In fact, the national consumer price index has shown annual growth rates below 3 percent, the target since 2003, consecutively over the past 15 months, resulting in 11 unprecedented since such an index exists. While these achievements cannot be attributed exclusively to the autonomy of the central bank, it is also true that they would hardly have been achieved in the absence of it. The decrease in inflation has brought benefits to families, companies, government and the Bank of Mexico itself. It should be noted, for example, that families currently have access to mortgage loans at fixed rates, in pesos, with terms of up to 30 years, which was impossible during times of high inflation. Likewise, the recovery we have seen recently in real wages has been determined not by larger nominal increases, but by lower inflation. Lower inflation has benefited companies not only through access to credit with longer terms and lower interest rates, but has also allowed them to plan their operations in an environment of greater certainty. For the government, the benefits have been, among others, the possibility of implementing a less onerous debt policy, extending the term of the government yield curve and improving the profile of public debt. As for the Bank, the strengthening of the credibility of its commitment to price stability resulting from these results has in turn resulted in greater effectiveness and efficiency of monetary policy, thus facilitating the continuity in achieving this objective. In short, the Bank of Mexico has played a significant role in the economic development of the country, through channels that have been modified over time in accordance with the requirements of the economy. In 12 Its most recent adjustment, the Bank's autonomy eliminated the possibility of using the Institution as a window for financing government spending, which has allowed significant progress in the fight against inflation, a necessary but not sufficient condition to lay the foundations for sustained economic growth. Efforts to strengthen the Bank and adapt to new needs must continue. It is also important to keep in mind that the Bank of Mexico represents only one piece of the institutional framework required to adequately support the country's economic development. Undoubtedly, we must continue to strive to achieve this goal. In conclusion, I would like to make one last comment. The development of an adequate institutional framework in any country requires the will and vision of the authorities to identify the measures to be implemented and the priorities for action. However, as I have already noted, given the nature and scope of changes of this magnitude, these efforts generally face resistance from some sectors of society. Hence, it will often be necessary, in addition to strong leadership, to achieve adequate levels of support from the political class and even civil society, to carry them out. The difficulties often faced in securing these endorsements are likely to help explain why, despite the obvious importance of institutions to economic performance, many countries continue to suffer from considerable weaknesses on this front. 13
